FJ3294.clinicalScenario: A patient with established psoriatic arthritis shows a swollen, sausage-like left third toe; radiographs reveal erosions at its interphalangeal joints.

FJ3302.name: Middle phalanx of right fourth toe
FJ3302.details: Middle segment of the right fourth toe; lesser-toe phalanges bear load during push-off and are vulnerable when heavy objects drop onto the forefoot.
FJ3302.clinicalCondition: Crush fracture — dropped objects fracture toe phalanges, sometimes with subungual haematoma in adjacent toes.
FJ3302.clinicalScenario: A warehouse worker drops a metal crate on his right forefoot; radiographs show a comminuted fracture of the fourth toe's middle phalanx.

FJ3303.name: Middle phalanx of right index finger
FJ3303.details: Middle segment of the dominant index finger for most people; carries the superficialis insertion and forms joints essential for precision pinch and grip.
FJ3303.clinicalCondition: Displaced phalangeal fracture — dominant-hand index injuries often need precise reduction to preserve pinch function.
FJ3303.clinicalScenario: A mechanic traps his right index finger in machinery; the middle phalanx is fractured and angulated, requiring closed reduction and a neighbour splint.

FJ3304.name: Middle phalanx of right little finger
FJ3304.details: Its middle segment is notably short; a wedge- or delta-shaped middle phalanx here is the usual anatomical basis of congenital incurving of the little finger.
FJ3304.clinicalCondition: Clinodactyly — a delta middle phalanx makes the little finger curve toward the ring finger.
FJ3304.clinicalScenario: Parents bring a 6-year-old whose right little finger curves inward; radiographs show a trapezoidal delta middle phalanx causing clinodactyly.

FJ3305.name: Middle phalanx of right little toe
FJ3305.details: Tiny fifth-toe segment, very often developmentally fused with the distal phalanx so the right little toe effectively has two phalanges instead of three.
FJ3305.clinicalCondition: Biphalangeal fifth toe — a common variant that must not be misread as post-traumatic ankylosis.
FJ3305.clinicalScenario: After kicking a door frame barefoot, a man's radiograph shows only a bruised toe; the apparently "missing" joint is the normal fused fifth-toe variant.

FJ3306.name: Middle phalanx of right middle finger
FJ3306.details: Middle segment of the central finger ray; the superficialis tendon splits and inserts on its palmar surface while the profundus continues deep to it.
FJ3306.clinicalCondition: Jammed-finger fracture — axial blows commonly fracture this phalanx and injure the interphalangeal joints.
FJ3306.clinicalScenario: A basketball player jams his right middle finger on the ball; the finger is swollen at the middle joint and radiographs confirm a nondisplaced fracture.

FJ3292.name: Middle phalanx of right ring finger
FJ3292.details: Base carries the central slip insertion of the extensor expansion; the joint below it is stabilised by the volar plate and collateral ligaments.
FJ3292.clinicalCondition: Central slip injury — unrecognised damage here progresses to boutonnière deformity over weeks.
FJ3292.clinicalScenario: A cricketer who "sprained" his right ring finger three weeks ago now cannot straighten the middle joint, which sits flexed with the tip extended.

FJ3300.name: Middle phalanx of right second toe
FJ3300.details: Middle segment of the second toe; imbalance between long extensors/flexors and weak intrinsics progressively flexes the joint it helps form.
FJ3300.clinicalCondition: Hammer toe deformity — fixed proximal interphalangeal flexion, often with the toe overriding its neighbours.
FJ3300.clinicalScenario: A diabetic patient develops a pressure sore over the knuckle of a hammered right second toe, raising concern for ulceration and infection.

FJ3301.name: Middle phalanx of right third toe
FJ3301.details: Middle segment of the third toe; lesser-toe phalanges are gripped by long flexor/extensor tendons and cushioned by the plantar fat pad during gait.
FJ3301.clinicalCondition: Lesser-toe fracture — usually stable, but displaced fractures may heal with toe deformity.
FJ3301.clinicalScenario: A child drops a heavy book on her bare right foot; the third toe is bruised and radiographs show a transverse middle phalanx fracture.

FJ3307.name: Navicular bone of left foot
FJ3307.details: Boat-shaped tarsal on the medial midfoot between the talar head and the cuneiforms; keystone of the medial longitudinal arch; tibialis posterior inserts on its tuberosity; its central third has a precarious blood supply.
FJ3307.clinicalCondition: Navicular stress fracture — the watershed central third heals poorly and risks nonunion in athletes.
FJ3307.clinicalScenario: A distance runner reports vague dorsal midfoot pain in the left foot for weeks; MRI shows a stress fracture through the navicular's central third.

FJ3308.name: Navicular bone of right foot
FJ3308.details: Medial midfoot tarsal articulating with the talus behind and three cuneiforms ahead; a separate ossicle, the accessory navicular, may persist beside its tuberosity within the tibialis posterior tendon.
FJ3308.clinicalCondition: Köhler disease — childhood avascular necrosis of the navicular causes midfoot pain and a limp.
FJ3308.clinicalScenario: A 5-year-old boy limps with right midfoot ache; radiographs show a dense, flattened, sclerotic navicular typical of Köhler disease.

FJ3175.name: Ninth thoracic vertebra
FJ3175.details: Typical lower thoracic vertebra with a heart-shaped body, demifacets for the ninth rib head, and a long overlapping spinous process; the spinal cord at this level carries lower-limb and trunk function.
FJ3175.clinicalCondition: Osteoporotic wedge fracture — lower thoracic vertebrae commonly collapse, producing kyphosis and height loss.
FJ3175.clinicalScenario: An elderly woman loses 4 cm of height and develops a rounded back; lateral imaging shows an anterior wedge compression fracture of T9.

FJ3309.name: Occipital bone
FJ3309.details: Forms the back and base of the skull; its foramen magnum transmits the medulla–cord junction, vertebral arteries and accessory nerve rootlets; condyles articulate with the atlas; hypoglossal canals carry cranial nerve XII.
FJ3309.clinicalCondition: Tonsillar herniation ("coning") — raised intracranial pressure forces cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum, compressing the medulla.
FJ3309.clinicalScenario: A head-injured patient develops hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing; the picture signals coning through the foramen magnum, a neurosurgical emergency.

FJ3329.name: Proximal phalanx of left big toe
FJ3329.details: First of only two hallux phalanges; its head forms the interphalangeal joint of the great toe while its base joins the first metatarsal at the weight-bearing metatarsophalangeal joint.
FJ3329.clinicalCondition: Turf toe — forced hyperextension sprains the metatarsophalangeal joint capsule and sesamoid complex of this toe.
FJ3329.clinicalScenario: An American football player is pushed backward with his left great toe planted and hyperextended; he cannot push off and has pain under the toe joint.

FJ3312.name: Proximal phalanx of left fourth toe
FJ3312.details: Longest segment of the fourth toe, articulating with the fourth metatarsal head; long flexor and extensor tendons cross it to reach the toe tip.
FJ3312.clinicalCondition: Metatarsophalangeal dislocation — barefoot stubbing injuries can dislocate the toe at this joint.
FJ3312.clinicalScenario: A man stubs his left fourth toe hard on a step; the toe sits shortened and deviated, and imaging shows dislocation at the metatarsophalangeal joint.

FJ3313.name: Proximal phalanx of left index finger
FJ3313.details: First long bone of the index ray; its base forms the metacarpophalangeal joint and its head the proximal interphalangeal joint; flexor tendons run in the fibrous sheath along its palmar face.
FJ3313.clinicalCondition: Proximal phalanx fracture — among the commonest hand fractures; rotation must be checked on fist closure.
FJ3313.clinicalScenario: A teenager slams a car door on her left index finger; radiographs show a transverse proximal phalanx fracture without rotation.

FJ3314.name: Proximal phalanx of left little finger
FJ3314.details: Short first segment of the little finger; hypothenar muscles arise nearby, and its metacarpophalangeal joint allows the abduction important for spreading the hand.
FJ3314.clinicalCondition: Extra-octave fracture — a child's little-finger proximal phalanx fracture angulating toward the ring finger.
FJ3314.clinicalScenario: A young pianist falls onto her left hand; the little finger's proximal phalanx is fractured and tilted, treated by "buddy" strapping to the ring finger.

FJ3315.name: Proximal phalanx of left little toe
FJ3315.details: First segment of the fifth toe, joined to the fifth metatarsal head; very commonly injured because the little toe projects at the foot's outer border.
FJ3315.clinicalCondition: "Bedpost fracture" — classic night-time stubbing fracture of the little toe's proximal phalanx.
FJ3315.clinicalScenario: A woman walking barefoot to the bathroom at night catches her left little toe on the bedpost; it points sideways and is exquisitely tender.

FJ3316.name: Proximal phalanx of left middle finger
FJ3316.details: Longest proximal phalanx; lies along the hand's central axis, so its alignment is the reference against which rotational deformity of other fingers is judged.
FJ3316.clinicalCondition: Collateral ligament avulsion — its base can chip where the interphalangeal collateral ligaments attach.
FJ3316.clinicalScenario: A volleyball player blocks a spike and jams his left middle finger; radiographs show a small avulsion fragment at the proximal phalanx base.

FJ3317.name: Proximal phalanx of left ring finger
FJ3317.details: First segment of the ring finger, transmitting grip forces between the metacarpal and the rest of the digit; encircled at its base by the digital neurovascular bundles.
FJ3317.clinicalCondition: Ring avulsion risk zone — rings catch at this segment, stripping skin and vessels in degloving injuries.
FJ3317.clinicalScenario: A labourer jumps from a truck and his wedding ring snags, nearly degloving the left ring finger down to this phalanx — a surgical emergency.

FJ3328.name: Proximal phalanx of left second toe
FJ3328.details: First segment of the second toe, often the longest toe; it bears significant load when the first ray is short or hypermobile.
FJ3328.clinicalCondition: Overload metatarsalgia pattern — a long second ray predisposes to stress injury along this toe.
FJ3328.clinicalScenario: A ballet dancer with a long left second toe develops aching under the forefoot; imaging excludes fracture but shows overload changes at the toe base.

FJ3311.name: Proximal phalanx of left third toe
FJ3311.details: First segment of the third toe; its metatarsophalangeal joint shares the forefoot load and is stabilised by the plantar plate underneath.
FJ3311.clinicalCondition: Plantar plate tear — hyperextension injury destabilises the toe, causing crossover drift.
FJ3311.clinicalScenario: A runner notices her left third toe drifting toward the second; examination and ultrasound confirm a plantar plate tear at the toe's base joint.

FJ3318.name: Proximal phalanx of left thumb
FJ3318.details: Short, stout first bone of the two-bone thumb; its base forms the metacarpophalangeal joint, guarded by two sesamoids in the flexor pollicis brevis and adductor tendons.
FJ3318.clinicalCondition: Thumb phalanx fracture — falls onto the thumb commonly fracture it and threaten pinch strength.
FJ3318.clinicalScenario: A cyclist goes over the handlebars and lands on her left thumb; radiographs show a displaced fracture of the proximal phalanx requiring splinting.

FJ3310.name: Proximal phalanx of right big toe
FJ3310.details: Hallux's first phalanx; aligns the great toe with the first metatarsal, and malalignment here drives the visible deformity of bunion formation.
FJ3310.clinicalCondition: Hallux valgus — this phalanx deviates laterally on the metatarsal head, producing the bunion deformity.
FJ3310.clinicalScenario: A 45-year-old woman shows a prominent right bunion with the great toe angled toward the second toe, painful in narrow shoes.

FJ3321.name: Proximal phalanx of right fourth toe
FJ3321.details: First segment of the right fourth toe, transmitting push-off load from the fourth metatarsal; protected by taping to the stable third toe when injured.
FJ3321.clinicalCondition: Buddy-taped toe fracture — nondisplaced fractures here heal well with neighbour strapping and stiff shoes.
FJ3321.clinicalScenario: A footballer kicks the ground instead of the ball; his right fourth toe swells, and radiographs show a nondisplaced proximal phalanx fracture.

FJ3322.name: Proximal phalanx of right index finger
FJ3322.details: First segment of the index ray of the (usually dominant) right hand; fine pinch depends on its stable, well-aligned length.
FJ3322.clinicalCondition: Intra-articular base fracture — joint involvement here risks stiffness in the hand's most skilled digit.
FJ3322.clinicalScenario: A joiner's right index finger is crushed by a falling beam; imaging shows a split fracture entering the metacarpophalangeal joint at the phalanx base.

FJ3323.name: Proximal phalanx of right little finger
FJ3323.details: First segment of the little finger; its growth plate in children lies at the base, making Salter–Harris injuries the typical paediatric pattern here.
FJ3323.clinicalCondition: Salter–Harris fracture — growth-plate injury of this phalanx is a common childhood hand fracture.
FJ3323.clinicalScenario: An 8-year-old falls off a climbing frame; his right little finger is bent at the base, and radiographs show a Salter–Harris type II fracture.

FJ3324.name: Proximal phalanx of right little toe
FJ3324.details: First segment of the fifth toe; exposed at the lateral border of the foot and the segment most frequently broken in barefoot household injuries.
FJ3324.clinicalCondition: Little-toe stubbing fracture — usually treated symptomatically despite being very painful.
FJ3324.clinicalScenario: A man catches his right little toe on a chair leg; it is purple and deviated, and radiographs confirm a proximal phalanx fracture.

FJ3325.name: Proximal phalanx of right middle finger
FJ3325.details: Long first segment of the middle ray; the flexor sheath and its annular pulleys hug this bone, so swelling or malunion quickly stiffens the finger.
FJ3325.clinicalCondition: Phalangeal fracture with stiffness risk — early mobilisation matters once this fracture is stable.
FJ3325.clinicalScenario: A goalkeeper's right middle finger is bent back by the ball; radiographs show a spiral proximal phalanx fracture, splinted briefly then mobilised.

FJ3326.name: Proximal phalanx of right ring finger
FJ3326.details: First segment of the ring finger; its base is a common site for benign cartilage-capped lesions arising within finger bones.
FJ3326.clinicalCondition: Enchondroma — the commonest primary bone tumour of the hand, often in this phalanx, presenting after pathological fracture.
FJ3326.clinicalScenario: A woman sustains a fracture of her right ring finger from trivial trauma; radiographs reveal it passed through a lucent enchondroma in the proximal phalanx.

FJ3319.name: Proximal phalanx of right second toe
FJ3319.details: First segment of the second toe; instability at its metatarsophalangeal joint lets the toe ride up and cross over the great toe.
FJ3319.clinicalCondition: Crossover toe — progressive plantar plate failure at this joint deforms the second toe.
FJ3319.clinicalScenario: An older man notices his right second toe crossing over the big toe with forefoot pain; examination confirms plantar plate insufficiency.

FJ3320.name: Proximal phalanx of right third toe
FJ3320.details: First segment of the right third toe; lesser-toe proximal phalanges commonly fracture when the forefoot is crushed or the toe is stubbed.
FJ3320.clinicalCondition: Toe crush fracture — often accompanied by nail-bed injury and subungual bleeding.
FJ3320.clinicalScenario: A steel-capped boot fails a factory worker; her right third toe is crushed, with a fractured proximal phalanx and a tense subungual haematoma.

FJ3327.name: Proximal phalanx of right thumb
FJ3327.details: Stout first thumb bone between the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints; the flexor pollicis longus tendon runs along its palmar surface within the thumb's digital sheath.
FJ3327.clinicalCondition: Skier's thumb context — forceful thumb abduction injuries centre on the joint just proximal to this bone.
FJ3327.clinicalScenario: A skier falls with his right thumb caught by the pole strap; he has pain and weak pinch from an ulnar collateral ligament tear at the thumb base joint.

FJ2792.name: Right arytenoid cartilage
FJ2792.details: Pyramidal laryngeal cartilage riding on the cricoid lamina; its vocal process anchors the vocal ligament and its muscular process receives the cricoarytenoid muscles that open and close the glottis.
FJ2792.clinicalCondition: Arytenoid dislocation — intubation trauma can displace this joint, leaving a breathy, hoarse voice.
FJ2792.clinicalScenario: Three weeks after emergency intubation, a patient remains hoarse; laryngoscopy shows the right arytenoid sitting displaced with an immobile vocal fold.

FJ3360.name: Right calcaneus
FJ3360.details: Largest tarsal bone forming the heel; receives the Achilles tendon posteriorly, articulates with the talus above and cuboid in front; Böhler's angle reflects its height; sustentaculum tali supports the talus medially.
FJ3360.clinicalCondition: Calcaneal fracture — axial falls flatten Böhler's angle; always check the spine for associated burst fractures.
FJ3360.clinicalScenario: A roofer falls three metres onto his heels; he has a comminuted right calcaneal fracture and an L1 compression fracture from the same impact.

FJ3361.name: Right capitate
FJ3361.details: Largest carpal bone, sitting centrally in the distal row; its rounded head fits the cup of lunate and scaphoid, and its base binds the third metacarpal along the hand's longitudinal axis.
FJ3361.clinicalCondition: Scaphocapitate syndrome — combined scaphoid and capitate fractures in high-energy perilunate wrist injuries.
FJ3361.clinicalScenario: A motorcyclist's right wrist is crushed in a crash; imaging shows perilunate dislocation with fractures of both the scaphoid and the capitate neck.

FJ3362.name: Right clavicle
FJ3362.details: S-shaped strut and the only bony link between arm and trunk; first bone to ossify; the subclavian vessels and brachial plexus pass behind its medial end, above the first rib.
FJ3362.clinicalCondition: Midshaft clavicle fracture — the commonest fracture of childhood and of the shoulder girdle, usually from falls.
FJ3362.clinicalScenario: A cyclist thrown over the handlebars lands on his right shoulder; radiographs show a displaced midshaft clavicle fracture with skin tenting.

FJ2793.name: Right corniculate cartilage
FJ2793.details: Tiny cone-shaped elastic cartilage perched on the apex of the arytenoid, enclosed in the aryepiglottic fold, where it raises the small corniculate tubercle visible at laryngoscopy.
FJ2793.clinicalCondition: Laryngoscopic landmark — its tubercle helps identify the laryngeal inlet during airway endoscopy and intubation.
FJ2793.clinicalScenario: During a difficult intubation, the anaesthetist orients the laryngoscope view by spotting the corniculate tubercles guarding the posterior glottis.

FJ3364.name: Right cuboid bone
FJ3364.details: Cube-shaped lateral midfoot tarsal between the calcaneus and the fourth and fifth metatarsals; its undersurface is grooved by the fibularis longus tendon; key to the lateral column of the foot.
FJ3364.clinicalCondition: Nutcracker fracture — the cuboid is crushed between calcaneus and metatarsals in severe midfoot trauma.
FJ3364.clinicalScenario: A horse steps on a rider's right foot; imaging shows the cuboid compressed and fractured, shortening the foot's lateral column.

FJ2795.name: Right cuneiform cartilage
FJ2795.details: Small rod-shaped elastic cartilage within the aryepiglottic fold, just in front of the corniculate cartilage, producing the cuneiform tubercle seen on the fold at laryngoscopy.
FJ2795.clinicalCondition: Endoscopic landmark — paired cuneiform and corniculate tubercles mark the posterior laryngeal inlet for intubation.
FJ2795.clinicalScenario: A trainee performing nasendoscopy identifies the cuneiform tubercles in the aryepiglottic folds to confirm a full view of the laryngeal inlet.

FJ3347.name: Right eighth rib
FJ3347.details: A false rib whose costal cartilage joins the cartilage above to form the costal margin; at the right side it overlies the upper pole region of the liver and the pleura.
FJ3347.clinicalCondition: Lower rib fracture with liver injury — right-sided fractures here threaten the liver beneath.
FJ3347.clinicalScenario: A passenger in a side-impact crash fractures the right eighth rib and is found to have a grade II liver laceration on CT.

FJ3331.name: Right eleventh rib
FJ3331.details: Floating rib with a single vertebral facet and a short cartilaginous tip ending in the lateral abdominal wall; posteriorly it lies near the pleura and the upper pole of the right kidney.
FJ3331.clinicalCondition: Eleventh rib fracture — flank blows can injure the kidney or pleura lying just deep to it.
FJ3331.clinicalScenario: A rugby player takes a knee to the right flank; he has a fractured eleventh rib and microscopic haematuria from a minor renal contusion.

FJ3365.name: Right femur
FJ3365.details: Longest and strongest bone; head and neck angle about 125° into the acetabulum, shaft bears the linea aspera for thigh muscle attachments, and distal condyles form the knee with the tibia.
FJ3365.clinicalCondition: Femoral neck fracture — intracapsular fractures threaten the head's retinacular blood supply, risking avascular necrosis.
FJ3365.clinicalScenario: An 82-year-old woman falls at home and cannot bear weight; her right leg lies shortened and externally rotated, the classic posture of a femoral neck fracture.

FJ3366.name: Right fibula
FJ3366.details: Slender lateral leg bone taking little weight; its head is circled by the common fibular nerve, and its distal lateral malleolus grips the talus as the outer wall of the ankle mortise.
FJ3366.clinicalCondition: Fibular neck fracture with foot drop — the winding common fibular nerve is injured at the neck.
FJ3366.clinicalScenario: A footballer struck on the outer knee develops a fractured fibular neck and cannot dorsiflex the foot, with numbness over its dorsum.

FJ1409.name: Right fibularis brevis
FJ1409.details: Lateral compartment muscle from the lower fibula; its tendon passes behind the lateral malleolus to insert on the tuberosity at the base of the fifth metatarsal; everts the foot; superficial fibular nerve.
FJ1409.clinicalCondition: Fifth metatarsal base avulsion — sudden brevis pull during inversion fractures the tuberosity ("pseudo-Jones").
FJ1409.clinicalScenario: A netball player inverts her right ankle and feels pain along the outer foot; radiographs show the brevis tendon has avulsed the fifth metatarsal base.

FJ1410.name: Right fibularis longus
FJ1410.details: Lateral compartment muscle from the upper fibula; its long tendon crosses the sole obliquely in the cuboid groove to reach the first metatarsal base; everts the foot and supports the transverse arch; superficial fibular nerve.
FJ1410.clinicalCondition: Fibularis longus tendinopathy — overuse pain along the lateral ankle and cuboid tunnel in runners.
FJ1410.clinicalScenario: A marathon runner develops aching under the right lateral midfoot; examination localises tenderness along the longus tendon as it turns into the sole.

FJ1411.name: Right fibularis tertius
FJ1411.details: Small anterior-compartment muscle, effectively the lateral slip of extensor digitorum longus, inserting on the dorsal base of the fifth metatarsal; assists dorsiflexion and eversion; deep fibular nerve; absent in some people.
FJ1411.clinicalCondition: Lost in deep fibular nerve palsy — its weakness contributes to the foot drop of anterior compartment lesions.
FJ1411.clinicalScenario: After a proximal fibular fracture, a patient drags his right toes when walking because the dorsiflexors, including fibularis tertius, are paralysed.

FJ3341.name: Right fifth costal cartilage
FJ3341.details: Bar of hyaline cartilage joining the fifth rib directly to the sternum, one of the true-rib cartilages forming the upper costochondral junctions beside the sternum.
FJ3341.clinicalCondition: Costochondritis — inflammation at these junctions causes localised chest pain that mimics cardiac pain.
FJ3341.clinicalScenario: A 30-year-old with sharp right parasternal pain is reassured when pressing the fifth costochondral junction exactly reproduces it and cardiac tests are normal.

FJ3358.name: Right fifth metacarpal bone
FJ3358.details: Short bone of the little-finger ray; its head forms the knuckle, and its neck is the classic fracture site when a clenched fist strikes a hard object.
FJ3358.clinicalCondition: Boxer's fracture — fifth metacarpal neck fracture; check rotation and accept only limited angulation.
FJ3358.clinicalScenario: A young man punches a wall and presents with a swollen right hand; radiographs show a fifth metacarpal neck fracture with 35° of angulation.

FJ3359.name: Right fifth metatarsal bone
FJ3359.details: Bone of the little-toe ray; its base bears a tuberosity for fibularis brevis, and the junction between metaphysis and diaphysis is a watershed zone with poor blood supply.
FJ3359.clinicalCondition: Jones fracture — fracture at the metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction heals slowly and often needs surgery in athletes.
FJ3359.clinicalScenario: A basketball player lands awkwardly and feels a crack on the outer right foot; radiographs show a Jones fracture just beyond the fifth metatarsal base.

FJ3342.name: Right fifth rib
FJ3342.details: A typical true rib articulating with the T4 and T5 vertebrae behind and its own cartilage in front; mid-ribs like this are the most frequently fractured in blunt chest trauma.
FJ3342.clinicalCondition: Flail chest component — fractures of consecutive mid-ribs can create a paradoxically moving chest segment.
FJ3342.clinicalScenario: A driver crushed against the steering wheel fractures ribs four to six on the right, producing a flail segment and laboured breathing.

FJ3333.name: Right first costal cartilage
FJ3333.details: Short cartilage uniting the first rib to the manubrium by a synchondrosis with no joint cavity; the subclavian vein crosses immediately in front of the scalene attachment just behind it.
FJ3333.clinicalCondition: Central-line landmark region — the vein's fixed relations here guide subclavian venous access and its risks.
FJ3333.clinicalScenario: During an emergency subclavian line insertion, the operator uses the first costal cartilage region as a landmark and watches for pneumothorax afterwards.

FJ3350.name: Right first metacarpal bone
FJ3350.details: Short, thick thumb metacarpal; its saddle-shaped base on the trapezium permits opposition, while its palmar base is pulled by abductor pollicis longus in fractures.
FJ3350.clinicalCondition: Bennett fracture — two-part intra-articular base fracture subluxes under the abductor pollicis longus pull.
FJ3350.clinicalScenario: A man falls onto his right thumb; radiographs show a Bennett fracture with the metacarpal shaft displaced radially from the small fixed base fragment.

FJ3351.name: Right first metatarsal bone
FJ3351.details: Shortest, thickest metatarsal, carrying the great toe; two sesamoids sit in the flexor hallucis brevis tendons beneath its head, and the ray bears a large share of forefoot load.
FJ3351.clinicalCondition: Sesamoiditis — inflamed sesamoids under this head cause push-off pain in dancers and runners.
FJ3351.clinicalScenario: A ballet dancer has pinpoint pain beneath her right big-toe joint on pointe work; imaging shows an inflamed tibial sesamoid.

FJ3334.name: Right first rib
FJ3334.details: Shortest, most curved rib, tucked behind the clavicle; scalene tubercle separates grooves for the subclavian vein (front) and artery with the lowest brachial plexus trunk (behind).
FJ3334.clinicalCondition: Thoracic outlet syndrome — structures crossing this rib are compressed, causing arm pain, numbness and vascular symptoms.
FJ3334.clinicalScenario: A young violinist develops right arm aching and hand tingling when practising; imaging shows compression of the neurovascular bundle at the first rib.

FJ3339.name: Right fourth costal cartilage
FJ3339.details: Hyaline bar linking the fourth rib to the sternum; together with the second to fifth cartilages it forms the costochondral junctions most often palpated in chest-wall pain.
FJ3339.clinicalCondition: Tietze syndrome — painful, visibly swollen costochondral junction, usually in the upper cartilages.
FJ3339.clinicalScenario: A woman notices a tender swelling beside her sternum at the right fourth cartilage; the localised, palpable swelling fits Tietze syndrome rather than costochondritis.

FJ3356.name: Right fourth metacarpal bone
FJ3356.details: Bone of the ring-finger ray; its base sits on the hamate, and its neck tolerates less post-fracture angulation than the fifth metacarpal because the ring ray is less mobile.
FJ3356.clinicalCondition: Metacarpal neck fracture — angulation beyond about 20° in this ray impairs grip and is corrected.
FJ3356.clinicalScenario: A boxer injures his right ring-finger knuckle; radiographs show a fourth metacarpal neck fracture angled 30°, referred for hand-surgery review.

FJ3357.name: Right fourth metatarsal bone
FJ3357.details: Slender lesser metatarsal sharing forefoot load; the webspace between its head and the third metatarsal head contains the interdigital nerve vulnerable to compression.
FJ3357.clinicalCondition: Morton neuroma neighbourhood — perineural fibrosis of the nerve between the third and fourth metatarsal heads causes burning forefoot pain.
FJ3357.clinicalScenario: A woman describes burning pain and clicking between her right third and fourth toes in tight shoes, typical of a Morton neuroma.

FJ3340.name: Right fourth rib
FJ3340.details: Typical true rib articulating with the T3 and T4 vertebrae; its undersurface groove shelters the intercostal nerve, artery and vein — the reason chest drains pass just above a rib's upper border.
FJ3340.clinicalCondition: Rib fracture with pneumothorax — displaced upper rib fractures can pierce the pleura and lung.
FJ3340.clinicalScenario: After a fall from scaffolding, a man has a fractured right fourth rib and a small apical pneumothorax requiring observation.

FJ3367.name: Right hamate
FJ3367.details: Distal-row carpal on the ulnar side bearing the hook of hamate on its palmar surface; the hook forms the medial wall of Guyon's canal, carrying the ulnar nerve and artery.
FJ3367.clinicalCondition: Hook of hamate fracture — golfers and batters fracture it, threatening the ulnar nerve in Guyon's canal.
FJ3367.clinicalScenario: A baseball player feels a crack on swinging; he has hypothenar pain and tingling in the little finger from a fractured hook of hamate.

FJ3152.name: Right hip bone
FJ3152.details: Fusion of ilium, ischium and pubis meeting in the acetabulum; iliac crest lies at the L4 level, the anterior superior iliac spine anchors the inguinal ligament, and the sacroiliac joint transfers trunk load.
FJ3152.clinicalCondition: Pelvic ring fracture — high-energy disruption bleeds heavily from presacral veins and fracture surfaces.
FJ3152.clinicalScenario: A pedestrian struck by a car arrives hypotensive with an unstable, open-book right pelvic fracture requiring a binder and massive transfusion.

FJ3368.name: Right humerus
FJ3368.details: Arm bone; surgical neck relates to the axillary nerve, the midshaft spiral groove carries the radial nerve, the distal medial epicondyle shelters the ulnar nerve, and the trochlea/capitulum form the elbow.
FJ3368.clinicalCondition: Midshaft fracture with radial nerve palsy — the nerve is tethered in the spiral groove and stretched by displacement.
FJ3368.clinicalScenario: After a motorcycle crash fractures his right humeral shaft, a man cannot extend his wrist or fingers — a wrist drop from radial nerve injury.

FJ1423.name: Right iliotibial tract
FJ1423.details: Thickened lateral fascia lata running from the iliac crest, receiving tensor fasciae latae and most of gluteus maximus, down to Gerdy's tubercle on the lateral tibial condyle; stabilises the extended knee.
FJ1423.clinicalCondition: Iliotibial band friction syndrome — the band rubs the lateral femoral epicondyle, causing runners' lateral knee pain.
FJ1423.clinicalScenario: A cyclist training for a race develops sharp pain over the outer right knee after twenty minutes of every ride, easing with rest.

FJ3370.name: Right intermediate cuneiform bone
FJ3370.details: Smallest cuneiform, wedged between the medial and lateral cuneiforms; its recessed joint with the second metatarsal base forms the mortise that locks the midfoot (the Lisfranc keystone).
FJ3370.clinicalCondition: Lisfranc injury centre — displacement at this recessed joint destabilises the whole midfoot arch.
FJ3370.clinicalScenario: A footballer whose foot was planted and twisted has midfoot swelling and plantar bruising; imaging shows widening at the second metatarsal–cuneiform joint.

FJ3373.name: Right lateral cuneiform bone
FJ3373.details: Midfoot tarsal between the intermediate cuneiform and cuboid, articulating with the third metatarsal base; part of the transverse arch and the Lisfranc joint complex.
FJ3373.clinicalCondition: Midfoot sprain involvement — lateral cuneiform injuries usually accompany broader Lisfranc-complex trauma rather than occurring alone.
FJ3373.clinicalScenario: CT after a crush injury to a builder's right foot shows a small lateral cuneiform fracture alongside cuboid and metatarsal injuries.

FJ1532.name: Right levator scapulae
FJ1532.details: Strap muscle from the transverse processes of C1–C4 to the superior medial border of the scapula; elevates the scapula and tilts the glenoid downward; supplied by the dorsal scapular nerve and C3–C4 branches.
FJ1532.clinicalCondition: Levator scapulae pain syndrome — myofascial trigger points here cause stiff, aching neck-to-shoulder pain.
FJ1532.clinicalScenario: A desk worker complains of chronic right-sided neck pain radiating to the top inner corner of the shoulder blade, tender exactly over the levator insertion.

FJ1272.name: Right lower central secondary incisor tooth
FJ1272.details: Permanent mandibular right central incisor (FDI 41); the smallest tooth in the mouth, with a narrow single root; its lingual surface faces the submandibular duct openings under the tongue.
FJ1272.clinicalCondition: Lingual calculus build-up — mineralised plaque accumulates fastest behind the lower incisors, driving gum disease.
FJ1272.clinicalScenario: A patient who rarely flosses shows heavy calculus behind the lower front teeth with inflamed, bleeding gums localised to this region.

FJ1268.name: Right lower first secondary molar tooth
FJ1268.details: Permanent mandibular right first molar (FDI 46); two roots (mesial and distal) overlying the mandibular canal region; erupts at about age six, before any baby teeth are shed.
FJ1268.clinicalCondition: Early carious loss — because it erupts first and is mistaken for a baby tooth, it is the most frequently lost permanent molar.
FJ1268.clinicalScenario: A 15-year-old has a grossly decayed lower right first molar; the treatment plan weighs root treatment against extraction near the inferior alveolar canal.

FJ1269.name: Right lower first secondary premolar tooth
FJ1269.details: Permanent mandibular right first premolar (FDI 44); single root, prominent buccal cusp and small lingual cusp; the mental foramen, carrying the mental nerve, usually lies just beyond its apex.
FJ1269.clinicalCondition: Mental nerve injury risk — surgery or implants near premolar apices can damage the mental nerve.
FJ1269.clinicalScenario: After implant placement beside this premolar, a patient reports persistent numbness of the right lower lip and chin from mental nerve injury.

FJ1273.name: Right lower lateral secondary incisor tooth
FJ1273.details: Permanent mandibular right lateral incisor (FDI 42); slightly larger than the central incisor, single-rooted, sitting in the most crowded segment of the lower dental arch.
FJ1273.clinicalCondition: Lower incisor crowding — this segment most often shows rotations and overlap needing orthodontics.
FJ1273.clinicalScenario: A teenager's orthodontic records show the right lower lateral incisor rotated and overlapped; alignment is planned with fixed braces.

FJ1270.name: Right lower second secondary molar tooth
FJ1270.details: Permanent mandibular right second molar (FDI 47); two roots lying close above the mandibular canal, which carries the inferior alveolar nerve and vessels.
FJ1270.clinicalCondition: Inferior alveolar nerve injury — molar roots near the canal risk nerve damage during extraction.
FJ1270.clinicalScenario: Following surgical removal of this molar, a patient has lasting numbness of the right lower lip; imaging had shown roots hugging the mandibular canal.

FJ1271.name: Right lower second secondary premolar tooth
FJ1271.details: Permanent mandibular right second premolar (FDI 45); single root and single canal in most cases; among the teeth most often congenitally absent after third molars.
FJ1271.clinicalCondition: Hypodontia — congenitally missing second premolars are a common incidental radiographic finding.
FJ1271.clinicalScenario: An orthodontic panoramic film for a 12-year-old reveals the right lower second premolar never developed, so the baby molar is retained in the plan.

FJ1274.name: Right lower secondary canine tooth
FJ1274.details: Permanent mandibular right canine (FDI 43); long, sturdy root anchoring the corner of the lower arch and guiding the jaw during side-to-side movements.
FJ1274.clinicalCondition: Retained deciduous canine — delayed exfoliation here can signal a displaced or impacted successor.
FJ1274.clinicalScenario: A 13-year-old still has his baby lower right canine; radiographs show the permanent canine erupting off-line, and orthodontic traction is planned.

FJ3374.name: Right lunate
FJ3374.details: Crescent-shaped proximal carpal articulating with the radius; central to carpal stability and perilunate injury patterns; its blood supply enters mainly distally, leaving the proximal pole vulnerable.
FJ3374.clinicalCondition: Kienböck disease — avascular necrosis of the lunate causes chronic wrist pain and collapse in young adults.
FJ3374.clinicalScenario: A 28-year-old manual worker has months of right wrist ache and stiffness; radiographs show a dense, sclerotic lunate consistent with Kienböck disease.

FJ2554.name: Right major alar cartilage
FJ2554.details: Curved nasal cartilage whose medial crus forms the columella and lateral crus forms the rim and roof of the nostril; it shapes the nasal tip and keeps the external nasal valve open.
FJ2554.clinicalCondition: Cleft-lip nasal deformity — the alar cartilage on the cleft side is displaced and flattened.
FJ2554.clinicalScenario: An infant with a right unilateral cleft lip shows a flattened, splayed nostril on that side from the malpositioned major alar cartilage.

FJ3375.name: Right maxilla
FJ3375.details: Upper-jaw bone carrying the upper teeth; contains the maxillary sinus, forms the orbital floor, and transmits the infraorbital nerve (V2) through its canal to the cheek.
FJ3375.clinicalCondition: Le Fort fracture — horizontal maxillary fractures separate the tooth-bearing segment from the midface.
FJ3375.clinicalScenario: A dashboard injury leaves a man's upper jaw mobile as one block with a deranged bite; CT shows a Le Fort I fracture pattern.

FJ3377.name: Right medial cuneiform bone
FJ3377.details: Largest cuneiform, articulating with the navicular behind and the first metatarsal in front; tibialis anterior and fibularis longus attach around its plantar surface, balancing the first ray.
FJ3377.clinicalCondition: First-ray Lisfranc disruption — separation between this bone and the second metatarsal signals midfoot instability.
FJ3377.clinicalScenario: After a twisting fall, a dancer's right midfoot shows a gap between the medial cuneiform and second metatarsal base on weight-bearing films.

FJ3378.name: Right nasal bone
FJ3378.details: Small paired bone forming the bridge of the nose, articulating with the frontal bone above and the maxilla laterally; thin and exposed, it is the most frequently fractured facial bone.
FJ3378.clinicalCondition: Nasal bone fracture — always examine for septal haematoma, which can necrose the septal cartilage.
FJ3378.clinicalScenario: A boxer takes a blow to the nose; alongside a fractured right nasal bone, examination finds a boggy septal swelling needing urgent drainage.

FJ3348.name: Right ninth rib
FJ3348.details: False rib contributing its cartilage to the costal margin; on the right it crosses in front of the liver's right lobe, with pleura and diaphragm interposed above it.
FJ3348.clinicalCondition: Lower rib fracture with hepatic injury — fractures of right ribs seven to ten should prompt liver imaging.
FJ3348.clinicalScenario: A seat-belted driver with a fractured right ninth rib has right upper quadrant tenderness; CT reveals a small liver capsular tear.

FJ3379.name: Right palatine bone
FJ3379.details: L-shaped bone whose horizontal plate forms the posterior quarter of the hard palate and whose perpendicular plate walls the nasal cavity; pierced by the greater palatine canal carrying vessels and nerve to the palate.
FJ3379.clinicalCondition: Cleft palate — failed fusion of the palatal shelves, including this bone, leaves the posterior palate open.
FJ3379.clinicalScenario: A newborn feeds poorly with milk escaping through the nose; examination shows a cleft extending through the posterior hard palate.

FJ3380.name: Right parietal bone
FJ3380.details: Curved vault bone forming the side and roof of the skull, meeting its pair at the sagittal suture; grooves for middle meningeal artery branches score its inner surface.
FJ3380.clinicalCondition: Fracture over meningeal grooves — tearing the middle meningeal artery causes an extradural haematoma.
FJ3380.clinicalScenario: A man struck on the side of the head has a right parietal fracture crossing a meningeal groove, then deteriorates from an expanding extradural haematoma.

FJ3381.name: Right patella
FJ3381.details: Largest sesamoid bone, embedded in the quadriceps tendon and linked to the tibial tuberosity by the patellar ligament; it lengthens the quadriceps lever arm and shields the knee's front.
FJ3381.clinicalCondition: Patellar fracture — direct blows split it; displaced fractures break the extensor mechanism.
FJ3381.clinicalScenario: A motorcyclist strikes his right knee on the kerb; he cannot straight-leg raise, and radiographs show a transverse patellar fracture with separation.

FJ3382.name: Right pisiform
FJ3382.details: Pea-shaped sesamoid bone inside the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon, articulating with the front of the triquetrum; it forms the lateral wall of Guyon's canal at the wrist.
FJ3382.clinicalCondition: Pisiform fracture — an uncommon fall injury causing ulnar-sided wrist pain over the heel of the hand.
FJ3382.clinicalScenario: A skater lands on the heel of her right hand; tenderness is pinpointed over the pisiform, and a dedicated view confirms its fracture.

FJ3349.name: Right radius
FJ3349.details: Lateral forearm bone; disc-shaped head rotates for pronation–supination, biceps inserts on its tuberosity, and its broad distal end forms most of the wrist joint; Lister's tubercle guides extensor tendons.
FJ3349.clinicalCondition: Colles fracture — distal radius fracture with dorsal displacement produces the "dinner fork" deformity.
FJ3349.clinicalScenario: An elderly woman falls on an outstretched right hand; her wrist shows the classic dinner-fork deformity of a Colles fracture.

FJ3383.name: Right scaphoid
FJ3383.details: Boat-shaped carpal bridging both carpal rows and flooring the anatomical snuffbox; blood reaches it retrogradely from its distal end, so proximal pole fractures risk avascular necrosis and nonunion.
FJ3383.clinicalCondition: Scaphoid fracture — occult fractures with snuffbox tenderness are splinted and re-imaged to prevent nonunion.
FJ3383.clinicalScenario: A snowboarder falls on his right wrist; initial films look normal, but snuffbox tenderness leads to a thumb spica and MRI confirming a waist fracture.

FJ3384.name: Right scapula
FJ3384.details: Flat triangular shoulder-blade bone gliding on the posterior chest wall; its spine ends in the acromion overhanging the shoulder, the coracoid anchors pectoralis minor and biceps, and the glenoid faces the humeral head.
FJ3384.clinicalCondition: Scapular fracture — requires high-energy trauma, so it flags associated rib, lung and brachial plexus injuries.
FJ3384.clinicalScenario: A motorcyclist in a high-speed crash has a comminuted right scapular body fracture alongside multiple rib fractures and a pulmonary contusion.

FJ3335.name: Right second costal cartilage
FJ3335.details: Cartilage joining the second rib to the sternum exactly at the sternal angle, the surface landmark from which all ribs and intercostal spaces are counted in clinical examination.
FJ3335.clinicalCondition: Examination landmark — the second intercostal space beside it is the auscultation site for the aortic area.
FJ3335.clinicalScenario: A student locates the sternal angle, slides onto the right second cartilage, and places the stethoscope in the space below to hear an aortic stenosis murmur.

FJ3352.name: Right second metacarpal bone
FJ3352.details: Longest metacarpal base, firmly wedged into the distal carpal row, making the index ray the hand's stable post for pinch against the thumb.
FJ3352.clinicalCondition: Metacarpal base fracture-dislocation — high-energy axial loads can disrupt this normally rigid carpometacarpal joint.
FJ3352.clinicalScenario: A punch thrown with the index knuckle leading leaves a man with a fractured, subluxed base of the right second metacarpal on imaging.

FJ3353.name: Right second metatarsal bone
FJ3353.details: Usually the longest metatarsal; its base is recessed between the cuneiforms as the Lisfranc keystone, and its slender shaft is the classic site of marching stress fractures.
FJ3353.clinicalCondition: March (stress) fracture — repetitive loading fractures this shaft in new runners and military recruits.
FJ3353.clinicalScenario: Three weeks into basic training, a recruit develops forefoot pain; radiographs show periosteal callus around a stress fracture of the right second metatarsal shaft.

FJ3336.name: Right second rib
FJ3336.details: Curved rib attached at the sternal angle, bearing the scalene tubercle region posteriorly and giving origin to serratus anterior digitations; the counting reference for ribs below it.
FJ3336.clinicalCondition: Rib-counting landmark — misidentifying this rib leads to wrongly sited chest drains and injections.
FJ3336.clinicalScenario: Before inserting an intercostal drain, a junior doctor counts down from the right second rib at the sternal angle to confirm the fifth intercostal space.

FJ3345.name: Right seventh costal cartilage
FJ3345.details: Cartilage of the seventh rib joining the sternum near the xiphoid and starting the costal margin, which it forms together with the eighth to tenth cartilages.
FJ3345.clinicalCondition: Costal margin pain — strain or inflammation at this junction produces upper abdominal/chest wall discomfort.
FJ3345.clinicalScenario: A weightlifter feels a pop and soreness at the right costal margin after heavy twisting; examination reproduces pain over the seventh costal cartilage.

FJ3346.name: Right seventh rib
FJ3346.details: Last true rib, attaching to the sternum by its own cartilage; posteriorly its level corresponds roughly to the inferior angle of the scapula when the arm rests at the side.
FJ3346.clinicalCondition: Rib fracture with haemothorax — mid-to-lower rib fractures can bleed into the pleural cavity.
FJ3346.clinicalScenario: A man kicked in the right chest develops breathlessness; imaging shows a fractured seventh rib with a moderate haemothorax needing drainage.

FJ3343.name: Right sixth costal cartilage
FJ3343.details: Cartilage joining the sixth rib to the sternum just above the xiphisternal region; one of the lower true-rib cartilages palpable along the upper costal margin.
FJ3343.clinicalCondition: Costochondritis — viral or strain-related inflammation here causes palpable, reproducible chest pain.
FJ3343.clinicalScenario: After a heavy cold with prolonged coughing, a woman develops aching over the right sixth costochondral junction that is tender to fingertip pressure.

FJ3344.name: Right sixth rib
FJ3344.details: Typical mid-series rib; counting to it identifies the fifth intercostal space below it in the midaxillary line — the standard site for chest drain insertion within the triangle of safety.
FJ3344.clinicalCondition: Safe drain landmark — the space below this rib avoids the diaphragm and abdominal organs on the right.
FJ3344.clinicalScenario: A trauma team counts the right ribs to site a chest drain in the fifth intercostal space, above the sixth rib's lower neighbour, inside the triangle of safety.

FJ1504.name: Right subscapularis
FJ1504.details: Large rotator-cuff muscle filling the scapula's costal (subscapular) fossa, inserting on the lesser tubercle of the humerus; the cuff's only internal rotator; supplied by the upper and lower subscapular nerves.
FJ1504.clinicalCondition: Subscapularis tear — traumatic anterior dislocations can rupture it, leaving weak internal rotation.
FJ1504.clinicalScenario: After a first-time anterior shoulder dislocation, a rugby player fails the belly-press test, and MRI confirms a full-thickness right subscapularis tear.

FJ3385.name: Right talus
FJ3385.details: Keystone ankle bone transmitting the whole body weight from tibia to foot; no muscles attach to it, and its blood supply enters largely through the neck, flowing backward into the body.
FJ3385.clinicalCondition: Talar neck fracture — displacement interrupts the retrograde flow, causing avascular necrosis of the talar body.
FJ3385.clinicalScenario: A driver in a head-on crash sustains a displaced right talar neck fracture; follow-up films are watched for the Hawkins sign of revascularisation.

FJ3386.name: Right temporal bone
FJ3386.details: Houses the ear within its petrous part, along with the facial nerve canal and carotid canal; the mastoid process anchors neck muscles and the squamous part forms the temple wall over the middle meningeal artery.
FJ3386.clinicalCondition: Temporal bone fracture — basal fractures cause Battle's sign, CSF otorrhoea and facial nerve palsy.
FJ3386.clinicalScenario: After a road accident, a patient has bruising behind the right ear and clear fluid leaking from it; CT confirms a longitudinal temporal bone fracture.

FJ3330.name: Right tenth rib
FJ3330.details: False rib whose cartilage joins the costal margin; its tip is palpable at the margin's lower end, overlying the upper pole of the right kidney behind and the liver in front.
FJ3330.clinicalCondition: Slipping rib syndrome — hypermobile eighth-to-tenth cartilages click and cause sharp lower chest pain.
FJ3330.clinicalScenario: A teenage gymnast reports a painful click at her right costal margin during twists; the hooking manoeuvre reproduces the slip of the tenth cartilage.

FJ3337.name: Right third costal cartilage
FJ3337.details: Cartilage of the third true rib joining the sternum; the second to fifth costochondral junctions are the sites most often involved in benign chest-wall pain syndromes.
FJ3337.clinicalCondition: Costochondritis — a leading benign cause of localised anterior chest pain in young adults.
FJ3337.clinicalScenario: A 24-year-old with two days of sharp right-sided chest pain is diagnosed after palpation of the third costochondral junction reproduces it exactly.

FJ3354.name: Right third metacarpal bone
FJ3354.details: Metacarpal of the middle finger, articulating with the capitate; the third ray is the hand's longitudinal axis, so its alignment is the reference for judging finger rotation.
FJ3354.clinicalCondition: Axial reference injury — malrotation after this fracture distorts the whole finger cascade.
FJ3354.clinicalScenario: After a crush injury, a man's right middle finger crosses over the index when he flexes; radiographs show a rotated third metacarpal shaft fracture.

FJ3355.name: Right third metatarsal bone
FJ3355.details: Slender central lesser metatarsal sharing forefoot load with its neighbours; stress injuries of its shaft occur with sudden increases in walking, running or dance training.
FJ3355.clinicalCondition: Stress fracture — the second and third metatarsal shafts are the classic sites of march fractures.
FJ3355.clinicalScenario: A dancer with forefoot ache has callus forming on the right third metatarsal shaft from a healing stress fracture.

FJ3338.name: Right third rib
FJ3338.details: Upper true rib curving from the T2/T3 vertebrae to its cartilage near the sternum; it roofs the upper lung field and is crossed by chest-wall muscles including pectoralis major.
FJ3338.clinicalCondition: Upper rib fracture — uncommon in isolation; suggests high-energy transfer and warrants vascular screening.
FJ3338.clinicalScenario: A motorcyclist fractures the right third rib in a crash; because upper-rib fractures imply severe force, CT angiography excludes subclavian vessel injury.

FJ3387.name: Right tibia
FJ3387.details: Main weight-bearing leg bone; expanded upper end forms the tibial plateau under the femoral condyles, the tuberosity receives the patellar ligament, and its subcutaneous medial surface forms the shin; medial malleolus braces the ankle.
FJ3387.clinicalCondition: Tibial shaft fracture with compartment syndrome — bleeding and swelling in tight fascial compartments threaten the leg.
FJ3387.clinicalScenario: Hours after a tibial shaft fracture, a patient reports pain out of proportion and pain on toe stretching; urgent fasciotomy treats acute compartment syndrome.

FJ1439.name: Right tibialis anterior
FJ1439.details: Anterior compartment muscle from the lateral tibia and interosseous membrane, inserting on the medial cuneiform and first metatarsal base; chief dorsiflexor and an invertor of the foot; deep fibular nerve, L4–L5.
FJ1439.clinicalCondition: Foot drop — weakness of this muscle is the hallmark deficit of deep fibular or L4/L5 lesions.
FJ1439.clinicalScenario: A patient with a common fibular nerve injury at the fibular neck cannot lift the right forefoot, and the toes drag with each step.

FJ1440.name: Right tibialis posterior
FJ1440.details: Deepest posterior leg muscle; its tendon hooks behind the medial malleolus (first in the "Tom, Dick And Harry" order) to fan into the navicular and midfoot; inverts, plantarflexes and dynamically holds the arch; tibial nerve.
FJ1440.clinicalCondition: Posterior tibial tendon dysfunction — failure of this dynamic arch support produces progressive flatfoot and hindfoot valgus.
FJ1440.clinicalScenario: A 58-year-old man notices his right arch collapsing and the heel drifting outward; from behind, "too many toes" are visible on that side.

FJ3388.name: Right trapezium
FJ3388.details: Distal-row carpal whose saddle joint with the first metacarpal base gives the thumb its wide range of opposition; the flexor carpi radialis tendon grooves its palmar surface inside the flexor retinaculum.
FJ3388.clinicalCondition: Trapeziometacarpal osteoarthritis — the saddle joint wears out, causing basal thumb pain and pinch weakness.
FJ3388.clinicalScenario: A seamstress develops aching at the base of her right thumb with a visible bump; radiographs show advanced trapezium–metacarpal joint arthritis.

FJ3389.name: Right trapezoid
FJ3389.details: Small, tightly bound distal carpal between trapezium and capitate, keyed firmly to the second metacarpal base so the index ray stays rigid for pinch.
FJ3389.clinicalCondition: Isolated trapezoid injury — so rare that its discovery should prompt search for wider carpal disruption.
FJ3389.clinicalScenario: CT performed for a perilunate injury pattern reveals an associated fracture of the right trapezoid among several carpal injuries.

FJ3390.name: Right triquetral
FJ3390.details: Ulnar proximal-row carpal articulating with hamate and lunate and separated from the ulnar head by the triangular fibrocartilage complex, which loads the ulnar wrist in gripping.
FJ3390.clinicalCondition: Triquetral chip fracture — dorsal avulsion chips are the second commonest carpal fracture, best seen on lateral views.
FJ3390.clinicalScenario: A goalkeeper falls backward onto his right hand; a lateral radiograph shows the tell-tale dorsal chip above the triquetrum.

FJ3332.name: Right twelfth rib
FJ3332.details: Short floating rib ending free in the abdominal wall musculature; used as a surgical landmark, since the pleura descends behind its medial half and the right kidney lies just deep to it.
FJ3332.clinicalCondition: Twelfth rib syndrome — a hypermobile, painful rib tip mimics renal or biliary colic.
FJ3332.clinicalScenario: A woman has recurrent right flank pain repeatedly investigated for kidney stones; pressing the twelfth rib tip reproduces it, confirming rib-tip syndrome.

FJ3391.name: Right ulna
FJ3391.details: Medial forearm bone whose subcutaneous posterior border can be felt end to end; the olecranon forms the elbow's point, and the distal head is cushioned from the carpus by the triangular fibrocartilage.
FJ3391.clinicalCondition: Nightstick fracture — an isolated ulnar shaft fracture from a direct defensive blow.
FJ3391.clinicalScenario: A man who raised his right forearm to block a stick blow has a transverse midshaft ulna fracture with an intact radius.

FJ1279.name: Right upper central secondary incisor tooth
FJ1279.details: Permanent maxillary right central incisor (FDI 11); the most prominent tooth in the smile, with a single conical root lying close beneath the floor of the nose.
FJ1279.clinicalCondition: Avulsion in sports trauma — rapid reimplantation offers the best chance of saving this tooth.
FJ1279.clinicalScenario: A hockey player's right central incisor is knocked out; a teammate stores it in milk, and it is reimplanted and splinted within forty minutes.

FJ1276.name: Right upper first secondary molar tooth
FJ1276.details: Permanent maxillary right first molar (FDI 16); three roots overlie the maxillary sinus floor, and the mesiobuccal root usually hides a second canal (MB2) that endodontists must find.
FJ1276.clinicalCondition: Missed MB2 canal — untreated second canals are a leading cause of root-treatment failure in this tooth.
FJ1276.clinicalScenario: A root-treated upper right first molar stays tender for months; CBCT reveals an unfilled MB2 canal, and retreatment resolves the symptoms.

FJ1277.name: Right upper first secondary premolar tooth
FJ1277.details: Permanent maxillary first premolar (FDI 14), between canine and second premolar; two cusps, frequently two roots/canals; key occlusal contact in lateral guidance.
FJ1277.clinicalCondition: Two-canal anatomy missed in root canal treatment — untreated canal causes persistent infection.
FJ1277.clinicalScenario: A 30-year-old has lingering cold sensitivity and night pain in the upper right premolar; radiograph shows deep caries approaching the pulp.

FJ1280.name: Right upper lateral secondary incisor tooth
FJ1280.details: Permanent maxillary lateral incisor (FDI 12), between central incisor and canine; slender root, prone to peg shape, palatal pit and dens invaginatus anomalies.
FJ1280.clinicalCondition: Dens invaginatus — enamel infolding lets bacteria reach pulp early.
FJ1280.clinicalScenario: A teenager presents with a palatal swelling and draining sinus tract over the upper right lateral incisor despite minimal visible decay.

FJ1275.name: Right upper second secondary molar tooth
FJ1275.details: Permanent maxillary second molar (FDI 17), distal to the first molar; three roots whose apices lie close to the floor of the maxillary sinus.
FJ1275.clinicalCondition: Oroantral communication after extraction — thin sinus floor perforates during removal.
FJ1275.clinicalScenario: After extraction of the upper right second molar, the patient reports fluid passing into the nose when drinking and air escaping on nose-blowing.

FJ1278.name: Right upper second secondary premolar tooth
FJ1278.details: Permanent maxillary second premolar (FDI 15), between first premolar and first molar; usually single-rooted with one canal, smaller buccal and palatal cusps.
FJ1278.clinicalCondition: Irreversible pulpitis from proximal caries — single canal makes endodontics comparatively straightforward.
FJ1278.clinicalScenario: A 25-year-old reports sharp pain on biting and prolonged ache from hot drinks localised to the upper right second premolar.

FJ1281.name: Right upper secondary canine tooth
FJ1281.details: Permanent maxillary canine (FDI 13), corner of the dental arch; longest root of any tooth, provides canine guidance; erupts around age 11–12.
FJ1281.clinicalCondition: Palatal impaction — maxillary canines commonly fail to erupt, often palatally displaced.
FJ1281.clinicalScenario: A 13-year-old still has a retained baby canine and no buccal canine bulge; imaging confirms a palatally impacted permanent canine.

FJ3392.name: Right zygomatic bone
FJ3392.details: Forms the cheek prominence and lateral orbital wall; articulates with frontal, sphenoid, temporal and maxilla; its temporal process completes the zygomatic arch.
FJ3392.clinicalCondition: Zygomaticomaxillary complex fracture — displaced fracture flattens cheek and restricts mouth opening.
FJ3392.clinicalScenario: A man punched in the right cheek has a flattened cheekbone, numbness below the eye and cannot open his mouth fully.

FJ3393.name: Sacrum
FJ3393.details: Five fused vertebrae forming the posterior pelvic wall; articulates with L5 above, coccyx below and ilia at sacroiliac joints; sacral canal ends at hiatus.
FJ3393.clinicalCondition: Sacral insufficiency fracture — fragile osteoporotic bone fails under normal load.
FJ3393.clinicalScenario: An elderly woman develops severe low pelvic and buttock pain after a minor fall; MRI shows bilateral sacral insufficiency fractures.

FJ3159.name: Second lumbar vertebra
FJ3159.details: Typical lumbar vertebra with massive kidney-shaped body; lies near the conus medullaris level (L1–L2), so fractures here threaten conus and cauda equina.
FJ3159.clinicalCondition: Burst fracture from axial loading — retropulsed fragments may narrow the canal.
FJ3159.clinicalScenario: A worker falls from scaffolding onto his feet and presents with severe mid-lumbar pain and weak ankle dorsiflexion.

FJ3160.name: Second thoracic vertebra
FJ3160.details: Upper thoracic vertebra with heart-shaped body and demifacets for the second rib; part of the kyphotic thoracic segment stiffened by the rib cage.
FJ3160.clinicalCondition: Osteoporotic wedge compression fracture — anterior body collapse increases kyphosis.
FJ3160.clinicalScenario: An elderly woman with chronic steroids develops acute upper back pain after lifting; radiograph shows an anterior wedge fracture at T2.

FJ3266.name: Sesamoid bone of left foot
FJ3266.details: One of two sesamoids embedded in the flexor hallucis brevis tendons beneath the first metatarsal head; they bear weight and increase flexor leverage.
FJ3266.clinicalCondition: Sesamoiditis — repetitive forefoot loading inflames the sesamoid apparatus.
FJ3266.clinicalScenario: A ballet dancer complains of aching pain under the ball of her left foot, worst when rising onto pointe.

FJ3270.name: Sesamoid bone of left foot
FJ3270.details: Companion sesamoid beneath the left first metatarsal head, within flexor hallucis brevis; the flexor hallucis longus tendon runs in the groove between the pair.
FJ3270.clinicalCondition: Sesamoid stress fracture — repetitive overload cracks the small bone.
FJ3270.clinicalScenario: A distance runner has focal pain under the left great toe for months; MRI shows a stress fracture of the sesamoid.

FJ3372.name: Sesamoid bone of right foot
FJ3372.details: Sesamoid beneath the right first metatarsal head, part of the plantar plate–sesamoid complex stabilising the great toe during push-off in gait.
FJ3372.clinicalCondition: Turf toe — hyperextension sprain injures the sesamoid–plantar plate complex.
FJ3372.clinicalScenario: A footballer forced his right great toe into hyperextension on the turf and now cannot push off without sharp forefoot pain.

FJ3376.name: Sesamoid bone of right foot
FJ3376.details: Second sesamoid of the right forefoot pair; in some people a sesamoid is naturally bipartite with smooth, corticated margins rather than fractured.
FJ3376.clinicalCondition: Bipartite sesamoid mimicking fracture — smooth margins distinguish variant from injury.
FJ3376.clinicalScenario: An X-ray after minor right foot trauma is reported as a sesamoid fracture, but smooth corticated edges indicate a bipartite variant.

FJ3172.name: Seventh cervical vertebra
FJ3172.details: Vertebra prominens, with the longest, non-bifid spinous process — a surface landmark for counting vertebrae; vertebral artery usually passes anterior to, not through, its foramen.
FJ3172.clinicalCondition: Clay-shoveler's fracture — avulsion of the prominent C7 spinous process.
FJ3172.clinicalScenario: A labourer shovelling heavy clay feels sudden pain between the shoulders; imaging shows an avulsed C7 spinous process.

FJ3173.name: Seventh thoracic vertebra
FJ3173.details: Mid-thoracic vertebra; its spinous process tip lies level with the inferior angle of the scapula, a useful surface landmark with arms at rest.
FJ3173.clinicalCondition: Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease) — vertebral destruction produces angular kyphosis (gibbus).
FJ3173.clinicalScenario: A young man with months of mid-back pain, weight loss and a sharp kyphotic bump is found to have T7 tuberculous collapse.

FJ3170.name: Sixth cervical vertebra
FJ3170.details: Its anterior tubercle is the carotid tubercle (of Chassaignac), against which the common carotid can be compressed; vertebral artery typically enters the foramen transversarium here.
FJ3170.clinicalCondition: Landmark for stellate ganglion block — C6 tubercle guides needle placement.
FJ3170.clinicalScenario: An anaesthetist palpates the C6 carotid tubercle while performing a stellate ganglion block for a patient with complex regional pain syndrome.

FJ3171.name: Sixth thoracic vertebra
FJ3171.details: Mid-thoracic vertebra within the narrowest part of the vertebral canal; oesophagus and thoracic duct lie anterior to the thoracic vertebral bodies.
FJ3171.clinicalCondition: Metastatic cord compression — tumour-filled body collapses onto the cord.
FJ3171.clinicalScenario: A patient with prostate cancer develops mid-back pain and progressive leg weakness; MRI shows a T6 metastasis compressing the cord.

FJ3394.name: Sphenoid bone
FJ3394.details: Central skull-base bone housing the pituitary in the sella turcica; contains optic canal and superior orbital fissure; cavernous sinuses lie along its body.
FJ3394.clinicalCondition: Basal skull fracture through sphenoid sinus — causes cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhoea.
FJ3394.clinicalScenario: After a head injury, a patient has persistent clear watery nasal discharge that tests positive for beta-2 transferrin.

FJ3154.name: Tenth thoracic vertebra
FJ3154.details: Lower thoracic vertebra with a single costal facet for the tenth rib; transitional toward lumbar form, still within the cord-bearing thoracic canal.
FJ3154.clinicalCondition: Osteoporotic compression fracture — common near the thoracolumbar transition.
FJ3154.clinicalScenario: A postmenopausal woman develops acute lower thoracic back pain after coughing; radiograph shows a T10 wedge compression fracture.

FJ3161.name: Third cervical vertebra
FJ3161.details: Typical cervical vertebra at the level of the hyoid bone; the phrenic nerve (C3–C5) originates at these levels, so high cervical injury threatens diaphragmatic breathing.
FJ3161.clinicalCondition: High cervical cord injury — diaphragmatic paralysis causes ventilator dependence.
FJ3161.clinicalScenario: A diver who struck his head on the pool floor sustains a C3 fracture and requires immediate ventilatory support.

FJ3162.name: Third lumbar vertebra
FJ3162.details: Largest lumbar vertebra near the apex of lumbar lordosis; the L3/L4 interspace, safely below the conus, is a standard lumbar puncture level.
FJ3162.clinicalCondition: Landmark for lumbar puncture — needle placed below cord termination avoids injury.
FJ3162.clinicalScenario: A febrile, photophobic teenager undergoes lumbar puncture at the L3/L4 space to investigate suspected bacterial meningitis.

FJ3163.name: Third thoracic vertebra
FJ3163.details: Upper thoracic vertebra whose spinous process lies level with the spine of the scapula; aortic arch structures lie anterior at nearby levels.
FJ3163.clinicalCondition: Pathological compression fracture from metastatic disease — weakens body until collapse.
FJ3163.clinicalScenario: A woman treated for breast cancer reports new upper back pain; imaging shows a lytic T3 lesion with partial collapse.

FJ2808.name: Thyroid cartilage
FJ2808.details: Largest laryngeal cartilage; two laminae meet anteriorly forming the laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple); superior horns join hyoid via the thyrohyoid membrane.
FJ2808.clinicalCondition: Laryngeal fracture from strangulation — cartilage breaks under direct compression.
FJ2808.clinicalScenario: A strangulation survivor is hoarse with neck tenderness and subcutaneous emphysema; CT reveals a fractured thyroid cartilage lamina.

FJ3156.name: Twelfth thoracic vertebra
FJ3156.details: Transitional thoracolumbar vertebra bearing lumbar-like features; the thoracolumbar junction is the most injury-prone spinal segment because stiff thoracic spine meets mobile lumbar spine.
FJ3156.clinicalCondition: Thoracolumbar burst fracture — junctional stress concentrates forces here.
FJ3156.clinicalScenario: A motorcyclist in a high-speed crash sustains a T12 burst fracture with early conus medullaris signs.

FJ3395.name: Vomer
FJ3395.details: Thin unpaired bone forming the posteroinferior nasal septum; articulates with sphenoid, ethmoid, palatines, maxillae and the septal cartilage anteriorly.
FJ3395.clinicalCondition: Septal deviation involving vomer — contributes to nasal airway obstruction.
FJ3395.clinicalScenario: A boxer with a previously fractured nose breathes poorly through the left nostril; examination shows a deviated septum over the vomer.

FJ3153.name: Xiphoid process
FJ3153.details: Small cartilaginous caudal tip of the sternum, ossifying with age; surface landmark for the central tendon level, liver edge and correct CPR hand position above it.
FJ3153.clinicalCondition: Xiphoid fracture during CPR — compressions over it can injure underlying liver.
FJ3153.clinicalScenario: A resuscitated patient complains of epigastric pain; imaging shows a fractured xiphoid process from chest compressions.

FJ1446M.name: Abdominal part of left pectoralis major
FJ1446M.details: Lowest fibers of left pectoralis major arising from the rectus sheath/external oblique aponeurosis, inserting on the humeral crest; adducts and medially rotates arm. Nerve: lateral and medial pectoral nerves (C5–T1).
FJ1446M.clinicalCondition: Poland syndrome — congenital absence of pectoralis major fibers causes chest asymmetry and weak adduction.
FJ1446M.clinicalScenario: A teenage boy notices his left chest looks flatter than the right; examination shows absent anterior axillary fold and weak arm adduction.

FJ1446.name: Abdominal part of right pectoralis major
FJ1446.details: Lowest fibers of right pectoralis major arising from the rectus sheath, converging with sternal fibers to insert on the humerus; assists adduction and medial rotation. Nerve: lateral and medial pectoral nerves (C5–T1).
FJ1446.clinicalCondition: Pectoralis major tendon rupture — forceful bench-press injury tears insertion, causing bruising and lost adduction strength.
FJ1446.clinicalScenario: A weightlifter feels a sudden pop in his right shoulder while bench-pressing; a painful swelling appears in the axilla with weak adduction.

FJ1390M.name: Abductor digiti minimi of left foot
FJ1390M.details: Origin: calcaneal tuberosity and plantar aponeurosis; insertion: lateral base of proximal phalanx of fifth toe. Abducts and flexes little toe. Nerve: lateral plantar nerve (S2–S3).
FJ1390M.clinicalCondition: Baxter neuropathy — entrapment of first branch of lateral plantar nerve near this muscle causes chronic medial heel pain.
FJ1390M.clinicalScenario: A runner reports stubborn left heel pain worst with first morning steps; tenderness sits just anterior to the calcaneal tuberosity.

FJ1466M.name: Abductor digiti minimi of left hand
FJ1466M.details: Hypothenar muscle; origin: pisiform and flexor carpi ulnaris tendon; insertion: medial base of proximal phalanx of little finger. Abducts fifth digit. Nerve: deep branch of ulnar nerve (C8–T1).
FJ1466M.clinicalCondition: Ulnar nerve lesion at Guyon canal — hypothenar wasting with weak little-finger abduction signals compression at wrist.
FJ1466M.clinicalScenario: A cyclist develops numbness along the left little finger and cannot spread her fingers apart after long rides pressing on the handlebars.

FJ1390.name: Abductor digiti minimi of right foot
FJ1390.details: Origin: calcaneal tuberosity; insertion: lateral side of proximal phalanx of fifth toe; forms the lateral border of the sole. Abducts little toe. Nerve: lateral plantar nerve (S2–S3).
FJ1390.clinicalCondition: Plantar heel pain syndromes — hypertrophy or strain of this muscle contributes to lateral plantar foot pain.
FJ1390.clinicalScenario: A nurse standing all day complains of aching along the outer border of her right foot, tender over the abductor digiti minimi belly.

FJ1466.name: Abductor digiti minimi of right hand
FJ1466.details: Hypothenar muscle; origin: pisiform; insertion: medial base of proximal phalanx of little finger and ulnar sesamoid region. Abducts the fifth digit away from midline. Nerve: deep branch, ulnar nerve (C8–T1).
FJ1466.clinicalCondition: Froment/Wartenberg sign complex — ulnar palsy makes the little finger rest abducted yet abduction power is weak.
FJ1466.clinicalScenario: After a fractured elbow, a man cannot bring his right little finger back against the ring finger and drops small objects.

FJ1467M.name: Acromial part of left deltoid
FJ1467M.details: Middle multipennate fibers of deltoid from the lateral acromion, inserting on the deltoid tuberosity of humerus; prime abductor of arm beyond 15 degrees. Nerve: axillary nerve (C5–C6).
FJ1467M.clinicalCondition: Axillary nerve injury — surgical neck humeral fracture damages the nerve, paralyzing deltoid abduction.
FJ1467M.clinicalScenario: A patient after a proximal humerus fracture cannot lift her left arm sideways and has numbness over the lateral shoulder.

FJ1467.name: Acromial part of right deltoid
FJ1467.details: Middle fibers of deltoid arising from the acromion, inserting on the humeral deltoid tuberosity; main abductor of the shoulder. Nerve: axillary nerve (C5–C6), tested with resisted abduction at 90 degrees.
FJ1467.clinicalCondition: Deltoid intramuscular injection injury — injections placed too low or medial risk axillary nerve damage and shoulder weakness.
FJ1467.clinicalScenario: A man develops right shoulder weakness weeks after an injection given low in the arm; deltoid wasting is visible on inspection.

FJ2419.name: Anterior papillary muscle of right ventricle
FJ2419.details: Largest right ventricular papillary muscle, arising from the anterior ventricular wall; its chordae tendineae support the anterior and posterior tricuspid cusps, preventing valve prolapse during systole.
FJ2419.clinicalCondition: Papillary muscle rupture after inferior myocardial infarction — chordal support fails, causing acute severe tricuspid regurgitation.
FJ2419.clinicalScenario: Three days after an inferior heart attack, a patient becomes abruptly breathless with a new pansystolic murmur and signs of right heart failure.

FJ2418.name: Anterolateral head of lateral papillary muscle of left ventricle
FJ2418.details: One head of the anterolateral papillary muscle of the left ventricle; chordae run to adjacent halves of the anterior and posterior mitral cusps. Supplied by both LAD and circumflex branches, so relatively infarction-resistant.
FJ2418.clinicalCondition: Mitral valve prolapse — elongated chordae from this muscle let a cusp billow into the atrium.
FJ2418.clinicalScenario: A young woman has a mid-systolic click and late systolic murmur; echocardiography shows prolapse of the posterior mitral leaflet.

FJ1520M.name: Ascending part of left trapezius
FJ1520M.details: Lower fibers of trapezius from lower thoracic spines, converging on the scapular spine; depresses and helps upwardly rotate the scapula. Nerve: spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) with C3–C4 proprioceptive fibers.
FJ1520M.clinicalCondition: Spinal accessory nerve palsy — neck dissection injury weakens trapezius, causing shoulder droop and poor arm abduction.
FJ1520M.clinicalScenario: After lymph node biopsy in the posterior triangle, a patient cannot shrug his left shoulder fully and the shoulder sits lower than the right.

FJ1520.name: Ascending part of right trapezius
FJ1520.details: Lower trapezius fibers sweeping up from T6–T12 spinous processes to the scapular spine; depresses scapula and steadies it during arm elevation. Nerve: spinal accessory nerve (CN XI).
FJ1520.clinicalCondition: Scapular dyskinesis — weak lower trapezius lets the scapula tilt and wing during overhead activity, causing impingement pain.
FJ1520.clinicalScenario: A swimmer reports right shoulder pain at the top of her stroke; her scapula visibly tips forward when she raises the arm.

FJ1468M.name: Clavicular part of left deltoid
FJ1468M.details: Anterior deltoid fibers from the lateral third of the clavicle, inserting on the deltoid tuberosity; flexes and medially rotates the arm and assists horizontal adduction. Nerve: axillary nerve (C5–C6).
FJ1468M.clinicalCondition: Anterior shoulder dislocation — deltoid contour flattens and its anterior fibers are stretched over the displaced humeral head.
FJ1468M.clinicalScenario: A rugby player falls on an outstretched arm; his left shoulder looks squared-off and he holds the arm slightly abducted, unable to move it.

FJ1447M.name: Clavicular part of left pectoralis major
FJ1447M.details: Origin: medial half of clavicle; insertion: lateral lip of intertubercular sulcus of humerus. Flexes, adducts and medially rotates the arm. Nerve: lateral pectoral nerve (C5–C7).
FJ1447M.clinicalCondition: Clavicular head strain — overstretch during dips or fly exercises produces pain just below the clavicle on resisted flexion.
FJ1447M.clinicalScenario: A gymnast feels a sharp pain under her left collarbone during ring work; resisted horizontal adduction reproduces the pain.

FJ1468.name: Clavicular part of right deltoid
FJ1468.details: Anterior deltoid fibers arising from the lateral clavicle, inserting on the humeral deltoid tuberosity; flexes the arm and assists medial rotation. Nerve: axillary nerve (C5–C6).
