FJ1468.clinicalCondition: Rotator cuff tendinopathy compensation — overactive anterior deltoid with weak cuff causes painful superior humeral migration.
FJ1468.clinicalScenario: A painter has right shoulder ache reaching overhead cupboards; the humeral head rides high on X-ray with a reduced subacromial space.

FJ1447.name: Clavicular part of right pectoralis major
FJ1447.details: Origin: medial half of right clavicle; insertion: crest of greater tubercle of humerus. Flexes and adducts the arm, working with anterior deltoid. Nerve: lateral pectoral nerve (C5–C7).
FJ1447.clinicalCondition: Pectoralis major rupture — usually involves this head's tendon, producing loss of the anterior axillary fold.
FJ1447.clinicalScenario: A powerlifter hears a tearing sound at the bottom of a bench press; his right chest swells and the front axillary fold disappears.

FJ1521M.name: Descending part of left trapezius
FJ1521M.details: Upper trapezius fibers from occiput and ligamentum nuchae descending to the lateral clavicle and acromion; elevates the scapula (shrug) and supports the shoulder girdle. Nerve: spinal accessory nerve (CN XI).
FJ1521M.clinicalCondition: Trapezius myalgia — sustained postural load causes aching pain and trigger points in the upper fibers.
FJ1521M.clinicalScenario: A desk worker complains of daily left neck-to-shoulder aching, worse by evening, with tender knots along the upper trapezius.

FJ1521.name: Descending part of right trapezius
FJ1521.details: Upper fibers of trapezius running from the skull and neck down to the lateral third of clavicle; elevates and retracts the scapula. Nerve: spinal accessory nerve (CN XI), tested by shrugging against resistance.
FJ1521.clinicalCondition: CN XI lesion in the posterior triangle — upper trapezius weakness causes visible shoulder droop on that side.
FJ1521.clinicalScenario: After a road accident with neck lacerations, a man cannot shrug his right shoulder and the shoulder girdle sags noticeably.

FJ3131.name: Diaphragm
FJ3131.details: Dome-shaped chief muscle of inspiration; sternal, costal and lumbar (crura) origins converge on the central tendon. Openings transmit IVC (T8), esophagus (T10), aorta (T12). Nerve: phrenic nerves (C3–C5).
FJ3131.clinicalCondition: Phrenic nerve palsy — one hemidiaphragm lies paralyzed and elevated, paradoxically moving up on inspiration.
FJ3131.clinicalScenario: After cardiac surgery, a patient is short of breath when lying flat; chest X-ray shows a raised right hemidiaphragm that rises on sniffing.

FJ1450M.name: External anal sphincter
FJ1450M.details: Voluntary striated sphincter around the anal canal with subcutaneous, superficial and deep parts; blends with puborectalis above. Maintains fecal continence. Nerve: inferior rectal branch of pudendal nerve (S2–S4) and perineal branch of S4.
FJ1450M.clinicalCondition: Obstetric sphincter injury — third-degree vaginal tear divides the sphincter, causing fecal incontinence.
FJ1450M.clinicalScenario: A woman develops leakage of flatus and stool six weeks after a forceps delivery complicated by a deep perineal tear.

FJ2543.name: External anal sphincter
FJ2543.details: Skeletal muscle encircling the lower anal canal, attached behind to the anococcygeal raphe and in front to the perineal body; contracts voluntarily to defer defecation. Nerve: pudendal nerve (S2–S4).
FJ2543.clinicalCondition: Fistula-in-ano surgery risk — dividing too much sphincter during fistulotomy can cause postoperative incontinence.
FJ2543.clinicalScenario: A man with a complex perianal fistula is warned that laying it open could damage the sphincter, so a seton is placed instead.

FJ2548.name: External anal sphincter
FJ2548.details: Three-part voluntary sphincter (subcutaneous, superficial, deep) surrounding the anal canal, continuous with the pelvic floor; its deep part merges with puborectalis. Nerve: inferior rectal nerve from pudendal (S2–S4).
FJ2548.clinicalCondition: Anal sphincter defect on endoanal ultrasound — occult tears explain incontinence years after childbirth.
FJ2548.clinicalScenario: A multiparous woman with worsening stool urgency has an ultrasound showing a gap in the anterior external sphincter ring.

FJ1451.name: external intercostal muscle
FJ1451.details: Fibers run downward and forward between adjacent ribs, from rib tubercle to costochondral junction, replaced anteriorly by the external intercostal membrane. Elevates ribs in inspiration. Nerve: corresponding intercostal nerves.
FJ1451.clinicalCondition: Flail chest — multiple rib fractures isolate a segment that moves paradoxically against intercostal action.
FJ1451.clinicalScenario: After a steering-wheel injury, a driver's chest wall segment sinks inward each time he breathes in, with severe pain and hypoxia.

FJ1451M.name: External intercostal muscle
FJ1451M.details: Outermost intercostal layer; fibers slope inferoanteriorly like hands-in-pockets direction, elevating ribs to increase thoracic volume. Its posterior part continues to the vertebral column. Nerve: intercostal nerves T1–T11.
FJ1451M.clinicalCondition: Intercostal muscle strain — sudden twisting or coughing tears fibers, producing localized chest wall pain.
FJ1451M.clinicalScenario: A cricketer feels a sharp side pain after bowling; breathing deeply and rotating the trunk reproduce tenderness over one intercostal space.

FJ1383M.name: First lumbrical of left foot
FJ1383M.details: Origin: medial side of first tendon of flexor digitorum longus; insertion: medial extensor expansion of second toe. Flexes metatarsophalangeal joint, extends interphalangeal joints. Nerve: medial plantar nerve (L4–L5).
FJ1383M.clinicalCondition: Claw toe deformity — intrinsic muscle imbalance from neuropathy lets long flexors/extensors deform the lesser toes.
FJ1383M.clinicalScenario: A diabetic patient develops clawing of the left second toe with callus under the metatarsal head and early ulceration.

FJ1383.name: First lumbrical of right foot
FJ1383.details: Origin: first flexor digitorum longus tendon; insertion: extensor hood of the second toe. Balances toe flexion and extension at the MTP joint. Nerve: medial plantar nerve (L4–L5).
FJ1383.clinicalCondition: Intrinsic-minus foot in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease — lumbrical weakness produces high arch and clawed toes.
FJ1383.clinicalScenario: A teenager with progressive right foot cavus and claw toes has wasted intrinsic muscles and a family history of similar feet.

FJ1384M.name: First plantar interosseous of left foot
FJ1384M.details: Origin: medial side of third metatarsal shaft; insertion: medial base of proximal phalanx of third toe. Adducts third toe toward the second-toe axis and flexes MTP joint. Nerve: lateral plantar nerve (S2–S3).
FJ1384M.clinicalCondition: Intermetatarsal (Morton) neuroma neighborhood — interosseous dysfunction contributes to forefoot splaying and metatarsalgia.
FJ1384M.clinicalScenario: A woman complains of burning pain between her left third and fourth toes, relieved by removing her shoes and massaging the forefoot.

FJ1384.name: First plantar interosseous of right foot
FJ1384.details: Small unipennate muscle from the third metatarsal to the third toe's proximal phalanx; adducts the toe and stabilizes the forefoot during push-off. Nerve: deep branch, lateral plantar nerve (S2–S3).
FJ1384.clinicalCondition: Metatarsalgia — intrinsic weakness overloads the metatarsal heads during gait, causing plantar forefoot pain.
FJ1384.clinicalScenario: A marathon runner develops aching under the ball of his right foot late in long runs, with tenderness over the third metatarsal head.

FJ1391M.name: Flexor digiti minimi brevis of left foot
FJ1391M.details: Origin: base of fifth metatarsal and long plantar ligament; insertion: lateral base of proximal phalanx of little toe. Flexes the fifth toe at the MTP joint. Nerve: lateral plantar nerve (S2–S3).
FJ1391M.clinicalCondition: Fifth metatarsal base pain — strain here mimics or accompanies peroneus brevis insertion problems at the same site.
FJ1391M.clinicalScenario: A footballer twists his left foot and has pain at the little-toe base; imaging excludes fracture, and resisted toe flexion reproduces symptoms.

FJ1470M.name: Flexor digiti minimi brevis of left hand
FJ1470M.details: Hypothenar muscle; origin: hook of hamate and flexor retinaculum; insertion: medial base of proximal phalanx of little finger. Flexes fifth digit at MCP joint. Nerve: deep branch of ulnar nerve (C8–T1).
FJ1470M.clinicalCondition: Guyon canal syndrome — compression beside the hamate hook weakens this muscle and other hypothenar muscles.
FJ1470M.clinicalScenario: A mechanic using vibrating tools notices weak left little-finger flexion and numbness confined to the ulnar one and a half fingers.

FJ1391.name: Flexor digiti minimi brevis of right foot
FJ1391.details: Origin: fifth metatarsal base; insertion: proximal phalanx of the fifth toe alongside abductor digiti minimi. Flexes the little toe. Nerve: superficial branch, lateral plantar nerve (S2–S3).
FJ1391.clinicalCondition: Tailor's bunion (bunionette) — lateral fifth-ray soft tissues including this muscle are irritated by footwear pressure.
FJ1391.clinicalScenario: A woman has a painful prominence at the base of her right little toe, inflamed after wearing narrow high-heeled shoes.

FJ1470.name: Flexor digiti minimi brevis of right hand
FJ1470.details: Hypothenar muscle deep to abductor digiti minimi; origin: hamate hook; insertion: proximal phalanx of little finger. Flexes the MCP joint of the fifth digit. Nerve: deep branch, ulnar nerve (C8–T1).
FJ1470.clinicalCondition: Hypothenar hammer syndrome — repetitive palm trauma thromboses the ulnar artery near this muscle, causing finger ischemia.
FJ1470.clinicalScenario: A carpenter who uses his right palm as a hammer develops a cold, pale, painful little finger with a tender hypothenar mass.

FJ1389M.name: Fourth lumbrical of left foot
FJ1389M.details: Origin: adjacent sides of third and fourth flexor digitorum longus tendons; insertion: extensor expansion of fifth toe. Flexes MTP and extends IP joints. Nerve: lateral plantar nerve (S2–S3).
FJ1389M.clinicalCondition: Clawing of the fifth toe — lumbrical failure from lateral plantar neuropathy deforms the digit and causes shoe friction sores.
FJ1389M.clinicalScenario: A diabetic man presents with a clawed left little toe and a dorsal corn that has broken down into a shallow ulcer.

FJ1389.name: Fourth lumbrical of right foot
FJ1389.details: Outermost foot lumbrical from flexor digitorum longus tendons to the fifth toe extensor hood; fine-tunes toe posture during gait. Nerve: lateral plantar nerve (S2–S3).
FJ1389.clinicalCondition: Intrinsic muscle wasting in peripheral neuropathy — lumbrical loss is an early sign of diabetic foot muscle imbalance.
FJ1389.clinicalScenario: A patient with long-standing diabetes shows guttering between the right metatarsals and early claw toes, prompting high-risk foot classification.

FJ1473M.name: Humeral head of left flexor carpi ulnaris
FJ1473M.details: One origin of flexor carpi ulnaris from the medial epicondyle via the common flexor origin; muscle inserts on pisiform, hamate and fifth metacarpal. Flexes and adducts wrist. Nerve: ulnar nerve (C7–T1), which passes between its two heads.
FJ1473M.clinicalCondition: Cubital tunnel syndrome — the ulnar nerve is compressed beneath the aponeurosis joining this head to the ulnar head.
FJ1473M.clinicalScenario: A man wakes nightly with tingling in his left ring and little fingers; symptoms worsen when he props on his elbows.

FJ1474M.name: Humeral head of left pronator teres
FJ1474M.details: Larger origin of pronator teres from the medial epicondyle and common flexor tendon; joins the ulnar head to insert on the radius midshaft. Pronates forearm. Nerve: median nerve (C6–C7), which passes between its heads.
FJ1474M.clinicalCondition: Pronator teres syndrome — median nerve compression between the heads causes aching forearm pain and paresthesia.
FJ1474M.clinicalScenario: A weightlifter reports left forearm aching and thumb-side tingling after repeated curls, with normal sensation over the thenar eminence.

FJ1473.name: Humeral head of right flexor carpi ulnaris
FJ1473.details: Medial epicondylar origin of flexor carpi ulnaris; the muscle crosses to the pisiform, acting as a sesamoid to boost wrist flexion and ulnar deviation. Nerve: ulnar nerve (C7–T1), entering forearm between its heads.
FJ1473.clinicalCondition: Medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow) — degeneration at this common flexor origin causes medial elbow pain.
FJ1473.clinicalScenario: A golfer has pain over the right medial epicondyle, aggravated by gripping and resisted wrist flexion with pronation.

FJ1474.name: Humeral head of right pronator teres
FJ1474.details: Origin: medial epicondyle and supracondylar ridge; with the ulnar head it forms pronator teres, inserting on the lateral radius. Chief pronator with pronator quadratus. Nerve: median nerve (C6–C7).
FJ1474.clinicalCondition: Anterior interosseous nerve passage — the nerve branches off as the median trunk passes this muscle, a site of entrapment.
FJ1474.clinicalScenario: A man cannot make the 'OK' sign with his right hand after forearm swelling, though skin sensation is completely normal.

FJ1557.name: Inferior oblique part of left longus colli
FJ1557.details: Lowest part of longus colli running from upper thoracic vertebral bodies up to the transverse processes of C5–C6; lies on the front of the vertebral column behind the esophagus. Flexes and slightly rotates neck. Nerve: ventral rami C2–C6.
FJ1557.clinicalCondition: Retropharyngeal/prevertebral swelling — infection or hematoma in front of this muscle presents with neck stiffness and dysphagia.
FJ1557.clinicalScenario: After a road accident, a patient has severe midline neck pain and painful swallowing; imaging shows a widened prevertebral soft-tissue shadow.

FJ1454.name: innermost intercostal muscle
FJ1454.details: Deepest intercostal layer, separated from internal intercostals by the intercostal nerve and vessels; fibers parallel the internal layer and span one or more spaces. Assists forced expiration. Nerve: intercostal nerves.
FJ1454.clinicalCondition: Intercostal nerve block plane — local anesthetic is deposited deep to the internal layer near this muscle for rib fracture analgesia.
FJ1454.clinicalScenario: An elderly man with three rib fractures receives an intercostal block; ultrasound shows injectate spreading beneath the internal intercostal layer.

FJ1454M.name: Innermost intercostal muscle
FJ1454M.details: Thin deep layer lining the inner chest wall within each intercostal space, continuous with transversus thoracis anteriorly; depresses ribs during active expiration. Nerve: adjacent intercostal nerves.
FJ1454M.clinicalCondition: Thoracentesis landmark relevance — the neurovascular bundle sits between internal and innermost layers, so needles pass just above the rib below.
FJ1454M.clinicalScenario: During pleural tap for an effusion, the operator inserts the needle along the upper border of the rib to avoid the intercostal vessels.

FJ1455.name: internal intercostal muscle
FJ1455.details: Middle intercostal layer; fibers run downward and backward from costal groove to rib below, replaced behind by the internal intercostal membrane. Depresses ribs in expiration. Nerve: intercostal nerves, which run deep to it.
FJ1455.clinicalCondition: Intercostal neuralgia — nerve irritation in the plane deep to this muscle causes band-like chest pain.
FJ1455.clinicalScenario: A patient recovering from shingles describes a burning strip of pain wrapping around one side of the chest along a rib.

FJ1455M.name: Internal intercostal muscle
FJ1455M.details: Fibers slope inferoposteriorly at right angles to the external layer; active mainly in forced expiration and coughing. The intercostal vessels and nerve lie between it and the innermost layer. Nerve: intercostal nerves T1–T11.
FJ1455M.clinicalCondition: Chest drain insertion — the drain traverses this layer in the safe triangle; staying above the rib avoids the bundle beneath it.
FJ1455M.clinicalScenario: A trauma patient needs an urgent chest drain for hemothorax; the tube is placed just above the rib through the intercostal muscles.

FJ1393M.name: Lateral head of left flexor hallucis brevis
FJ1393M.details: Origin: cuboid and lateral cuneiform; insertion: lateral sesamoid and base of proximal phalanx of great toe, sharing insertion with adductor hallucis. Flexes the hallux MTP joint. Nerve: lateral plantar nerve (S1–S2).
FJ1393M.clinicalCondition: Sesamoiditis — inflammation beneath the first metatarsal head involves the sesamoids embedded in these flexor tendons.
FJ1393M.clinicalScenario: A ballet dancer has pain under her left big toe when rising onto pointe, tender over the lateral sesamoid.

FJ1394M.name: Lateral head of left gastrocnemius
FJ1394M.details: Origin: lateral femoral condyle (contains the fabella sesamoid in some people); joins soleus via the Achilles tendon to calcaneus. Plantarflexes ankle, flexes knee. Nerve: tibial nerve (S1–S2).
FJ1394M.clinicalCondition: Gastrocnemius strain — tearing at the musculotendinous junction causes sudden calf pain (the classic 'tennis leg' is specifically a tear of the medial head).
FJ1394M.clinicalScenario: A squash player feels a snap in his left calf lunging for a shot and limps off with swelling in the upper calf.

FJ1477M.name: Lateral head of left triceps brachii
FJ1477M.details: Origin: posterior humerus above the radial groove; converges with other heads onto the olecranon. Extends the elbow, forming the lateral bulk of the arm. Nerve: radial nerve (C6–C8).
FJ1477M.clinicalCondition: Radial nerve palsy in spiral groove — triceps is usually spared because its branches leave before the groove, unlike wrist extension.
FJ1477M.clinicalScenario: A man wakes after sleeping with his arm over a chair ('Saturday night palsy') unable to extend his left wrist, but elbow extension is intact.

FJ1393.name: Lateral head of right flexor hallucis brevis
FJ1393.details: Origin: plantar cuboid/lateral cuneiform; insertion: lateral sesamoid of the great toe with adductor hallucis. Stabilizes and flexes the first MTP joint in push-off. Nerve: lateral plantar nerve (S1–S2).
FJ1393.clinicalCondition: Hallux valgus imbalance — lateral structures including this head tighten as the great toe drifts, worsening the bunion deformity.
FJ1393.clinicalScenario: A woman with a progressive right bunion has her great toe overlapping toward the second toe, with pain over the first MTP joint.

FJ1394.name: Lateral head of right gastrocnemius
FJ1394.details: Origin: lateral condyle of femur; forms the upper lateral calf and contributes to the Achilles tendon. Plantarflexes foot and assists knee flexion. Nerve: tibial nerve (S1–S2).
FJ1394.clinicalCondition: Baker cyst rupture mimic — gastrocnemius tear and ruptured popliteal cyst both cause acute calf pain and swelling needing differentiation.
FJ1394.clinicalScenario: A runner presents with sudden right calf swelling; ultrasound shows a gastrocnemius tear rather than deep vein thrombosis.

FJ1477.name: Lateral head of right triceps brachii
FJ1477.details: Origin: posterolateral humerus above the spiral groove; inserts via the common triceps tendon on the olecranon process. Powerful elbow extensor. Nerve: radial nerve (C6–C8).
FJ1477.clinicalCondition: Triceps tendon rupture — forced elbow flexion against contraction avulses the tendon, losing active extension.
FJ1477.clinicalScenario: A snowboarder falls on his right elbow and cannot straighten it against gravity; a palpable gap sits above the olecranon.

FJ1547.name: lateral lumbar intertransversarius
FJ1547.details: Small slips between adjacent lumbar transverse processes, lateral divisions; assist lateral flexion and stabilize the lumbar spine. Lie near the lumbar plexus within psoas. Nerve: ventral rami of lumbar spinal nerves.
FJ1547.clinicalCondition: Lumbar plexus block landmark — the intertransverse plane guides needle placement, with muscle layers marking depth to the plexus.
FJ1547.clinicalScenario: For hip fracture analgesia, an anesthetist uses ultrasound of the lumbar transverse processes to locate the plexus deep to these muscles.

FJ1547M.name: Lateral lumbar intertransversarius
FJ1547M.details: Paired small muscles bridging lumbar transverse processes; segmental stabilizers working with medial intertransversarii and multifidus. Nerve: lumbar ventral rami (lateral branches).
FJ1547M.clinicalCondition: Quadratus lumborum/intertransverse strain — deep lateral trunk strain causes flank pain mistaken for renal colic.
FJ1547M.clinicalScenario: A warehouse worker lifting boxes develops deep flank pain with normal urine tests; pain is reproduced by side-bending against resistance.

FJ2429.name: Lateral papillary muscle of left ventricle
FJ2429.details: Anterolateral papillary muscle of the left ventricle; its chordae support adjacent halves of both mitral cusps. It has dual coronary supply (LAD diagonal and circumflex marginal), so rupture is less common than the posteromedial muscle.
FJ2429.clinicalCondition: Ischemic mitral regurgitation — papillary displacement from ventricular remodeling tethers the leaflets without rupturing the muscle.
FJ2429.clinicalScenario: Months after a large myocardial infarction, a patient has exertional breathlessness and a soft apical murmur; echo shows tethered mitral leaflets.

FJ1400M.name: Left abductor hallucis
FJ1400M.details: Origin: medial calcaneal tuberosity, flexor retinaculum and plantar aponeurosis; insertion: medial base of proximal phalanx of great toe. Abducts and flexes hallux; supports medial arch. Nerve: medial plantar nerve (S1–S2).
FJ1400M.clinicalCondition: Tarsal tunnel entrapment — the muscle's fascial edge can compress the posterior tibial nerve branches beneath the retinaculum.
FJ1400M.clinicalScenario: A woman reports burning pain and tingling in her left sole at night, with tenderness behind the medial malleolus.

FJ1483M.name: Left abductor pollicis brevis
FJ1483M.details: Thenar muscle; origin: scaphoid, trapezium and flexor retinaculum; insertion: lateral base of proximal phalanx of thumb. Abducts thumb perpendicular to palm. Nerve: recurrent branch of median nerve (C8–T1); key test of median function.
FJ1483M.clinicalCondition: Carpal tunnel syndrome — late compression wastes this muscle, flattening the thenar eminence and weakening thumb abduction.
FJ1483M.clinicalScenario: A typist with years of nocturnal hand tingling now shows a hollowed left thenar eminence and cannot raise her thumb against resistance.

FJ1484M.name: Left abductor pollicis longus
FJ1484M.details: Origin: posterior radius, ulna and interosseous membrane; insertion: base of first metacarpal. Abducts and extends the thumb and forms the anterior border of the anatomical snuffbox. Nerve: posterior interosseous nerve (C7–C8).
FJ1484M.clinicalCondition: De Quervain tenosynovitis — its tendon and extensor pollicis brevis inflame within the first dorsal wrist compartment.
FJ1484M.clinicalScenario: A new mother has pain at the radial side of her left wrist when lifting her baby; Finkelstein test is sharply positive.

FJ1401M.name: Left adductor brevis
FJ1401M.details: Origin: inferior pubic ramus; insertion: upper linea aspera of femur, deep to pectineus and adductor longus. Adducts and flexes the thigh. Nerve: obturator nerve, anterior division (L2–L4).
FJ1401M.clinicalCondition: Adductor strain ('groin pull') — sudden change of direction tears medial thigh muscles including this one.
FJ1401M.clinicalScenario: A footballer feels a tearing pain in his left groin sprinting for the ball and cannot continue; resisted adduction is painful and weak.

FJ1402M.name: Left adductor longus
FJ1402M.details: Origin: front of pubis below the crest; insertion: middle third of linea aspera. Most superficial medial thigh muscle; adducts, flexes and laterally rotates thigh. Nerve: obturator nerve, anterior division (L2–L4).
FJ1402M.clinicalCondition: Adductor longus tendinopathy — chronic overload at its pubic origin causes persistent groin pain in kicking athletes.
FJ1402M.clinicalScenario: A hockey player has six months of left groin pain at the pubic origin, worst when striking the puck.

FJ1403M.name: Left adductor magnus
FJ1403M.details: Largest medial thigh muscle; adductor part from ischiopubic ramus (obturator nerve L2–L4) and hamstring part from ischial tuberosity to adductor tubercle (sciatic nerve L4). Adducts thigh; hamstring part extends it. Forms the adductor hiatus transmitting femoral vessels.
FJ1403M.clinicalCondition: Adductor hiatus landmark — femoral artery passes through it to become popliteal, a level used in vascular examination and bypass surgery.
FJ1403M.clinicalScenario: A vascular surgeon plans a femoropopliteal bypass, marking where the femoral vessels exit behind the knee through the adductor hiatus.

FJ1404M.name: Left adductor minimus
FJ1404M.details: Upper, often incomplete part of adductor magnus running from the inferior pubic ramus to the gluteal tuberosity and upper linea aspera; assists adduction and lateral rotation of thigh. Nerve: obturator nerve (L2–L4).
FJ1404M.clinicalCondition: Obturator nerve entrapment — compression in the obturator canal weakens this and other adductors, causing medial thigh pain and gait instability.
FJ1404M.clinicalScenario: A postpartum woman reports left medial thigh aching and a tendency for the leg to drift outward when walking.

FJ1485M.name: Left anconeus
FJ1485M.details: Small triangular muscle; origin: lateral epicondyle of humerus; insertion: lateral olecranon and upper ulna. Assists triceps in elbow extension and stabilizes the ulna in pronation. Nerve: radial nerve (C7–C8).
FJ1485M.clinicalCondition: Posterolateral elbow pain — anconeus irritation contributes to lateral elbow pain syndromes near the lateral epicondyle.
FJ1485M.clinicalScenario: A tennis player has pain over the back of the left lateral elbow distinct from classic epicondylitis, tender over the anconeus triangle.

FJ2774.name: Left aryepiglotticus
FJ2774.details: Fibers continuing from oblique arytenoid into the aryepiglottic fold, from arytenoid apex to epiglottis edge; helps close the laryngeal inlet during swallowing. Nerve: recurrent laryngeal branch of vagus (CN X).
FJ2774.clinicalCondition: Laryngomalacia — floppy aryepiglottic folds collapse inward in infants, producing inspiratory stridor.
FJ2774.clinicalScenario: A six-week-old baby has noisy breathing worse when feeding and lying flat; endoscopy shows prolapsing aryepiglottic folds.

FJ1486M.name: Left brachialis
FJ1486M.details: Origin: lower half of anterior humerus; insertion: ulnar tuberosity and coronoid process, deep to biceps. Pure elbow flexor in all forearm positions. Nerve: musculocutaneous nerve (C5–C6), small radial contribution.
FJ1486M.clinicalCondition: Brachialis strain — eccentric overload ('climber's elbow') causes deep anterior elbow pain beneath the biceps.
FJ1486M.clinicalScenario: A rock climber reports deep aching in the front of his left elbow after training, with full but painful resisted flexion.

FJ1487M.name: Left brachioradialis
FJ1487M.details: Origin: lateral supracondylar ridge of humerus; insertion: distal radius above the styloid. Flexes elbow best in mid-prone position and forms the lateral boundary of the cubital fossa. Nerve: radial nerve (C5–C7). Its tendon is used for the brachioradialis reflex.
FJ1487M.clinicalCondition: Brachioradialis reflex testing — tapping its tendon checks C5–C6 arc; an inverted reflex suggests cord lesion at C5.
FJ1487M.clinicalScenario: A patient with neck myelopathy shows a paradoxical finger-flexion response when the examiner taps the left brachioradialis tendon.

FJ1524M.name: Left cervical rotator
FJ1524M.details: Rotatores cervicis: short deep muscles from transverse process to lamina of the vertebra above; fine-tune rotation and proprioception of the cervical spine. Nerve: dorsal rami of cervical spinal nerves.
FJ1524M.clinicalCondition: Cervical facet dysfunction — spasm of deep rotators accompanies whiplash, producing segmental neck stiffness and pain.
FJ1524M.clinicalScenario: After a rear-end collision, a driver has a stiff, painful neck with restricted rotation but a normal neurological examination.

FJ1449M.name: Left coccygeus
FJ1449M.details: Triangular pelvic floor muscle from the ischial spine to the coccyx and lower sacrum, lying on the sacrospinous ligament; supports pelvic viscera and flexes the coccyx. Nerve: branches from S4–S5.
FJ1449M.clinicalCondition: Coccydynia — spasm or strain of coccygeus causes pain sitting on hard surfaces after a fall.
FJ1449M.clinicalScenario: A woman who slipped onto ice has persistent tailbone pain when sitting, eased by a ring cushion and leaning forward.

FJ2542.name: Left coccygeus
FJ2542.details: Posterior part of the pelvic diaphragm with levator ani; spans ischial spine to coccyx, reinforcing the pelvic outlet behind the rectum. Nerve: sacral ventral rami S4–S5.
FJ2542.clinicalCondition: Pelvic floor hypertonicity — overactive coccygeus contributes to chronic pelvic pain and painful sitting.
FJ2542.clinicalScenario: A cyclist develops deep perineal aching after long rides; pelvic floor examination finds a tender, tight left coccygeus.

FJ1488M.name: Left coracobrachialis
FJ1488M.details: Origin: tip of coracoid process with biceps short head; insertion: middle of medial humeral shaft. Flexes and adducts the arm. Nerve: musculocutaneous nerve (C5–C7), which pierces this muscle.
FJ1488M.clinicalCondition: Musculocutaneous nerve entrapment — compression where the nerve pierces coracobrachialis causes lateral forearm sensory loss and weak flexion.
FJ1488M.clinicalScenario: A bodybuilder notices numbness along the outer left forearm and weaker elbow flexion after heavy coracoid-region training.

FJ1555.name: Left digastric
FJ1555.details: Two bellies joined by an intermediate tendon slung to the hyoid: posterior belly from mastoid notch (facial nerve), anterior belly from mandible (nerve to mylohyoid, V3). Depresses mandible and elevates hyoid in swallowing.
FJ1555.clinicalCondition: Submandibular triangle landmark — the digastric bellies bound the triangle used to locate the submandibular gland and lingual artery.
FJ1555.clinicalScenario: During excision of a submandibular stone, the surgeon defines the triangle by the two digastric bellies to protect nearby vessels.

FJ1560.name: Left digastric
FJ1560.details: Suprahyoid muscle whose posterior belly runs forward from the mastoid and anterior belly back from the chin, meeting at the hyoid sling; opens the jaw when the hyoid is fixed. Nerves: CN VII (posterior), V3 (anterior).
FJ1560.clinicalCondition: Eagle syndrome neighborhood — the digastric region overlies the styloid apparatus; pain here can mimic elongated styloid symptoms.
FJ1560.clinicalScenario: A woman with throat pain radiating to the ear has tenderness along the posterior digastric; imaging assesses the styloid process length.

FJ1578.name: Left digastric
FJ1578.details: Paired suprahyoid muscle forming the floor framework of the submental and submandibular regions; its intermediate tendon is anchored to the hyoid body by a fibrous loop. Assists jaw depression and hyoid elevation. Nerves: facial and trigeminal branches.
FJ1578.clinicalCondition: Digastric (anterior belly) hypertrophy — asymmetric fullness under the chin can be mistaken for a submental mass.
FJ1578.clinicalScenario: A young man worries about a lump beneath his jaw; examination shows a prominent digastric belly that firms when he opens his mouth.

FJ1489M.name: Left extensor carpi radialis brevis
FJ1489M.details: Origin: lateral epicondyle via common extensor origin; insertion: base of third metacarpal. Extends and abducts the wrist. Nerve: posterior interosseous nerve (C7–C8).
FJ1489M.clinicalCondition: Lateral epicondylitis ('tennis elbow') — degeneration of this muscle's origin is the main lesion, causing lateral elbow pain on gripping.
FJ1489M.clinicalScenario: A plumber has pain over the left lateral epicondyle when wringing a cloth; resisted wrist extension with elbow straight is painful.

FJ1490M.name: Left extensor carpi radialis longus
FJ1490M.details: Origin: lateral supracondylar ridge of humerus; insertion: base of second metacarpal. Extends and radially deviates the wrist and helps fix the wrist during finger flexion. Nerve: radial nerve (C6–C7).
FJ1490M.clinicalCondition: Intersection syndrome — its tendon crosses over the thumb extensors in the forearm, where friction causes painful crepitus.
FJ1490M.clinicalScenario: A rower develops swelling and squeaking pain on the back of her left forearm a few centimeters above the wrist.

FJ1472M.name: Left extensor carpi ulnaris
FJ1472M.details: Origin: lateral epicondyle and posterior ulna; insertion: base of fifth metacarpal. Extends and adducts the wrist; its tendon sits in the sixth dorsal compartment within its own subsheath. Nerve: posterior interosseous nerve (C7–C8).
FJ1472M.clinicalCondition: ECU tendinopathy/subluxation — subsheath tear lets the tendon snap out of the ulnar groove during rotation.
FJ1472M.clinicalScenario: A tennis player feels a painful click on the ulnar side of the left wrist when supinating to hit a topspin forehand.

FJ1517M.name: Left extensor carpi ulnaris
FJ1517M.details: Superficial ulnar-sided wrist extensor arising from the common extensor origin and ulna; stabilizes the distal radioulnar joint and wrist during grip. Nerve: posterior interosseous nerve (C7–C8).
FJ1517M.clinicalCondition: Triangular fibrocartilage complex pain — ECU pathology is a key mimic of TFCC tears on the ulnar wrist.
FJ1517M.clinicalScenario: A weightlifter has ulnar wrist pain pressing up from a bench; the ECU synergy test reproduces it while TFCC tests are negative.

FJ1491M.name: Left extensor digiti minimi
FJ1491M.details: Origin: lateral epicondyle (common extensor origin); its tendon passes through the fifth dorsal compartment to the little finger's extensor expansion. Extends the fifth digit independently. Nerve: posterior interosseous nerve (C7–C8).
FJ1491M.clinicalCondition: Vaughan-Jackson syndrome — attritional rupture of this tendon over a deformed distal radioulnar joint in rheumatoid arthritis.
FJ1491M.clinicalScenario: A woman with rheumatoid arthritis suddenly cannot straighten her left little finger; the tendon has ruptured over the arthritic wrist.

FJ1492M.name: Left extensor digitorum
FJ1492M.details: Origin: lateral epicondyle; four tendons pass under the extensor retinaculum (fourth compartment) to extensor expansions of fingers 2–5. Extends MCP joints and assists IP extension. Nerve: posterior interosseous nerve (C7–C8).
FJ1492M.clinicalCondition: Extensor tendon injury (zones) — laceration over the MCP joint ('fight bite') risks tendon division and joint sepsis.
FJ1492M.clinicalScenario: A man who punched someone presents with a cut over his left knuckle and cannot fully extend the middle finger.

FJ1406M.name: Left extensor digitorum longus
FJ1406M.details: Origin: lateral tibial condyle, fibula and interosseous membrane; tendons split to the four lesser toes, with fibularis tertius to the fifth metatarsal. Extends toes and dorsiflexes ankle. Nerve: deep fibular (peroneal) nerve (L4–L5).
FJ1406M.clinicalCondition: Anterior compartment syndrome — swelling of this compartment after trauma compresses the deep fibular nerve and anterior tibial artery.
FJ1406M.clinicalScenario: After a tibial fracture, a patient has severe shin pain, worse on passive toe flexion, with numbness in the first web space.

FJ1407M.name: Left extensor hallucis brevis
FJ1407M.details: Actually the medial belly of extensor digitorum brevis on the dorsum of the foot; origin: calcaneus; insertion: proximal phalanx of great toe. Extends the hallux MTP joint. Nerve: deep fibular nerve (L5–S1).
FJ1407M.clinicalCondition: Dorsal foot ganglion — cysts near this muscle's tendon on the midfoot are a common presentation mimicking a tumor.
FJ1407M.clinicalScenario: A runner notices a firm, painless swelling on top of her left foot that transilluminates, arising near the extensor tendons.

FJ1408M.name: Left extensor hallucis longus
FJ1408M.details: Origin: mid-fibula and interosseous membrane; tendon crosses in front of the ankle to the distal phalanx of the great toe. Extends hallux and dorsiflexes ankle; the dorsalis pedis pulse lies lateral to its tendon. Nerve: deep fibular nerve (L4–L5).
FJ1408M.clinicalCondition: EHL tendon rupture — laceration or attrition over the midfoot causes loss of great-toe extension and a cock-up toe.
FJ1408M.clinicalScenario: A worker drops a metal sheet on his left foot; later he cannot lift the big toe, though ankle dorsiflexion is preserved.

FJ1493M.name: Left extensor indicis
FJ1493M.details: Origin: posterior ulna and interosseous membrane; tendon joins the index finger's extensor expansion on its ulnar side, allowing independent index extension. Nerve: posterior interosseous nerve (C7–C8).
FJ1493M.clinicalCondition: Posterior interosseous nerve syndrome — compression in the forearm paralyzes this and other extensors while wrist extension persists with radial deviation.
FJ1493M.clinicalScenario: A man develops gradual inability to extend his left fingers and thumb, with no numbness and preserved, radially-deviating wrist extension.

FJ1494M.name: Left extensor pollicis brevis
FJ1494M.details: Origin: posterior radius and interosseous membrane; insertion: base of proximal phalanx of thumb. Forms the posterior border of the anatomical snuffbox and extends the thumb MCP joint. Nerve: posterior interosseous nerve (C7–C8).
FJ1494M.clinicalCondition: De Quervain tenosynovitis — shares the stenosed first compartment with abductor pollicis longus, causing radial wrist pain.
FJ1494M.clinicalScenario: A cashier has thumb-side wrist pain when gripping the till; stretching the thumb across the palm sharply reproduces it.

FJ1495M.name: Left extensor pollicis longus
FJ1495M.details: Origin: posterior ulna and interosseous membrane; tendon hooks around Lister's tubercle (third compartment) to the distal phalanx of thumb. Extends the thumb IP joint and forms the medial snuffbox border. Nerve: posterior interosseous nerve (C7–C8).
FJ1495M.clinicalCondition: EPL attritional rupture — tendon frays over Lister's tubercle weeks after a distal radius fracture.
FJ1495M.clinicalScenario: Six weeks after a wrist fracture heals, a patient suddenly cannot extend the tip of his left thumb or lift it off a flat table.

FJ1452M.name: Left external oblique
FJ1452M.details: Superficial anterolateral abdominal wall muscle; origin: outer surfaces of ribs 5–12; fibers run inferomedially to linea alba, pubic crest, and form the inguinal ligament and external inguinal ring. Rotates and flexes trunk. Nerve: thoracoabdominal nerves (T7–T12).
FJ1452M.clinicalCondition: Spigelian hernia — protrusion through the semilunar line at this muscle's aponeurotic edge, hard to palpate and prone to strangulation.
FJ1452M.clinicalScenario: An elderly woman has intermittent left lower abdominal pain and a subtle bulge at the lateral rectus border, confirmed on CT.

FJ1412M.name: Left flexor accessorius
FJ1412M.details: Quadratus plantae; origin: medial and plantar surfaces of calcaneus; insertion: tendon of flexor digitorum longus. Straightens the oblique pull of FDL so toes flex in line. Nerve: lateral plantar nerve (S1–S3).
FJ1412M.clinicalCondition: Plantar heel pain differential — strain of quadratus plantae is an under-recognized cause of medial plantar heel pain.
FJ1412M.clinicalScenario: A warehouse worker has deep left heel pain unresponsive to plantar fascia treatment; ultrasound shows quadratus plantae tendinopathy.

FJ1496M.name: Left flexor carpi radialis
FJ1496M.details: Origin: medial epicondyle (common flexor origin); tendon passes through its own compartment in the flexor retinaculum to the bases of metacarpals 2–3. Flexes and abducts the wrist. Nerve: median nerve (C6–C7).
FJ1496M.clinicalCondition: FCR tendinitis — overuse inflames the tendon in its fibro-osseous tunnel, causing radial-volar wrist pain.
FJ1496M.clinicalScenario: A badminton player has pain along the front of her left wrist on smashing, tender over the FCR tendon near the trapezium.

FJ1413M.name: Left flexor digitorum brevis
FJ1413M.details: Origin: medial calcaneal tuberosity and plantar aponeurosis; splits into four tendons that divide (Camper chiasm) around FDL tendons to insert on middle phalanges of toes 2–5. Flexes PIP joints. Nerve: medial plantar nerve (L4–L5).
FJ1413M.clinicalCondition: Plantar fasciitis association — this muscle shares the calcaneal origin with the plantar fascia and can be strained in heel pain syndromes.
FJ1413M.clinicalScenario: A runner with plantar heel pain also has mid-arch aching and pain on resisted toe flexion at the proximal joints.

FJ1414M.name: Left flexor digitorum longus
FJ1414M.details: Origin: posterior tibia below soleal line; tendon passes behind the medial malleolus, crosses flexor hallucis longus ('knot of Henry'), and inserts on distal phalanges of toes 2–5. Flexes toes and plantarflexes ankle. Nerve: tibial nerve (S1–S2).
FJ1414M.clinicalCondition: Posterior tibial/FDL tenosynovitis — pain and swelling behind the medial malleolus occur in dancers and runners.
FJ1414M.clinicalScenario: A ballet dancer complains of pain behind her left inner ankle in pointe work, with crepitus along the flexor tendons.

FJ1497M.name: Left flexor digitorum profundus
FJ1497M.details: Origin: upper ulna and interosseous membrane; four tendons pass through the split superficialis tendons to insert on distal phalanges. Flexes DIP joints. Medial part: ulnar nerve; lateral part: anterior interosseous branch of median nerve (C8–T1).
FJ1497M.clinicalCondition: Jersey finger — forced extension of a flexed DIP joint avulses the profundus tendon from the distal phalanx.
FJ1497M.clinicalScenario: A rugby player's left ring finger is caught on a jersey; he cannot bend the fingertip and the tendon has retracted into the palm.

FJ1475M.name: Left flexor digitorum superficialis
FJ1475M.details: Origin: humeroulnar head (medial epicondyle, coronoid) and radial head; tendons split around profundus (Camper chiasm) to insert on middle phalanges. Flexes PIP joints and fingers. Nerve: median nerve (C7–T1).
FJ1475M.clinicalCondition: Trigger finger — thickening at the A1 pulley catches the superficialis tendon, locking the finger in flexion.
FJ1475M.clinicalScenario: A diabetic woman finds her left middle finger clicks and locks each morning, needing her other hand to straighten it.

FJ1499M.name: Left flexor digitorum superficialis
FJ1499M.details: Intermediate forearm flexor forming the bulk between pronator teres and profundus; its four tendons travel in the carpal tunnel, superficialis to digits 3–4 lying superficial. Flexes PIP joints. Nerve: median nerve (C7–T1).
FJ1499M.clinicalCondition: Carpal tunnel crowding — tenosynovitis of these tendons within the tunnel raises pressure and compresses the median nerve.
FJ1499M.clinicalScenario: A pregnant woman develops night-time tingling in her left thumb, index and middle fingers from flexor tenosynovial swelling.

FJ1415M.name: Left flexor hallucis longus
FJ1415M.details: Origin: posterior fibula and interosseous membrane; tendon grooves the talus and passes under the sustentaculum tali to the distal phalanx of the great toe. Flexes hallux, key in push-off and pointe work. Nerve: tibial nerve (S1–S3).
FJ1415M.clinicalCondition: Dancer's tendinitis (FHL tenosynovitis) — stenosis at the talus tunnel causes posterior ankle pain and triggering of the great toe.
FJ1415M.clinicalScenario: A dancer reports pain behind her left ankle and a catching big toe when rising en pointe.

FJ1469.name: Left flexor pollicis brevis
FJ1469.details: Thenar muscle; superficial head from flexor retinaculum/trapezium (median nerve), deep head from trapezoid/capitate (ulnar nerve); insertion via lateral sesamoid into proximal phalanx of thumb. Flexes thumb MCP joint.
FJ1469.clinicalCondition: Sesamoiditis of the thumb — inflammation at its sesamoids causes pain on pinch grip at the thumb base.
FJ1469.clinicalScenario: A potter has aching at the base of her left thumb when wedging clay, tender over the palmar sesamoids.

FJ1498M.name: Left flexor pollicis longus
FJ1498M.details: Origin: anterior radius and interosseous membrane; its tendon runs in its own compartment of the carpal tunnel to the distal phalanx of the thumb. Flexes the thumb IP joint. Nerve: anterior interosseous nerve (C8–T1).
FJ1498M.clinicalCondition: Anterior interosseous nerve palsy — loss of FPL (and index profundus) prevents the pinch 'OK' sign.
FJ1498M.clinicalScenario: A man after a viral illness cannot pinch a sheet of paper with his left hand; the thumb tip stays straight and sensation is normal.

FJ1416M.name: Left gemellus inferior
FJ1416M.details: Small short external rotator below the obturator internus tendon, from the ischial tuberosity to the medial surface of the greater trochanter; laterally rotates and stabilizes the hip. Nerve: nerve to quadratus femoris (L4–S1).
FJ1416M.clinicalCondition: Deep gluteal syndrome — the gemelli-obturator complex can irritate the adjacent sciatic nerve, mimicking radicular pain.
FJ1416M.clinicalScenario: A cyclist has deep left buttock pain radiating down the thigh with normal lumbar imaging and tenderness below the piriformis.

FJ1417M.name: Left gemellus superior
FJ1417M.details: Small muscle above the obturator internus tendon, from the ischial spine to the greater trochanter; blends with the obturator tendon. Laterally rotates the extended thigh. Nerve: nerve to obturator internus (L5–S2).
FJ1417M.clinicalCondition: Posterior hip arthroplasty relevance — the short rotators including gemelli are detached and repaired in the posterior approach to the hip.
FJ1417M.clinicalScenario: After total hip replacement via a posterior approach, a patient is kept on dislocation precautions while the short rotator repair heals.

FJ2738.name: Left genioglossus
FJ2738.details: Fan-shaped extrinsic tongue muscle from the mental spine of the mandible into the tongue body and hyoid; protrudes and depresses the tongue. Nerve: hypoglossal nerve (CN XII). Its tone keeps the airway open.
FJ2738.clinicalCondition: Hypoglossal nerve lesion — tongue deviates toward the lesion on protrusion because the opposite genioglossus acts unopposed.
FJ2738.clinicalScenario: After carotid surgery, a patient's tongue points to the left when stuck out, with slurred articulation of lingual sounds.

FJ1559.name: Left geniohyoid
FJ1559.details: Narrow suprahyoid muscle from the inferior mental spine of the mandible to the hyoid body, lying above mylohyoid; elevates the hyoid and helps depress the mandible. Nerve: C1 fibers via hypoglossal nerve.
FJ1559.clinicalCondition: Swallowing rehabilitation target — strengthening suprahyoid muscles including geniohyoid improves hyoid excursion after stroke dysphagia.
FJ1559.clinicalScenario: A stroke patient aspirates thin fluids; therapy includes chin-tuck and effortful swallows to recruit the suprahyoid group.

FJ1418M.name: Left gluteus maximus
FJ1418M.details: Largest hip muscle; origin: ilium behind posterior gluteal line, sacrum and sacrotuberous ligament; insertion: iliotibial band and gluteal tuberosity of femur. Chief extensor and lateral rotator of thigh. Nerve: inferior gluteal nerve (L5–S2).
FJ1418M.clinicalCondition: Inferior gluteal nerve injury — weak hip extension gives difficulty rising from a chair and climbing stairs ('gluteus maximus gait' lurch).
FJ1418M.clinicalScenario: After a misplaced buttock injection, a man lurches his trunk backward each time his left foot lands and struggles to stand up.

FJ1419M.name: Left gluteus medius
FJ1419M.details: Origin: external ilium between anterior and posterior gluteal lines; insertion: lateral surface of greater trochanter. Abducts thigh and, via anterior fibers, medially rotates; keeps pelvis level in single-leg stance. Nerve: superior gluteal nerve (L4–S1).
FJ1419M.clinicalCondition: Trendelenburg gait — medius weakness lets the opposite pelvis drop during stance on the affected leg.
FJ1419M.clinicalScenario: After hip surgery, a woman's pelvis dips to the right each time she stands on her left leg; the Trendelenburg test is positive.

FJ1420M.name: Left gluteus minimus
FJ1420M.details: Deepest gluteal muscle, from external ilium below medius to the anterior greater trochanter; abducts and medially rotates the thigh and stabilizes the pelvis. Nerve: superior gluteal nerve (L4–S1).
FJ1420M.clinicalCondition: Greater trochanteric pain syndrome — minimus tendinopathy and tears at its trochanteric insertion cause lateral hip pain, often mislabeled bursitis.
FJ1420M.clinicalScenario: A middle-aged woman has pain lying on her left side and tenderness over the greater trochanter; MRI shows a gluteus minimus tear.

FJ1421M.name: Left gracilis
FJ1421M.details: Long strap muscle from pubic symphysis/inferior ramus to the upper medial tibia in the pes anserinus; adducts thigh and flexes knee. Nerve: obturator nerve, anterior division (L2–L4). Commonly harvested as a free muscle flap.
FJ1421M.clinicalCondition: Gracilis flap harvest — its expendability and reliable pedicle make it a workhorse for perineal and facial reanimation surgery.
FJ1421M.clinicalScenario: A patient with long-standing facial paralysis receives a free gracilis transfer powered by the masseteric nerve to restore a smile.

FJ2739.name: Left hyoglossus
FJ2739.details: Flat extrinsic tongue muscle from the greater horn of the hyoid up into the side of the tongue; depresses and retracts the tongue. The lingual artery passes deep to it; hypoglossal nerve and lingual vein run on its surface. Nerve: CN XII.
FJ2739.clinicalCondition: Ranula/submandibular surgery landmark — the hypoglossal nerve on hyoglossus is at risk during submandibular gland excision.
FJ2739.clinicalScenario: After removal of a submandibular gland, a patient cannot protrude the tongue straight; the hypoglossal nerve was stretched during dissection.

FJ1422M.name: Left iliacus
FJ1422M.details: Origin: iliac fossa and sacral ala; joins psoas major as iliopsoas, inserting on the lesser trochanter. Powerful hip flexor; the femoral nerve lies in the groove between iliacus and psoas. Nerve: femoral nerve (L2–L4).
FJ1422M.clinicalCondition: Iliacus hematoma — bleeding into the muscle in anticoagulated patients compresses the femoral nerve, causing quadriceps weakness.
FJ1422M.clinicalScenario: A man on warfarin develops groin pain and cannot extend his left knee or straighten the hip; CT shows an iliacus hematoma.

FJ1453M.name: Left iliococcygeus
FJ1453M.details: Posterior sheet of levator ani from the arcus tendineus and ischial spine to the anococcygeal raphe and coccyx; supports pelvic organs and resists intra-abdominal pressure. Nerve: levator ani nerve (S3–S5) and pudendal branches.
FJ1453M.clinicalCondition: Pelvic organ prolapse — levator ani weakness/avulsion widens the hiatus, allowing bladder or uterine descent.
FJ1453M.clinicalScenario: A multiparous woman reports a vaginal bulge by evening; examination shows stage II prolapse with a palpable levator defect.

FJ2544.name: Left iliococcygeus
FJ2544.details: Thin levator ani component forming the posterolateral pelvic floor shelf with pubococcygeus; elevates the pelvic floor and supports the rectum and vagina/ prostate. Nerve: sacral branches S3–S5.
FJ2544.clinicalCondition: Levator avulsion after vaginal delivery — detachment from the pubis correlates with later prolapse and recurrence after repair.
FJ2544.clinicalScenario: Translabial ultrasound after a difficult first delivery shows the left levator insertion detached, predicting higher prolapse risk.

FJ1526M.name: Left iliocostalis cervicis
FJ1526M.details: Lateral column of erector spinae in the neck, from angles of ribs 3–6 to transverse processes of C4–C6; extends and laterally flexes the cervical spine. Nerve: dorsal rami of cervical and upper thoracic nerves.
FJ1526M.clinicalCondition: Cervical erector spinae strain — whiplash overload of these extensors contributes to chronic post-traumatic neck pain.
FJ1526M.clinicalScenario: A passenger from a car crash has persistent deep pain beside the left cervical spine, tender over the lateral extensor mass.

FJ1527M.name: Left iliocostalis lumborum
FJ1527M.details: Lateral erector spinae in the loin, from the sacrum and iliac crest to the angles of the lower six ribs; extends and side-flexes the lumbar spine and stabilizes the trunk. Nerve: dorsal rami of lumbar nerves.
FJ1527M.clinicalCondition: Mechanical low back pain — fatty infiltration and deconditioning of lumbar extensors including iliocostalis accompany chronic back pain.
FJ1527M.clinicalScenario: A sedentary man with years of back pain has MRI showing fatty replacement of the lumbar extensor muscles.

FJ1528M.name: Left iliocostalis thoracis
FJ1528M.details: Middle link of the iliocostalis column, from angles of lower ribs to angles of upper ribs and C7 transverse process; extends the thoracic spine. Nerve: dorsal rami of thoracic spinal nerves.
FJ1528M.clinicalCondition: Thoracic extensor myofascial pain — trigger points here refer pain around the posterolateral chest wall, mimicking rib pathology.
FJ1528M.clinicalScenario: A seamstress has aching beside the left mid-thoracic spine, reproduced by palpation of a taut band in the iliocostalis.

FJ1294.name: Left inferior oblique
FJ1294.details: Extraocular muscle from the medial orbital floor (maxilla) to the posterolateral sclera below the lateral rectus; extorts, elevates and abducts the eye, acting mainly in adduction. Nerve: oculomotor nerve, inferior division (CN III).
FJ1294.clinicalCondition: Brown syndrome — restricted inferior oblique elevation in adduction from superior oblique tendon sheath tightness mimics its palsy.
FJ1294.clinicalScenario: A child cannot elevate the left eye when looking right and up, with a compensatory head posture but normal elevation in abduction.

FJ1295.name: Left inferior rectus
FJ1295.details: Extraocular muscle from the common tendinous ring to the inferior sclera 6.5 mm behind the limbus; depresses, adducts and extorts the eye, acting best in abduction. Nerve: inferior division of oculomotor nerve (CN III).
FJ1295.clinicalCondition: Thyroid eye disease — inferior rectus fibrosis is the commonest restriction, causing vertical diplopia and limited upgaze.
FJ1295.clinicalScenario: A woman with Graves disease sees double looking upward; forced duction shows a tight left inferior rectus and CT confirms muscle enlargement.

FJ1500M.name: Left infraspinatus muscle
FJ1500M.details: Rotator cuff muscle filling the infraspinous fossa of the scapula, inserting on the middle facet of the greater tubercle; chief external rotator of the arm. Nerve: suprascapular nerve (C5–C6).
FJ1500M.clinicalCondition: Infraspinatus tendinopathy/tear — posterior cuff failure weakens external rotation and causes posterior shoulder pain in throwers.
FJ1500M.clinicalScenario: A volleyball player has deep posterior left shoulder ache and weak external rotation; imaging shows an infraspinatus tendon tear.

FJ1551M.name: Left interspinalis thoracis
FJ1551M.details: Small paired muscles between adjacent thoracic spinous processes (often rudimentary in mid-thoracic region); assist extension and provide proprioceptive feedback on spinal position. Nerve: dorsal rami of thoracic spinal nerves.
FJ1551M.clinicalCondition: Segmental spinal stiffness — these deep muscles are part of the stabilizer system retrained in thoracic back pain rehabilitation.
FJ1551M.clinicalScenario: A manual therapist finds a stiff T7–T8 segment in a patient with focal mid-back pain and prescribes segmental extension exercises.

FJ2778.name: Left lateral crico-arytenoid
FJ2778.details: Intrinsic laryngeal muscle from the lateral cricoid arch to the muscular process of the arytenoid; rotates the arytenoid medially to adduct and close the vocal folds for phonation. Nerve: recurrent laryngeal nerve (CN X).
FJ2778.clinicalCondition: Recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy — adductor failure leaves the cord paramedian, causing a breathy weak voice.
FJ2778.clinicalScenario: After thyroid surgery, a woman speaks in a whispery voice; endoscopy shows the left vocal fold barely moving.

FJ1304.name: Left lateral rectus
FJ1304.details: Extraocular muscle from the common tendinous ring to the lateral sclera; purely abducts the eye. Nerve: abducens nerve (CN VI), whose long intracranial course makes it vulnerable to raised intracranial pressure.
FJ1304.clinicalCondition: Sixth nerve palsy — failure of abduction causes horizontal double vision worse looking toward the affected side.
FJ1304.clinicalScenario: A diabetic man reports double vision when looking left; his left eye cannot cross the midline outward, indicating abducens palsy.

FJ1306.name: Left levator palpebrae superioris
FJ1306.details: Muscle from the sphenoid lesser wing above the optic canal to the tarsal plate and eyelid skin; elevates the upper lid. Nerve: superior division of oculomotor nerve (CN III); its aponeurosis forms the lid crease. Müller's muscle assists sympathetically.
FJ1306.clinicalCondition: Ptosis — aponeurotic dehiscence in aging drops the lid despite intact nerve and good levator excursion when severe.
FJ1306.clinicalScenario: An elderly woman has a gradually drooping left upper lid with a high lid crease; pupil and eye movements are normal.

FJ2741.name: Left levator veli palatini
FJ2741.details: Muscle from the petrous temporal bone and Eustachian cartilage descending into the soft palate; elevates the palate to close the nasopharynx in swallowing and speech. Nerve: pharyngeal plexus (CN X with cranial XI fibers).
FJ2741.clinicalCondition: Velopharyngeal insufficiency — cleft palate disrupts this muscle's sling, causing hypernasal speech and nasal regurgitation.
FJ2741.clinicalScenario: A child repaired for cleft palate still has nasal speech; nasendoscopy shows poor palatal elevation from a scarred levator sling.

FJ1533M.name: Left longissimus capitis
FJ1533M.details: Intermediate erector spinae column continuing into the neck, from upper thoracic/cervical transverse processes to the mastoid process; extends the head and rotates it to the same side. Nerve: dorsal rami of cervical spinal nerves.
FJ1533M.clinicalCondition: Cervicogenic headache contribution — trigger points in the posterior neck extensors refer pain toward the mastoid and temple.
FJ1533M.clinicalScenario: A patient with chronic neck stiffness points to pain behind the left ear; palpation of the longissimus capitis reproduces her headache.

FJ1534M.name: Left longissimus cervicis
FJ1534M.details: From transverse processes of T1–T5 to transverse processes of C2–C6, medial to iliocostalis cervicis; extends and laterally flexes the neck. Nerve: dorsal rami of spinal nerves.
FJ1534M.clinicalCondition: Post-whiplash extensor weakness — impaired deep and superficial cervical extensors, including longissimus, underlie persistent post-traumatic neck pain.
FJ1534M.clinicalScenario: Six months after whiplash, a man fatigues holding his head upright at a desk, with weak resisted neck extension.

FJ1535M.name: Left longissimus thoracis
FJ1535M.details: Largest erector spinae part; from the sacrum and lumbar transverse processes to lower nine/ten ribs and thoracic transverse processes; main extensor of the trunk against gravity. Nerve: dorsal rami of thoracic and lumbar nerves.
FJ1535M.clinicalCondition: Erector spinae atrophy in chronic back pain — selective wasting of longissimus/multifidus reduces spinal load tolerance.
FJ1535M.clinicalScenario: A laborer with recurrent back strains shows poor trunk-extension endurance; rehabilitation targets the erector spinae group progressively.

FJ1561.name: Left longus capitis
FJ1561.details: Prevertebral muscle from transverse processes of C3–C6 to the basal occipital bone, in front of the vertebral column; flexes the head and neck. Nerve: ventral rami C1–C3. Key deep neck flexor tested by the craniocervical flexion test.
FJ1561.clinicalCondition: Deep neck flexor insufficiency — longus capitis/colli weakness after whiplash leads to forward head posture and recurrent neck pain.
FJ1561.clinicalScenario: A patient post-whiplash substitutes with sternocleidomastoid when asked to nod; retraining targets the deep flexors with a pressure cuff.

FJ1522M.name: Left lumbar rotator
FJ1522M.details: Rotatores lumborum: deepest short spinal muscles from the mamillary process of one lumbar vertebra to the lamina above; rich in proprioceptors, they fine-tune segmental rotation. Nerve: medial branches of dorsal rami.
FJ1522M.clinicalCondition: Medial branch blocks — the dorsal ramus branch supplying these muscles and facet joints is targeted for facet pain diagnosis and denervation.
FJ1522M.clinicalScenario: A patient with facet-mediated left lumbar pain gets temporary complete relief from a medial branch block, confirming the pain source.

FJ1308.name: Left medial rectus
FJ1308.details: Extraocular muscle from the common tendinous ring to the medial sclera, 5.5 mm behind the limbus (closest rectus insertion); purely adducts the eye. Nerve: inferior division of oculomotor nerve (CN III).
FJ1308.clinicalCondition: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia — MLF lesion disconnects medial rectus activation in horizontal gaze, causing failed adduction with nystagmus of the other eye.
FJ1308.clinicalScenario: A young woman with multiple sclerosis cannot adduct her left eye on rightward gaze, while convergence remains intact.

FJ1562.name: Left mylohyoid
FJ1562.details: Flat suprahyoid sheet from the mylohyoid line of the mandible to the hyoid and midline raphe; forms the floor of the mouth, elevating it and the tongue in swallowing. Nerve: nerve to mylohyoid from inferior alveolar nerve (V3).
FJ1562.clinicalCondition: Ludwig angina — submandibular space infection above/below this muscle spreads across the floor of mouth and threatens the airway.
FJ1562.clinicalScenario: A man with a decayed molar develops a brawny, board-like swelling under the jaw and cannot open his mouth; airway support is readied.

FJ2780.name: Left oblique arytenoid
FJ2780.details: Intrinsic laryngeal muscle crossing from the muscular process of one arytenoid to the apex of the opposite, continuing as aryepiglotticus; approximates the arytenoids and closes the laryngeal inlet. Nerve: recurrent laryngeal nerve (CN X).
FJ2780.clinicalCondition: Laryngeal inlet incompetence — weak inlet closure contributes to aspiration in neurological bulbar disease.
FJ2780.clinicalScenario: A patient with motor neuron disease coughs on liquids; endoscopy shows pooled secretions and sluggish arytenoid approximation.

FJ1563.name: Left obliquus capitis inferior
FJ1563.details: Suboccipital muscle from the spinous process of the axis (C2) to the transverse process of the atlas (C1); the only capitis muscle not attached to the skull. Rotates atlas and head to the same side. Nerve: suboccipital nerve (dorsal ramus C1).
FJ1563.clinicalCondition: Atlanto-axial rotatory subluxation — spasm of this rotator helps fix the torticollis posture in children after throat infections (Grisel syndrome).
FJ1563.clinicalScenario: A child develops a painful cock-robin head tilt after tonsillitis; CT shows C1 rotated and fixed on C2.

FJ1564.name: Left obliquus capitis superior
FJ1564.details: Suboccipital muscle from the transverse process of the atlas to the occipital bone between the nuchal lines; extends and laterally flexes the head at the atlanto-occipital joint. Nerve: suboccipital nerve (C1 dorsal ramus). Forms the lateral boundary of the suboccipital triangle.
FJ1564.clinicalCondition: Suboccipital neuralgia (occipital neuralgia) — pain from the greater occipital nerve crossing this region radiates over the back of the scalp.
FJ1564.clinicalScenario: A woman describes electric-shock pains starting at the base of her skull and shooting to the vertex, tender over the suboccipital muscles.

FJ1425M.name: Left obturator externus
FJ1425M.details: Flat muscle covering the outer surface of the obturator membrane and surrounding pubic/ischial rami; tendon passes behind the femoral neck to the trochanteric fossa. Laterally rotates the thigh. Nerve: obturator nerve, posterior division (L3–L4).
FJ1425M.clinicalCondition: Obturator canal hernia — although deep, this muscle region overlies the canal through which hernias cause medial thigh (Howship-Romberg) pain.
FJ1425M.clinicalScenario: A thin elderly woman has small bowel obstruction with pain down the inner left thigh; CT reveals an obturator hernia.

FJ1426M.name: Left obturator internus
FJ1426M.details: Fan-shaped muscle lining the inner pelvic wall over the obturator membrane; its tendon exits through the lesser sciatic foramen, bending sharply around the ischium to reach the greater trochanter. Laterally rotates extended thigh. Nerve: nerve to obturator internus (L5–S2).
FJ1426M.clinicalCondition: Obturator internus tendinopathy — deep buttock pain in runners from injury at its ischial bend point.
FJ1426M.clinicalScenario: A distance runner has deep left buttock ache late in runs, with MRI showing obturator internus tendon thickening.

FJ1565.name: Left omohyoid
FJ1565.details: Slender infrahyoid strap muscle with two bellies joined by a tendon tethered to the clavicle; runs from scapula to hyoid, crossing the carotid sheath superficially. Depresses the hyoid. Nerve: ansa cervicalis (C1–C3). Divides the posterior triangle into occipital and supraclavicular parts.
FJ1565.clinicalCondition: Neck surgery landmark — the omohyoid marks levels for carotid endarterectomy; its intermediate tendon overlies the internal jugular vein.
FJ1565.clinicalScenario: During carotid surgery, the team identifies the omohyoid crossing the carotid sheath to define the upper limit of dissection.

FJ1501M.name: Left opponens pollicis
FJ1501M.details: Triangular thenar muscle deep to abductor pollicis brevis, from the trapezium and flexor retinaculum to the lateral border of the first metacarpal shaft; flexes and medially rotates the metacarpal to oppose the thumb. Nerve: recurrent median branch (C8–T1).
FJ1501M.clinicalCondition: Loss of opposition in median nerve injury — 'ape hand' deformity develops when thenar opposition fails.
FJ1501M.clinicalScenario: A patient with a high median nerve injury holds the left thumb flat in the plane of the palm, unable to touch the little fingertip.

FJ1502M.name: Left palmaris longus
FJ1502M.details: Slender superficial flexor from the medial epicondyle to the flexor retinaculum and palmar aponeurosis; weak wrist flexor, absent in about 15% of people. Nerve: median nerve (C7–C8). Its tendon is a common graft donor and landmark for median nerve location.
FJ1502M.clinicalCondition: Palmaris longus absence — a normal variant checked before tendon grafting; the median nerve may be exposed and mistaken for the tendon.
FJ1502M.clinicalScenario: Before harvesting a tendon graft, the surgeon tests wrist flexion with opposed fingers and finds the left palmaris longus congenitally absent.

FJ1427M.name: Left pectineus
FJ1427M.details: Flat quadrangular muscle from the pecten pubis to the femur below the lesser trochanter; forms the medial floor of the femoral triangle. Adducts, flexes and medially rotates thigh. Dual nerve supply: femoral nerve (L2–L3) and obturator nerve.
FJ1427M.clinicalCondition: Femoral triangle relations — pectineus lies just medial to the femoral vessels, a landmark in femoral catheterization and hernia examination.
FJ1427M.clinicalScenario: Examining a groin swelling, a clinician finds it lateral and below relative to the pubic tubercle, suggesting a femoral hernia above the pectineus floor.

FJ1456M.name: Left pectoralis minor
FJ1456M.details: Thin triangular muscle from ribs 3–5 to the coracoid process, deep to pectoralis major; protracts and depresses the scapula and lifts ribs in forced inspiration. The axillary vessels and brachial plexus cords pass behind it. Nerve: medial pectoral nerve (C8–T1).
FJ1456M.clinicalCondition: Pectoralis minor syndrome — a tight or hypertrophied muscle compresses the neurovascular bundle, mimicking thoracic outlet syndrome.
FJ1456M.clinicalScenario: A swimmer reports left arm heaviness and tingling when reaching overhead; hyperabduction reproduces symptoms with a diminished pulse.

FJ1428M.name: Left piriformis
FJ1428M.details: Key gluteal landmark from the anterior sacrum through the greater sciatic foramen to the top of the greater trochanter; laterally rotates the thigh. The sciatic nerve usually exits below it; superior gluteal vessels/nerve exit above. Nerve: nerve to piriformis (S1–S2).
FJ1428M.clinicalCondition: Piriformis syndrome — muscle spasm or a split sciatic nerve through it compresses the nerve, causing buttock and leg pain.
FJ1428M.clinicalScenario: A runner has deep left buttock pain radiating down the leg, worse sitting on a wallet, with straight leg raise nearly normal.

FJ1429M.name: Left plantaris
FJ1429M.details: Small muscle from the lateral supracondylar ridge of the femur with a very long thin tendon descending between gastrocnemius and soleus to the calcaneus/medial Achilles border; weak plantarflexor, absent in some. Nerve: tibial nerve (S1–S2). Used as a tendon graft source.
FJ1429M.clinicalCondition: Plantaris tendon rupture — sudden calf 'pop' during push-off mimics gastrocnemius tear or Achilles rupture but spares strong plantarflexion.
FJ1429M.clinicalScenario: A badminton player feels a snap in his left calf; he can still plantarflex strongly and Thompson test is negative, pointing to plantaris rupture.

FJ1558.name: Left platysma
FJ1558.details: Thin superficial neck muscle in the superficial fascia, from upper thoracic/deltoid fascia to mandible and lower face; cervical branch of facial nerve (CN VII); tenses neck skin, depresses lip corners.
FJ1558.clinicalCondition: Platysmal banding of the aging neck — vertical bands appear because the thin muscle separates and its edges become prominent.
FJ1558.clinicalScenario: A 58-year-old woman requests rejuvenation for vertical neck bands that appear when she grimaces; bands accentuate when she tenses her neck against resistance.

FJ1430M.name: Left popliteus
FJ1430M.details: From lateral femoral condyle to posterior proximal tibia above the soleal line; tibial nerve; unlocks the knee by laterally rotating the femur on the tibia to initiate flexion.
FJ1430M.clinicalCondition: Posterolateral corner injury — popliteus damage with the lateral collateral ligament permits posterolateral rotatory instability of the knee.
FJ1430M.clinicalScenario: A skier twists his flexed knee, later complains of posterolateral knee pain and instability descending stairs; dial test shows increased external rotation.

FJ2782.name: Left posterior crico-arytenoid
FJ2782.details: From posterior cricoid lamina to the muscular process of the arytenoid; recurrent laryngeal nerve; the only abductor of the vocal folds, opening the rima glottidis.
FJ2782.clinicalCondition: Bilateral abductor paralysis — both folds lie near the midline after recurrent laryngeal injury, obstructing the airway.
FJ2782.clinicalScenario: Hours after total thyroidectomy a woman develops inspiratory stridor and respiratory distress; laryngoscopy shows both vocal folds paramedian and immobile.

FJ1503M.name: Left pronator quadratus
FJ1503M.details: Deep quadrilateral muscle between distal ulna and radius on their volar surfaces; anterior interosseous nerve (median); principal pronator of the forearm, binds the distal radioulnar joint.
FJ1503M.clinicalCondition: Anterior interosseous nerve syndrome — weakness of this muscle with flexor pollicis longus and index profundus paralyses pronation against resistance.
FJ1503M.clinicalScenario: A man cannot make the 'OK' sign and pronates weakly with the elbow fully flexed, excluding pronator teres from the movement.

FJ1431M.name: Left psoas major
FJ1431M.details: From T12–L5 vertebrae and discs, passing under the inguinal ligament to the lesser trochanter with iliacus; ventral rami L1–L3; powerful hip flexor and trunk stabilizer.
FJ1431M.clinicalCondition: Psoas abscess — infection, classically tuberculous from Pott disease, tracks within the psoas sheath to present below the inguinal ligament.
FJ1431M.clinicalScenario: A man with treated spinal tuberculosis presents with flank pain, fever, and keeps his hip flexed; extending the hip sharply increases the pain.

FJ1457M.name: Left pubococcygeus
FJ1457M.details: Main part of levator ani, from the posterior pubis to the coccyx and anococcygeal raphe; pudendal and S3–S4 branches; supports pelvic viscera and assists urinary and fecal continence.
FJ1457M.clinicalCondition: Pelvic organ prolapse — levator avulsion or denervation during childbirth removes visceral support, allowing bladder or uterine descent.
FJ1457M.clinicalScenario: A multiparous woman reports a vaginal bulge worse on standing and straining; examination shows a cystocele descending to the introitus.

FJ2545.name: Left pubococcygeus
FJ2545.details: Levator ani component running from pubis around the viscera to the coccyx; its pubovaginal/puboprostatic fibers form the visceral sling; supplied by inferior rectal (pudendal) and direct sacral branches.
FJ2545.clinicalCondition: Levator ani syndrome — chronic spasm of this muscle group causes dull rectal aching relieved by sitting on a hard surface.
FJ2545.clinicalScenario: A woman describes months of vague rectal pressure and aching, worse when sitting; rectal examination reveals a tender, tight levator sling.

FJ1458M.name: Left puborectalis
FJ1458M.details: U-shaped sling of levator ani looping behind the anorectal junction from both pubic bones; pudendal/S4 supply; maintains the anorectal angle and hence fecal continence.
FJ1458M.clinicalCondition: Dyssynergic defecation — failure of the sling to relax, or paradoxical contraction, obstructs defecation despite normal colonic transit.
FJ1458M.clinicalScenario: A patient with chronic constipation strains excessively and uses manual maneuvers; anorectal manometry shows paradoxical puborectalis contraction during attempted defecation.

FJ2546.name: Left puborectalis
FJ2546.details: Fibers arising from the pubic rami that decussate behind the rectum without a posterior bony insertion; tonic contraction keeps the anorectal junction angled forward.
FJ2546.clinicalCondition: Fecal incontinence after obstetric sphincter injury — damage to this sling complex opens the anorectal angle and weakens continence.
FJ2546.clinicalScenario: Years after a forceps delivery complicated by a tear, a woman leaks liquid stool; imaging shows a disrupted, lax puborectalis sling.

FJ1432M.name: Left quadratus femoris
FJ1432M.details: Flat muscle from the lateral ischial tuberosity to the quadrate tubercle of the femur; nerve to quadratus femoris (L4–S1); lateral rotator and stabilizer of the hip joint.
FJ1432M.clinicalCondition: Ischiofemoral impingement — narrowing between ischial tuberosity and lesser trochanter crushes this muscle, causing deep buttock pain.
FJ1432M.clinicalScenario: A woman has deep buttock pain on long strides after hip surgery; MRI shows quadratus femoris edema in a narrowed ischiofemoral space.

FJ1566.name: Left rectus capitis anterior
FJ1566.details: Small prevertebral muscle from the lateral mass of the atlas to the basilar occipital bone anterior to the foramen magnum; ventral rami C1–C2; flexes the head at the atlanto-occipital joint.
FJ1566.clinicalCondition: Whiplash strain of the deep prevertebral flexors — hyperextension injury leaves deep neck flexor weakness and poor head control.
FJ1566.clinicalScenario: After a rear-end collision, a patient has anterior neck pain and cannot lift her head from the pillow without discomfort.

FJ1569.name: Left rectus capitis lateralis
FJ1569.details: From the transverse process of the atlas to the jugular process of the occipital bone; ventral ramus C1; laterally flexes the head and stabilizes the atlanto-occipital joint.
FJ1569.clinicalCondition: Surgical landmark relevance only — it overlies the jugular foramen region and guides the far-lateral approach to the foramen magnum.
FJ1569.clinicalScenario: During a far-lateral craniotomy for a foramen magnum meningioma, this muscle is reflected to expose the jugular tubercle and vertebral artery.

FJ1567.name: Left rectus capitis posterior major
FJ1567.details: From the spinous process of the axis to the lateral inferior nuchal line; suboccipital nerve (C1); forms the superolateral boundary of the suboccipital triangle; extends and rotates the head.
FJ1567.clinicalCondition: Cervicogenic headache — spasm and trigger points in the suboccipital muscles refer pain from the occiput over the vertex.
FJ1567.clinicalScenario: An office worker has occipital headaches radiating to the forehead, with tender suboccipital muscles and restricted upper cervical rotation.

FJ1568.name: Left rectus capitis posterior minor
FJ1568.details: From the posterior tubercle of the atlas to the medial inferior nuchal line; suboccipital nerve (C1); extends the head; linked to the cervical dura by the myodural bridge.
FJ1568.clinicalCondition: Tension-type and cervicogenic headache — its dural connection may transmit abnormal tension to pain-sensitive dura during sustained contraction.
FJ1568.clinicalScenario: A patient with chronic daily occipital headache and neck stiffness improves with suboccipital release and postural correction physiotherapy.

FJ1433M.name: Left rectus femoris
FJ1433M.details: Quadriceps head from the anterior inferior iliac spine and acetabular rim, joining the quadriceps tendon to the patella; femoral nerve (L2–L4); extends knee and flexes hip.
FJ1433M.clinicalCondition: Rectus femoris strain or AIIS apophyseal avulsion — its two-joint span makes it vulnerable during forceful kicking and sprinting.
FJ1433M.clinicalScenario: A teenage footballer feels a tearing pain at the front of the hip while striking the ball; hip flexion and knee extension are both weak.

FJ1536M.name: Left rhomboid major
FJ1536M.details: From spinous processes T2–T5 to the medial scapular border below the spine; dorsal scapular nerve (C4–C5); retracts and rotates the scapula, fixing it to the thoracic wall.
FJ1536M.clinicalCondition: Rhomboid strain — overuse in rowing or throwing produces aching interscapular pain and tenderness along the medial scapular border.
FJ1536M.clinicalScenario: A competitive rower reports aching between the shoulder blades during the pull-through phase, reproduced by scapular retraction against resistance.

FJ1537M.name: Left rhomboid minor
FJ1537M.details: From ligamentum nuchae and spinous processes C7–T1 to the medial scapular border at the root of the spine; dorsal scapular nerve; retracts and stabilizes the scapula.
FJ1537M.clinicalCondition: Snapping scapula syndrome association — altered scapular control from weak rhomboids lets the scapula grate audibly over the ribs.
FJ1537M.clinicalScenario: A young woman hears and feels grinding under her shoulder blade when raising her arm; symptoms ease with scapular stabilization exercises.

FJ1434M.name: Left sartorius
FJ1434M.details: Long strap muscle from the anterior superior iliac spine to the upper medial tibia (pes anserinus); femoral nerve; flexes hip and knee, the 'tailor's muscle'; forms the lateral border of the femoral triangle.
