FJ1659.clinicalCondition: Temporal lobe ischemia — contributes to receptive language and auditory symptoms when dominant-side branches are involved.
FJ1659.clinicalScenario: A patient with an MCA embolus shows early infarction of the right temporal pole on CT, sparing motor cortex but causing agitation and auditory hallucinations.

FJ2130.name: Right anterior tibial artery
FJ2130.details: Smaller terminal branch of the popliteal artery passing forward through the interosseous membrane into the anterior compartment of the leg, continuing as the dorsalis pedis at the ankle.
FJ2130.clinicalCondition: Anterior compartment syndrome — injury or swelling raises compartment pressure, threatening this artery's muscles and the deep fibular nerve.
FJ2130.clinicalScenario: A footballer with a tibial fracture complains of severe shin pain and pain on passive toe stretch; compartment pressures confirm acute compartment syndrome needing fasciotomy.

FJ2131.name: Right anterior tibial recurrent artery
FJ2131.details: First branch of the anterior tibial artery, ascending through tibialis anterior to join the genicular anastomosis around the knee.
FJ2131.clinicalCondition: Collateral to the knee — helps maintain leg perfusion in popliteal artery occlusion via the genicular network.
FJ2131.clinicalScenario: Angiography in a patient with popliteal occlusion shows the anterior compartment reconstituted through enlarged recurrent and genicular collateral branches.

FJ2311.name: Right anterior ulnar recurrent artery
FJ2311.details: Small branch of the ulnar artery just below the elbow, ascending in front of the medial epicondyle to anastomose with the inferior ulnar collateral artery.
FJ2311.clinicalCondition: Elbow collateral network — preserves forearm flow after brachial artery injury at the elbow.
FJ2311.clinicalScenario: A child with a displaced supracondylar fracture has a pulseless but pink hand; the ulnar collateral network maintains perfusion while urgent reduction proceeds.

FJ2133.name: Right arcuate artery
FJ2133.details: Branch of the dorsalis pedis artery running laterally across the bases of the metatarsals, giving the second to fourth dorsal metatarsal arteries to the toes.
FJ2133.clinicalCondition: Foot ischemia assessment — its pulse territory helps judge forefoot perfusion in peripheral arterial disease and diabetes.
FJ2133.clinicalScenario: A diabetic patient with a forefoot ulcer has absent distal signals beyond the arcuate level; vascular imaging guides revascularization planning.

FJ2371.name: Right arteria princeps pollicis
FJ2371.details: Branch of the radial artery in the palm, descending along the first metacarpal to divide into proper palmar digital arteries supplying both sides of the thumb.
FJ2371.clinicalCondition: Thumb ischemia — injury here threatens thumb viability because it is the thumb's dominant arterial supply.
FJ2371.clinicalScenario: A glass laceration deep in the thenar palm bleeds briskly; surgical exploration ligates a divided princeps pollicis while confirming thumb perfusion via collaterals.

FJ2372.name: Right arteria princeps pollicis
FJ2372.details: Passes deep to adductor pollicis and the flexor pollicis longus tendon region, emerging to supply the palmar and dorsal aspects of the thumb.
FJ2372.clinicalCondition: Surgical landmark in hand trauma — must be identified and protected in thenar space exploration and replantation surgery.
FJ2372.clinicalScenario: During thumb replantation after a saw injury, the microsurgeon anastomoses the princeps pollicis to restore arterial inflow before venous repair.

FJ2342.name: Right arteria radialis indicis
FJ2342.details: Branch of the radial artery (often sharing origin with princeps pollicis) running along the lateral side of the index finger to supply its palmar and dorsal aspects.
FJ2342.clinicalCondition: Index finger ischemia — dominant supply to the index makes its injury significant in hand lacerations.
FJ2342.clinicalScenario: A machinist sustains a deep cut at the index finger base; the finger remains viable through palmar arch collaterals after this branch is found divided.

FJ2363.name: Right arteria radialis indicis
FJ2363.details: Courses distally on the first dorsal interosseous muscle toward the index finger, anastomosing with the palmar digital circulation at the fingertip.
FJ2363.clinicalCondition: Variation awareness — it may arise from the superficial palmar arch or princeps pollicis, altering flap and graft planning.
FJ2363.clinicalScenario: Preoperative Doppler mapping for a hand reconstruction identifies a variant radialis indicis origin, changing the planned vascular pedicle.

FJ2268.name: Right axillary artery
FJ2268.details: Continuation of the subclavian artery from the first rib to the lower border of teres major, divided by pectoralis minor into three parts; closely related to the brachial plexus cords, which are named after it.
FJ2268.clinicalCondition: Axillary artery injury — trauma or shoulder dislocation can rupture it, threatening the entire upper limb, especially in elderly atherosclerotic patients.
FJ2268.clinicalScenario: An elderly man falls and dislocates his shoulder; after reduction the radial pulse is absent and CT angiography shows an axillary artery intimal tear.

FJ2271.name: Right brachial artery
FJ2271.details: Continuation of the axillary artery from teres major to the cubital fossa, where it bifurcates into radial and ulnar arteries; the median nerve crosses it in the arm, and its pulse is used for blood pressure measurement.
FJ2271.clinicalCondition: Brachial artery occlusion — embolism or injury causes acute limb ischemia; it is also the standard access site for BP and neonatal resuscitation checks.
FJ2271.clinicalScenario: A child with a supracondylar fracture presents with a cold, pulseless hand; brachial artery exploration reveals the vessel trapped in the fracture site.

FJ1676.name: Right callosomarginal artery
FJ1676.details: Major branch of the pericallosal (distal ACA) running in the cingulate sulcus, giving frontal and parietal branches including supply to the paracentral lobule.
FJ1676.clinicalCondition: ACA territory stroke — occlusion produces contralateral leg weakness from paracentral lobule involvement.
FJ1676.clinicalScenario: A patient develops isolated left foot drop after an anterior communicating artery aneurysm rupture; imaging shows vasospasm affecting the right callosomarginal territory.

FJ2273.name: Right circumflex scapular artery
FJ2273.details: Branch of the subscapular artery winding through the triangular space around the lateral scapular border, supplying subscapularis, teres muscles and the scapular anastomosis.
FJ2273.clinicalCondition: Scapular collateral — key link in the anastomosis that sustains arm perfusion in axillary artery occlusion.
FJ2273.clinicalScenario: Angiography for chronic axillary occlusion demonstrates the arm reconstituted through a hypertrophied subscapular–circumflex scapular collateral pathway.

FJ3590.name: Right colic artery
FJ3590.details: Branch of the superior mesenteric artery supplying the ascending colon; divides into ascending and descending branches joining the marginal artery of Drummond.
FJ3590.clinicalCondition: Ischemic colitis risk — its watershed anastomosis with the ileocolic and middle colic arteries can fail in hypotension.
FJ3590.clinicalScenario: An elderly patient after cardiac surgery develops bloody diarrhea; colonoscopy shows segmental ischemia of the ascending colon in the right colic territory.

FJ3564.name: Right common carotid artery
FJ3564.details: Arises from the brachiocephalic trunk behind the right sternoclavicular joint, ascends within the carotid sheath lateral to the trachea, bifurcating at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C4) into external and internal carotid arteries.
FJ3564.clinicalCondition: Carotid stenosis — atherosclerosis at its bifurcation causes TIAs and stroke; auscultation may reveal a bruit.
FJ3564.clinicalScenario: A smoker reports transient left-hand weakness and speech slurring; duplex ultrasound shows 80% stenosis at the right carotid bifurcation, and endarterectomy is planned.

FJ3565.name: Right common iliac artery
FJ3565.details: Formed by the aortic bifurcation at L4, it descends to the sacroiliac joint where it divides into external and internal iliac arteries; the ureter crosses its bifurcation anteriorly.
FJ3565.clinicalCondition: Aortoiliac occlusive disease (Leriche syndrome) — bilateral disease causes buttock claudication, impotence and absent femoral pulses.
FJ3565.clinicalScenario: A middle-aged man describes thigh and buttock pain on walking with erectile dysfunction; CT angiography shows occlusion at the aortic bifurcation involving both common iliac arteries.

FJ2275.name: Right common interosseous artery
FJ2275.details: Short branch of the ulnar artery in the proximal forearm, immediately dividing into anterior and posterior interosseous arteries that run on either side of the interosseous membrane.
FJ2275.clinicalCondition: Forearm compartment supply — its branches feed both flexor and extensor compartments, relevant in forearm compartment syndrome decompression.
FJ2275.clinicalScenario: During fasciotomy for forearm compartment syndrome, the surgeon identifies the interosseous vessels while releasing the deep flexor compartment.

FJ2670.name: Right conus artery
FJ2670.details: First branch of the right coronary artery, arising near its ostium and circling the pulmonary conus (right ventricular outflow tract), often forming Vieussens' arterial ring with a left coronary twig.
FJ2670.clinicalCondition: Collateral significance — this ring is an early collateral pathway between right and left coronary systems in proximal LAD occlusion.
FJ2670.clinicalScenario: Angiography in chronic total LAD occlusion shows the conus artery enlarged, feeding retrograde filling of the distal LAD through Vieussens' ring.

FJ2676.name: Right conus artery
FJ2676.details: Small branch supplying the infundibulum of the right ventricle; in about half of hearts it arises independently from the aorta as a 'third coronary artery'.
FJ2676.clinicalCondition: Variation awareness — a separate ostium can be missed at angiography or complicate selective cannulation during intervention.
FJ2676.clinicalScenario: During coronary angiography the operator notes a tiny separate right-sided ostium; recognizing the third coronary (conus) ostium avoids misreading it as an occluded RCA.

FJ2276.name: Right costocervical trunk
FJ2276.details: Branch of the posterior aspect of the second part of the subclavian artery, arching over the neck of the first rib to divide into the deep cervical and superior intercostal arteries.
FJ2276.clinicalCondition: Surgical landmark — lies near the stellate ganglion and thoracic duct region, at risk in supraclavicular and apical thoracic surgery.
FJ2276.clinicalScenario: During resection of a Pancoast tumor, the surgeon identifies the costocervical trunk while clearing the thoracic inlet, preserving it to limit chest wall ischemia.

FJ2277.name: Right deep brachial artery
FJ2277.details: Large branch of the brachial artery (profunda brachii) accompanying the radial nerve through the spiral groove and lateral intermuscular septum, supplying the posterior compartment of the arm and the humerus.
FJ2277.clinicalCondition: At risk in humeral fractures — tethered with the radial nerve in the spiral groove, so midshaft fractures threaten both.
FJ2277.clinicalScenario: A patient with a spiral humeral fracture cannot extend the wrist; imaging and exploration show the radial nerve and profunda vessels stretched over the fracture.

FJ2278.name: Right deep cervical artery
FJ2278.details: Branch of the costocervical trunk passing backward between the neck of the first rib and C7 transverse process to supply the deep posterior neck muscles, anastomosing with the occipital and vertebral arteries.
FJ2278.clinicalCondition: Collateral in subclavian steal — contributes to posterior neck collateral flow when the proximal subclavian or vertebral artery is occluded.
FJ2278.clinicalScenario: Angiography for vertebrobasilar insufficiency demonstrates deep cervical collaterals reconstituting the distal vertebral artery beyond a proximal occlusion.

FJ2279.name: Right deep palmar arch
FJ2279.details: Formed mainly by the terminal radial artery, completed by the deep palmar branch of the ulnar artery; lies deep to the flexor tendons at the level of the metacarpal bases, giving palmar metacarpal arteries.
FJ2279.clinicalCondition: Hand perfusion testing — patency assessed with the modified Allen test before radial artery harvest or cannulation.
FJ2279.clinicalScenario: Before using the radial artery as a bypass conduit, a surgeon performs an Allen test confirming ulnar collateral flow through the palmar arches.

FJ2136.name: Right deep plantar artery
FJ2136.details: Branch of the dorsalis pedis artery passing between the heads of the first dorsal interosseous muscle into the sole, where it joins the lateral plantar artery to complete the plantar arch.
FJ2136.clinicalCondition: Foot collateral — key link between dorsal and plantar circulations, assessed in forefoot ischemia and flap planning.
FJ2136.clinicalScenario: A vascular surgeon planning a forefoot amputation checks Doppler signals showing flow through the deep plantar connection, predicting adequate stump healing.

FJ2137.name: Right descending genicular artery
FJ2137.details: Last branch of the femoral artery before the adductor hiatus, descending with the saphenous nerve to supply the medial knee and join the genicular anastomosis; gives articular and saphenous branches.
FJ2137.clinicalCondition: Knee collateral — contributes to limb perfusion in superficial femoral or popliteal occlusion; its saphenous branch is used in vascularized flaps.
FJ2137.clinicalScenario: In a patient with popliteal occlusion, angiography shows the descending genicular artery feeding the genicular network that reconstitutes the tibial vessels.

FJ3592.name: Right dorsal artery of penis
FJ3592.details: Terminal branch of the internal pudendal artery running on the dorsum of the penis deep to Buck's fascia, lateral to the deep dorsal vein, supplying the glans and penile skin.
FJ3592.clinicalCondition: Vasculogenic erectile dysfunction — atherosclerotic disease of the pudendal–dorsal arterial axis reduces penile inflow.
FJ3592.clinicalScenario: A diabetic man with erectile dysfunction undergoes penile Doppler showing reduced peak systolic velocity in the dorsal arteries, supporting arterial insufficiency.

FJ3593.name: Right dorsal artery of penis
FJ3593.details: Accompanies the dorsal nerve of the penis within the neurovascular bundle on the dorsum, a relation protected during penile surgery and fracture repair.
FJ3593.clinicalCondition: Injury in penile fracture — rupture of the tunica can damage the dorsal neurovascular structures causing hematoma and sensory loss.
FJ3593.clinicalScenario: After a penile fracture injury, examination shows an 'eggplant' deformity; surgical repair inspects the dorsal vessels and nerves for associated damage.

FJ2288.name: Right dorsal carpal branch of ulnar artery
FJ2288.details: Small branch arising just proximal to the pisiform, passing dorsally deep to flexor carpi ulnaris to join the dorsal carpal arch supplying the dorsum of the wrist and hand.
FJ2288.clinicalCondition: Minor collateral — contributes to dorsal hand perfusion; relevant when planning ulnar artery flaps and wrist arthroscopy portals.
FJ2288.clinicalScenario: Preoperative mapping for a dorsal hand flap confirms dorsal carpal arch flow, allowing safe elevation of the flap on its pedicle.

FJ2284.name: Right dorsal scapular artery
FJ2284.details: Arises from the second or third part of the subclavian artery (or as the deep branch of the transverse cervical), piercing the brachial plexus to run deep to levator scapulae and rhomboids along the medial scapular border.
FJ2284.clinicalCondition: Scapular anastomosis — participates in collateral flow around a blocked subclavian or axillary artery.
FJ2284.clinicalScenario: Imaging in subclavian occlusion shows a prominent dorsal scapular artery carrying collateral flow toward the circumflex scapular system and the arm.

FJ2055.name: Right dorsalis pedis artery
FJ2055.details: Continuation of the anterior tibial artery on the dorsum of the foot, running lateral to extensor hallucis longus toward the first intermetatarsal space; its pulse is palpated between the first and second metatarsals.
FJ2055.clinicalCondition: Peripheral arterial disease marker — absent dorsalis pedis pulse signals significant lower-limb arterial disease (though absent in some healthy people as a variant).
FJ2055.clinicalScenario: A diabetic patient with a non-healing toe ulcer has no palpable dorsalis pedis pulse; ankle-brachial index confirms severe peripheral arterial disease.

FJ3567.name: Right external iliac artery
FJ3567.details: Larger terminal branch of the common iliac artery, running along the medial border of psoas major and passing behind the inguinal ligament to become the femoral artery; gives the inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac branches.
FJ3567.clinicalCondition: Iliac stenosis — atherosclerosis here causes thigh and calf claudication; it is also the access route for endovascular procedures.
FJ3567.clinicalScenario: A smoker with calf claudication at 100 meters has a diminished femoral pulse; CT angiography shows a tight right external iliac stenosis treated by stenting.

FJ2143.name: Right femoral artery
FJ2143.details: Continuation of the external iliac artery behind the inguinal ligament, traversing the femoral triangle and adductor canal to exit through the adductor hiatus as the popliteal artery; gives the profunda femoris and superficial branches.
FJ2143.clinicalCondition: Common access and injury site — used for angiography and cannulation; pseudoaneurysm and AV fistula are classic access complications.
FJ2143.clinicalScenario: Two days after cardiac catheterization, a patient notices a painful pulsatile groin swelling with a bruit; ultrasound confirms a femoral artery pseudoaneurysm.

FJ2343.name: Right first common palmar digital artery
FJ2343.details: First branch of the superficial palmar arch, dividing into proper palmar digital arteries supplying the adjacent sides of the index and middle fingers.
FJ2343.clinicalCondition: Digital ischemia — small-vessel occlusion here contributes to fingertip ischemia in vasculitis and scleroderma.
FJ2343.clinicalScenario: A woman with systemic sclerosis develops a painful fingertip ulcer; assessment maps digital artery patency in the palmar arch distribution.

FJ1939.name: Right first posterior intercostal artery
FJ1939.details: Branch of the superior intercostal artery (from the costocervical trunk) supplying the first intercostal space, running below the first rib with its vein and nerve.
FJ1939.clinicalCondition: Surgical hazard — lies close to the neck of the first rib and stellate ganglion, at risk during first rib resection for thoracic outlet syndrome.
FJ1939.clinicalScenario: During transaxillary first rib resection, careful subperiosteal dissection protects the first posterior intercostal vessels from troublesome bleeding.

FJ2370.name: Right fourth common palmar digital artery
FJ2370.details: Distal branch of the superficial palmar arch (occasionally supplemented by a persistent median artery) supplying the third webspace and adjacent sides of the ring and little fingers.
FJ2370.clinicalCondition: Variant anatomy — a persistent median artery contributing here is associated with carpal tunnel symptoms and pronator syndrome.
FJ2370.clinicalScenario: Ultrasound in a patient with carpal tunnel syndrome reveals a persistent median artery and bifid median nerve, altering the surgical release plan.

FJ3594.name: Right gastric artery
FJ3594.details: Branch of the proper hepatic artery (variable origin) running along the lesser curvature of the stomach within the lesser omentum, anastomosing with the left gastric artery; supplies the pyloric region.
FJ3594.clinicalCondition: Bleeding peptic ulcer — erosion of this vessel or its branches by a lesser-curvature ulcer causes major upper GI hemorrhage.
FJ3594.clinicalScenario: A patient with NSAID use presents with hematemesis; endoscopy shows a lesser curvature ulcer with a visible vessel, treated with clips and adrenaline injection.

FJ3596.name: Right gastro-epiploic artery
FJ3596.details: Terminal branch of the gastroduodenal artery running along the greater curvature of the stomach within the greater omentum, anastomosing with the left gastro-epiploic artery and giving omental branches.
FJ3596.clinicalCondition: Bypass conduit — the right gastro-epiploic artery is harvested as an arterial graft for coronary bypass to the posterior descending artery.
FJ3596.clinicalScenario: A cardiac surgeon uses the skeletonized right gastro-epiploic artery as an in-situ graft to the PDA in a patient with poor venous conduits.

FJ3604.name: Right inferior epigastric artery
FJ3604.details: Branch of the external iliac artery just above the inguinal ligament, ascending behind the rectus abdominis within the rectus sheath; forms the lateral border of Hesselbach's triangle.
FJ3604.clinicalCondition: Surgical landmark and hazard — separates direct from indirect inguinal hernias and is injured by misplaced laparoscopic ports or rectus sheath hematoma.
FJ3604.clinicalScenario: After laparoscopic surgery, a patient develops a painful abdominal wall swelling; CT shows a rectus sheath hematoma from inferior epigastric artery injury.

FJ2150.name: Right inferior lateral genicular artery
FJ2150.details: Branch of the popliteal artery passing laterally deep to the lateral head of gastrocnemius, supplying the lateral knee joint and joining the genicular anastomosis.
FJ2150.clinicalCondition: Knee collateral network — helps sustain the joint and leg in popliteal disease; vulnerable in lateral knee surgery.
FJ2150.clinicalScenario: During lateral meniscus surgery the arthroscopist notes brisk bleeding from a genicular branch, controlled with careful cautery near the joint line.

FJ2152.name: Right inferior medial genicular artery
FJ2152.details: Branch of the popliteal artery descending medially below the knee joint, supplying the medial joint and upper tibia and joining the genicular anastomosis.
FJ2152.clinicalCondition: Bleeding in knee arthroplasty — genicular branches are coagulated during total knee replacement to reduce postoperative hemarthrosis.
FJ2152.clinicalScenario: A patient develops a tense hemarthrosis after knee replacement; angiography identifies a bleeding medial genicular branch treated by embolization.

FJ3619.name: Right inferior phrenic artery
FJ3619.details: First paired branch of the abdominal aorta (or celiac trunk), ascending on the crus of the diaphragm to supply its inferior surface and giving the superior suprarenal branches.
FJ3619.clinicalCondition: Collateral tumor supply — hepatocellular carcinoma near the dome recruits this artery, requiring its embolization during TACE.
FJ3619.clinicalScenario: Angiography for a dome-of-liver tumor shows significant supply from the right inferior phrenic artery, which is embolized along with the hepatic branches.

FJ3620.name: Right inferior phrenic artery
FJ3620.details: Divides into medial and lateral branches over the undersurface of the right hemidiaphragm, anastomosing with musculophrenic and lower intercostal arteries.
FJ3620.clinicalCondition: Diaphragmatic collateral — enlarges in chronic celiac or hepatic arterial occlusion to support upper abdominal viscera.
FJ3620.clinicalScenario: Follow-up imaging in celiac occlusion shows hypertrophied inferior phrenic collaterals supplying the liver dome region.

FJ3621.name: Right inferior phrenic artery
FJ3621.details: Its superior suprarenal twigs are a principal arterial source to the right suprarenal (adrenal) gland, complementing middle and inferior suprarenal arteries.
FJ3621.clinicalCondition: Adrenal perfusion — relevant in adrenal surgery where multiple small arterial sources cause diffuse oozing rather than a single pedicle bleed.
FJ3621.clinicalScenario: During right adrenalectomy for a pheochromocytoma, the surgeon controls multiple small arterial twigs from the phrenic, aortic and renal sources.

FJ3622.name: Right inferior phrenic artery
FJ3622.details: Crosses the right crus close to the IVC and esophageal opening region, a relation of note in hiatal and diaphragmatic surgery.
FJ3622.clinicalCondition: Iatrogenic bleeding — can be torn during mobilization of the right liver lobe or diaphragmatic hernia repair.
FJ3622.clinicalScenario: During liver mobilization, brisk bleeding from the diaphragmatic surface is traced to an inferior phrenic branch and secured with clips.

FJ3623.name: Right inferior phrenic artery
FJ3623.details: May arise from the celiac trunk, aorta, or occasionally the renal artery; variant origins are common and mapped before upper abdominal interventions.
FJ3623.clinicalCondition: Variant origin awareness — an origin from the renal artery matters in renal embolization and donor nephrectomy planning.
FJ3623.clinicalScenario: Preoperative CT for a living kidney donor shows the inferior phrenic artery arising from the renal artery, modifying the vascular clamping plan.

FJ3624.name: Right inferior phrenic artery
FJ3624.details: Supplies the central tendon periphery and posterolateral diaphragm, with branches contributing to the inferior surface of the pericardium region via anastomoses.
FJ3624.clinicalCondition: Referred shoulder pain link — diaphragmatic irritation in its territory refers pain to the right shoulder via the phrenic nerve (C3–C5).
FJ3624.clinicalScenario: A patient with a subphrenic abscess complains of right shoulder-tip pain, explained by diaphragmatic irritation in the phrenic nerve distribution.

FJ3625.name: Right inferior phrenic artery
FJ3625.details: Gives esophageal and capsular twigs near the bare area of the liver, forming part of the extrahepatic collateral network of the liver.
FJ3625.clinicalCondition: Extrahepatic collateral — parasitized supply to liver tumors from this vessel is a common cause of incomplete chemoembolization.
FJ3625.clinicalScenario: A recurrent liver tumor after TACE is found to draw supply from inferior phrenic collaterals, prompting a repeat targeted embolization session.

FJ3626.name: Right inferior phrenic artery
FJ3626.details: Its terminal branches anastomose across the midline with the left inferior phrenic artery over the central tendon of the diaphragm.
FJ3626.clinicalCondition: Cross-midline collateral — unilateral occlusion rarely ischemizes the diaphragm because of these midline anastomoses.
FJ3626.clinicalScenario: After embolization of the right inferior phrenic artery for tumor supply, diaphragmatic function remains normal thanks to left-sided collateral inflow.

FJ3584.name: Right inferior suprarenal artery
FJ3584.details: Branch of the right renal artery reaching the inferior aspect of the right suprarenal gland, one of three arterial sources (superior, middle, inferior) supplying the gland.
FJ3584.clinicalCondition: Adrenal arterial redundancy — the triple supply means the gland rarely infarcts, but is vulnerable in Waterhouse–Friderichsen hemorrhage.
FJ3584.clinicalScenario: A patient with meningococcal sepsis develops adrenal hemorrhage and acute adrenal insufficiency, requiring immediate stress-dose steroids.

FJ2209.name: Right inferior thyroid artery
FJ2209.details: Branch of the thyrocervical trunk curving medially behind the carotid sheath to supply the posterior thyroid gland; the recurrent laryngeal nerve crosses it near the gland — a variable, surgically critical relation.
FJ2209.clinicalCondition: Thyroid surgery hazard — the nerve's variable relation to this artery is the classic cause of vocal cord palsy after thyroidectomy.
FJ2209.clinicalScenario: After total thyroidectomy, a patient has a breathy voice; laryngoscopy shows a paralyzed right vocal cord from recurrent laryngeal nerve injury near the artery.

FJ2267.name: Right inferior ulnar collateral artery
FJ2267.details: Branch of the brachial artery just above the elbow, descending anterior to the medial epicondyle to join the anterior ulnar recurrent artery in the elbow anastomosis.
FJ2267.clinicalCondition: Elbow collateral — preserves hand perfusion when the brachial artery is occluded or injured at the elbow.
FJ2267.clinicalScenario: In a pulseless pink hand after elbow fracture reduction, Doppler shows collateral flow around the elbow maintaining capillary refill, supporting observation over immediate exploration.

FJ1682.name: Right internal carotid artery
FJ1682.details: Arises at the carotid bifurcation (C4) and ascends without branches in the neck, entering the carotid canal, traversing the cavernous sinus and ending by dividing into anterior and middle cerebral arteries; supplies brain, eye and forehead.
FJ1682.clinicalCondition: Carotid stenosis and dissection — atherosclerosis or traumatic dissection causes embolic stroke and Horner syndrome; occlusion produces major hemispheric infarction.
FJ1682.clinicalScenario: A young woman develops neck pain, a droopy eyelid and then left arm weakness after minor neck trauma; MRI shows right internal carotid dissection with embolic stroke.

FJ3569.name: Right internal iliac artery
FJ3569.details: Smaller terminal branch of the common iliac artery entering the pelvis at the sacroiliac joint, dividing into anterior and posterior divisions supplying the pelvic viscera, perineum, gluteal region and pelvic walls.
FJ3569.clinicalCondition: Pelvic hemorrhage control — surgical ligation or angiographic embolization of this artery controls postpartum and pelvic fracture bleeding.
FJ3569.clinicalScenario: A woman with uncontrollable postpartum hemorrhage fails medical therapy; interventional radiology embolizes both internal iliac arteries and bleeding stops.

FJ1937.name: Right internal thoracic artery
FJ1937.details: Branch of the first part of the subclavian artery descending vertically 1 cm lateral to the sternal edge behind the costal cartilages, ending by dividing into superior epigastric and musculophrenic arteries.
FJ1937.clinicalCondition: Premier bypass conduit — the left/right internal thoracic (mammary) artery graft to the LAD has the best long-term patency in coronary surgery.
FJ1937.clinicalScenario: A triple-vessel disease patient receives a LIMA-to-LAD graft plus a right internal thoracic graft, chosen for superior ten-year patency.

FJ2158.name: Right lateral circumflex femoral artery
FJ2158.details: Large lateral branch of the profunda femoris (occasionally the femoral artery) passing between divisions of the femoral nerve, giving ascending, transverse and descending branches; the descending branch supplies the anterolateral thigh flap.
FJ2158.clinicalCondition: Flap pedicle and knee collateral — its descending branch feeds the ALT flap and anastomoses at the knee with the superior lateral genicular artery.
FJ2158.clinicalScenario: For a head and neck reconstruction, surgeons harvest an anterolateral thigh free flap based on the descending branch of this artery.

FJ1685.name: Right lateral frontobasal artery
FJ1685.details: Cortical branch of the right ACA (orbitofrontal group) supplying the lateral orbital surface of the frontal lobe and gyrus rectus region.
FJ1685.clinicalCondition: Frontal lobe ischemia — small ACA branch infarcts contribute to personality change and disinhibition after anterior circulation stroke.
FJ1685.clinicalScenario: Following anterior communicating aneurysm repair, a patient becomes disinhibited and apathetic; imaging shows orbitofrontal infarction in ACA branch territory.

FJ1686.name: Right lateral frontobasal artery
FJ1686.details: Runs on the orbital surface of the frontal lobe, supplying olfactory region cortex; lies near the olfactory tract, linking its territory to smell pathway lesions.
FJ1686.clinicalCondition: Anosmia in ACA events — basal frontal ischemia or aneurysm surgery here can damage olfactory apparatus causing loss of smell.
FJ1686.clinicalScenario: After clipping of an ACom aneurysm, a patient reports complete loss of smell, attributed to basal frontal retraction and small frontobasal branch injury.

FJ1687.name: Right lateral occipital artery
FJ1687.details: The P3 (quadrigeminal) continuation territory of the right PCA in its lateral occipital distribution, giving anterior, middle and posterior inferior temporal branches to the undersurface of the temporal lobe.
FJ1687.clinicalCondition: Inferior temporal ischemia — occlusion contributes to ventral visual stream deficits and color processing problems.
FJ1687.clinicalScenario: A patient with a PCA stroke cannot name colors despite seeing them; imaging shows inferior temporo-occipital infarction in this distribution.

FJ2159.name: Right lateral plantar artery
FJ2159.details: Larger terminal branch of the posterior tibial artery running diagonally across the sole, then curving medially as the deep plantar arch, completed by the deep plantar branch of dorsalis pedis; supplies most of the sole.
FJ2159.clinicalCondition: Plantar arch perfusion — its patency underlies forefoot viability in diabetic foot disease and guides amputation levels.
FJ2159.clinicalScenario: A diabetic patient with heel and forefoot ulcers has Doppler signals in the lateral plantar artery, supporting a limb-salvage revascularization attempt.

FJ2162.name: Right lateral superior genicular artery
FJ2162.details: Branch of the popliteal artery passing laterally above the knee deep to biceps femoris, supplying the lateral joint and femur and joining the genicular anastomosis.
FJ2162.clinicalCondition: Knee collateral — part of the periarticular network sustaining the leg in femoral/popliteal occlusion; at risk in lateral knee approaches.
FJ2162.clinicalScenario: Angiography in chronic superficial femoral occlusion shows genicular collaterals including this branch bridging flow into the popliteal segment.

FJ2163.name: Right lateral tarsal artery
FJ2163.details: Branch of the dorsalis pedis artery crossing the tarsal bones beneath extensor digitorum brevis, supplying the lateral dorsum of the foot and anastomosing with the arcuate artery.
FJ2163.clinicalCondition: Dorsal foot supply — contributes to extensor digitorum brevis flap perfusion used in foot reconstruction.
FJ2163.clinicalScenario: A plastic surgeon raises a dorsalis pedis flap for ankle coverage, preserving the lateral tarsal branch to keep the flap perfused.

FJ1938.name: Right lateral thoracic artery
FJ1938.details: Branch of the second part of the axillary artery descending along the lateral border of pectoralis minor, supplying pectoral muscles, serratus anterior and the lateral breast.
FJ1938.clinicalCondition: Breast and chest wall supply — relevant in mastectomy flap perfusion and lateral thoracic artery perforator flaps.
FJ1938.clinicalScenario: During mastectomy, the surgeon preserves lateral thoracic perforators where possible to maintain skin flap viability in an immediate reconstruction case.

FJ1924.name: Right lobe branch of right hepatic artery
FJ1924.details: The right hepatic artery's distribution to the right lobe (segments V–VIII), typically arising from the proper hepatic artery within the hepatoduodenal ligament, running posterior to the common hepatic duct.
FJ1924.clinicalCondition: Bile duct ischemia — because the bile duct depends on hepatic arterial flow, injury here causes ischemic strictures after transplant or cholecystectomy.
FJ1924.clinicalScenario: A liver transplant recipient develops multiple biliary strictures; angiography shows hepatic artery stenosis at the anastomosis requiring stenting.

FJ2394.name: Right lobe branch of right hepatic artery
FJ2394.details: Passes behind the biliary confluence and gives the cystic artery usually within Calot's triangle, a relation central to safe cholecystectomy.
FJ2394.clinicalCondition: Replaced right hepatic artery — in ~10% it arises from the SMA and runs behind the pancreas, vulnerable in pancreaticoduodenectomy.
FJ2394.clinicalScenario: Preoperative CT before a Whipple procedure reveals a replaced right hepatic artery from the SMA; the dissection plan is modified to protect it.

FJ1690.name: Right medial frontobasal artery
FJ1690.details: Medial orbitofrontal branch of the right ACA supplying the medial orbital frontal cortex and olfactory bulb region along the basal frontal lobe.
FJ1690.clinicalCondition: Basal frontal ischemia — contributes to apathy and executive dysfunction in ACA territory infarction.
FJ1690.clinicalScenario: An ACA stroke patient shows profound apathy and poor initiation; MRI confirms medial basal frontal involvement including this branch's territory.

FJ1691.name: Right medial occipital artery
FJ1691.details: Terminal P4 distribution of the right PCA supplying the medial occipital lobe, including the calcarine (visual) cortex via its calcarine branch and parieto-occipital branch.
FJ1691.clinicalCondition: PCA stroke — occlusion produces contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing from collateral supply at the occipital pole.
FJ1691.clinicalScenario: A man suddenly cannot see the left half of his visual world but reads the center of the chart fine; MRI shows a right calcarine infarct.

FJ2164.name: Right medial plantar artery
FJ2164.details: Smaller terminal branch of the posterior tibial artery running along the medial side of the sole with the medial plantar nerve, supplying the medial foot and great toe plantar surface.
FJ2164.clinicalCondition: Medial foot perfusion — supplies the medial plantar (instep) flap used for heel and sole reconstruction.
FJ2164.clinicalScenario: A patient with a heel pressure sore is reconstructed with a medial plantar artery flap, chosen for its durable, sensate skin.

FJ2166.name: Right medial superior genicular artery
FJ2166.details: Branch of the popliteal artery passing medially above the knee deep to semimembranosus, supplying the medial joint and distal femur within the genicular anastomosis.
FJ2166.clinicalCondition: Knee collateral and surgical bleeding — encountered in medial knee approaches and arthroplasty, where it may need coagulation.
FJ2166.clinicalScenario: During total knee replacement, the medial superior genicular branch is cauterized as part of routine hemostasis of the periarticular tissues.

FJ2167.name: Right middle genicular artery
FJ2167.details: Small branch from the anterior surface of the popliteal artery piercing the oblique popliteal ligament to supply the cruciate ligaments and synovium inside the knee joint.
FJ2167.clinicalCondition: Intra-articular supply — it nourishes the ACL and PCL; its rupture can contribute to hemarthrosis after cruciate injury.
FJ2167.clinicalScenario: A footballer twists his knee and develops a rapid tense swelling; aspiration confirms hemarthrosis from an ACL tear with intra-articular bleeding.

FJ3586.name: Right middle suprarenal artery
FJ3586.details: Small direct branch of the abdominal aorta at L1 level running laterally over the crus to the medial aspect of the right suprarenal gland.
FJ3586.clinicalCondition: Adrenal supply redundancy — one of three sources making adrenal infarction rare except in fulminant sepsis or antiphospholipid syndrome.
FJ3586.clinicalScenario: A patient with antiphospholipid syndrome presents with abdominal pain and hyponatremia; CT shows bilateral adrenal infarcts including middle suprarenal territories.

FJ1969.name: Right musculophrenic artery
FJ1969.details: One of two terminal branches of the internal thoracic artery, descending obliquely behind the lower costal cartilages, supplying the diaphragm and the seventh to ninth intercostal spaces.
FJ1969.clinicalCondition: Chest wall collateral — anastomoses with lower intercostals and phrenic branches, relevant when the internal thoracic artery is harvested for bypass.
FJ1969.clinicalScenario: After internal thoracic artery harvest for CABG, lower chest wall perfusion is maintained through musculophrenic and intercostal collateral pathways.

FJ1695.name: Right ophthalmic artery
FJ1695.details: First major branch of the internal carotid artery, entering the orbit through the optic canal inferolateral to the optic nerve; gives the central retinal artery and branches to the lacrimal gland, extraocular muscles and ethmoid sinuses.
FJ1695.clinicalCondition: Amaurosis fugax and retinal ischemia — emboli from carotid disease pass through this artery to cause transient or permanent monocular blindness.
FJ1695.clinicalScenario: A man describes a curtain descending over his right eye for two minutes; fundoscopy shows a cholesterol embolus at a retinal bifurcation — a Hollenhorst plaque.

FJ2289.name: Right palmar metacarpal artery
FJ2289.details: One of three small arteries from the deep palmar arch running distally on the interosseous muscles to join the common palmar digital arteries from the superficial arch.
FJ2289.clinicalCondition: Deep–superficial arch link — these junctions provide collateral flow protecting fingers when one arch is injured.
FJ2289.clinicalScenario: After a deep palmar laceration severing the superficial arch, the fingers stay perfused through deep arch connections via the palmar metacarpal arteries.

FJ1699.name: Right pericallosal artery
FJ1699.details: The distal continuation of the right ACA beyond the anterior communicating artery, arching backward in the pericallosal sulcus above the corpus callosum and giving callosomarginal and parietal branches.
FJ1699.clinicalCondition: Distal ACA aneurysm — pericallosal aneurysms rupture causing interhemispheric hemorrhage with leg-predominant deficits.
FJ1699.clinicalScenario: CT after thunderclap headache shows blood along the falx and corpus callosum; angiography reveals a small pericallosal artery aneurysm.

FJ2169.name: Right plantar arch
FJ2169.details: Formed by the lateral plantar artery curving across the sole and completed medially by the deep plantar branch of the dorsalis pedis, lying on the interosseous muscles at the metatarsal bases; gives four plantar metatarsal arteries.
FJ2169.clinicalCondition: Key perfusion index — a complete plantar arch predicts healing of foot wounds and success of distal bypass.
FJ2169.clinicalScenario: Angiography before toe amputation in a diabetic patient demonstrates a complete plantar arch, favoring a limited ray amputation with good healing prospects.

FJ1712.name: Right polar temporal artery
FJ1712.details: Anterior temporal branch of the right PCA arising near its temporal division, supplying the temporal pole and anterior inferior temporal cortex.
FJ1712.clinicalCondition: Temporal pole ischemia — may contribute to semantic and naming deficits when the dominant side is affected.
FJ1712.clinicalScenario: A patient after herpes encephalitis shows bilateral temporal pole damage with loss of word meaning; vascular imaging maps the polar temporal territories involved.

FJ2170.name: Right popliteal artery
FJ2170.details: Continuation of the femoral artery from the adductor hiatus through the popliteal fossa — the deepest structure there — ending at the lower border of popliteus by dividing into anterior tibial and tibioperoneal trunk; pulse palpated deep in the fossa.
FJ2170.clinicalCondition: Popliteal aneurysm and entrapment — aneurysms threaten the leg by thrombosis and embolism; entrapment compresses the artery in young athletes.
FJ2170.clinicalScenario: An elderly man has a pulsatile mass behind the knee and blue toes; ultrasound confirms a popliteal aneurysm with distal embolic occlusion.

FJ2291.name: Right posterior circumflex humeral artery
FJ2291.details: Branch of the third part of the axillary artery passing backward through the quadrangular space with the axillary nerve, winding around the surgical neck of the humerus to supply deltoid and the shoulder joint.
FJ2291.clinicalCondition: Quadrangular space syndrome — compression of this artery and the axillary nerve causes posterior shoulder pain and deltoid weakness in overhead athletes.
FJ2291.clinicalScenario: A volleyball player reports aching posterior shoulder pain and weak abduction; MR angiography shows posterior circumflex humeral artery compression in the quadrangular space.

FJ2292.name: Right posterior circumflex humeral artery
FJ2292.details: Its ascending branch is the principal blood supply to the humeral head, so surgical neck fractures and fracture-dislocations jeopardize humeral head viability.
FJ2292.clinicalCondition: Avascular necrosis risk — disruption of this vessel in proximal humeral fractures predisposes the humeral head to AVN.
FJ2292.clinicalScenario: Follow-up imaging six months after a four-part humeral fracture shows humeral head sclerosis consistent with avascular necrosis from circumflex vessel injury.

FJ1713.name: Right posterior communicating artery
FJ1713.details: Connects the internal carotid artery to the posterior cerebral artery, completing the posterior part of the circle of Willis; the oculomotor nerve runs just inferolateral to it.
FJ1713.clinicalCondition: PCom aneurysm — classically presents with painful third-nerve palsy with a dilated pupil from external compression of CN III.
FJ1713.clinicalScenario: A woman presents with sudden headache, ptosis and a blown pupil; CT angiography reveals a posterior communicating artery aneurysm compressing the oculomotor nerve.

FJ1700.name: Right posterior inferior cerebellar artery
FJ1700.details: Largest branch of the vertebral artery, winding around the medulla to supply the lateral medulla, inferior cerebellum, tonsil and vermis; its medullary branches are critical brainstem perforators.
FJ1700.clinicalCondition: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome — occlusion causes vertigo, dysphagia, Horner syndrome, ipsilateral facial and contralateral body sensory loss.
FJ1700.clinicalScenario: A man suddenly develops vertigo, hoarseness and difficulty swallowing, with loss of pain sensation on the right face and left limbs — classic Wallenberg syndrome.

FJ1701.name: Right posterior inferior cerebellar artery
FJ1701.details: Divided into anterior medullary, lateral medullary, tonsillomedullary, telovelotonsillar and cortical segments as it loops around the cerebellar tonsil — a key microsurgical anatomy reference.
FJ1701.clinicalCondition: PICA aneurysm — aneurysms here present with subarachnoid hemorrhage and lower cranial nerve palsies.
FJ1701.clinicalScenario: CT shows posterior fossa subarachnoid blood; angiography identifies a dissecting aneurysm of the right PICA requiring endovascular treatment.

FJ1702.name: Right posterior inferior cerebellar artery
FJ1702.details: Gives the posterior spinal artery near its origin and supplies the choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle through its medial branches.
FJ1702.clinicalCondition: Cerebellar infarction with swelling — large PICA territory strokes can compress the fourth ventricle causing obstructive hydrocephalus.
FJ1702.clinicalScenario: A patient with a PICA stroke deteriorates on day two with vomiting and drowsiness; CT shows cerebellar swelling compressing the fourth ventricle, needing EVD and decompression.

FJ1703.name: Right posterior inferior cerebellar artery
FJ1703.details: Supplies the inferior vermis and inferolateral cerebellar hemisphere, anastomosing with AICA and superior cerebellar branches at the cerebellar border zones.
FJ1703.clinicalCondition: Cerebellar borderzone ischemia — hypotension can infarct the watershed between PICA and superior cerebellar territories.
FJ1703.clinicalScenario: After prolonged intraoperative hypotension, a patient awakens with gait ataxia; MRI shows borderzone cerebellar infarcts between PICA and SCA distributions.

FJ1704.name: Right posterior inferior cerebellar artery
FJ1704.details: Its lateral medullary branches supply the spinal trigeminal nucleus, nucleus ambiguus, spinothalamic tract and inferior cerebellar peduncle — explaining the crossed signs of its stroke syndrome.
FJ1704.clinicalCondition: Crossed sensory loss explained — ipsilateral facial pain-temperature loss with contralateral body loss is the anatomical signature of PICA occlusion.
FJ1704.clinicalScenario: Neurology examination of a stroke patient demonstrates exactly this crossed pattern, localizing the lesion to the right lateral medulla before imaging confirms it.

FJ1705.name: Right posterior inferior cerebellar artery
FJ1705.details: Origin is variable — it may arise extracranially below the foramen magnum in up to a fifth of people, a variant important in posterior fossa surgery and angiography.
FJ1705.clinicalCondition: Low PICA origin — an extracranial origin risks injury during C1 lateral mass screw placement and upper cervical surgery.
FJ1705.clinicalScenario: Preoperative imaging for atlantoaxial fixation shows a low-lying right PICA origin at C1 level; the screw trajectory is redesigned to avoid it.

FJ1706.name: Right posterior inferior cerebellar artery
FJ1706.details: Loops caudally around the cerebellar tonsil (the tonsillomedullary segment), a landmark used to identify the vessel during foramen magnum decompression.
FJ1706.clinicalCondition: Chiari malformation surgery — the tonsillar loop of PICA lies in the operative field during decompression and must be protected.
FJ1706.clinicalScenario: During suboccipital decompression for Chiari I malformation, the surgeon identifies and preserves the PICA loop draped over the herniated tonsil.

FJ1707.name: Right posterior inferior cerebellar artery
FJ1707.details: Common site of vertebral artery dissection extension; dissection can occlude its origin while sparing the medullary perforators, producing cerebellar-only infarction.
FJ1707.clinicalCondition: Vertebral dissection — presents with neck pain and cerebellar stroke in young patients after minor trauma or neck manipulation.
FJ1707.clinicalScenario: A 35-year-old develops occipital headache and ataxia after a chiropractic session; MRA shows vertebral dissection occluding the PICA origin.

FJ1708.name: Right posterior inferior cerebellar artery
FJ1708.details: Telovelotonsillar segment courses in the cerebellomedullary fissure, supplying the tela choroidea and choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle roof region.
FJ1708.clinicalCondition: Surgical corridor landmark — this segment is mobilized in the trans–cerebellomedullary fissure approach to fourth ventricular tumors.
FJ1708.clinicalScenario: A child with a fourth-ventricular ependymoma undergoes resection where the surgeon works around the telovelotonsillar PICA segments to reach the tumor.

FJ1709.name: Right posterior inferior cerebellar artery
FJ1709.details: Cortical (hemispheric and vermian) branches spread over the suboccipital surface of the cerebellum, ending in borderzone anastomoses with the superior cerebellar artery.
FJ1709.clinicalCondition: Cerebellar stroke recovery — isolated cortical branch infarcts often cause transient vertigo and ataxia with good recovery.
FJ1709.clinicalScenario: An elderly woman presents with isolated vertigo and limb ataxia; MRI shows a small cortical-branch PICA infarct managed conservatively with rehabilitation.

FJ1710.name: Right posterior inferior cerebellar artery
FJ1710.details: When hypoplastic or absent, its territory is taken over by an enlarged AICA — the AICA–PICA dominance spectrum seen on angiography.
FJ1710.clinicalCondition: AICA–PICA variant — misreading this variant can lead to wrong stroke localization and wrong vessel treatment decisions.
FJ1710.clinicalScenario: Angiography in a cerebellar stroke patient shows a dominant AICA supplying the usual PICA territory, explaining the unexpectedly large infarct pattern.

FJ1711.name: Right posterior inferior cerebellar artery
FJ1711.details: Closely related to the glossopharyngeal, vagus and accessory nerve rootlets as it passes between them near the medulla — relevant in neurovascular compression syndromes.
FJ1711.clinicalCondition: Neurovascular conflict — a tortuous PICA can compress the glossopharyngeal nerve causing glossopharyngeal neuralgia.
FJ1711.clinicalScenario: A patient with lancinating throat pain triggered by swallowing has MRI showing a PICA loop compressing the ninth nerve, treated by microvascular decompression.

FJ1715.name: Right posterior inferior cerebellar artery
FJ1715.details: Its choroidal branches supply part of the fourth ventricular choroid plexus, sharing supply with AICA branches near the lateral recess and foramen of Luschka.
FJ1715.clinicalCondition: Posterior fossa bleeding source — distal PICA aneurysm rupture can present as isolated fourth-ventricular hemorrhage.
FJ1715.clinicalScenario: A patient presents with severe headache and vomiting; CT shows blood confined to the fourth ventricle from a ruptured distal PICA aneurysm.

FJ1727.name: Right posterior medial choroidal artery
FJ1727.details: Branch of the P2 segment of the PCA curving around the midbrain within the ambient cistern to supply the choroid plexus of the third ventricle, midbrain and medial thalamus.
FJ1727.clinicalCondition: Deep cerebral ischemia — small branch occlusion contributes to thalamic and midbrain lacunar syndromes.
FJ1727.clinicalScenario: A hypertensive patient develops vertical gaze difficulty and memory lapses; MRI shows a small infarct in the medial thalamic territory of this artery.

FJ1716.name: Right posterior parietal artery
FJ1716.details: Posterior cortical branch of the right MCA supplying the posterior parietal lobe, including the angular and supramarginal region watershed with PCA branches.
FJ1716.clinicalCondition: Non-dominant parietal stroke — occlusion causes hemispatial neglect and constructional apraxia.
FJ1716.clinicalScenario: After a right parietal stroke, a patient eats only from the right side of the plate and shaves half his face, demonstrating left-sided neglect.

FJ2172.name: Right posterior tibial artery
FJ2172.details: Larger terminal branch of the popliteal artery descending in the posterior compartment deep to soleus, passing behind the medial malleolus (where its pulse is felt) and dividing into medial and lateral plantar arteries.
FJ2172.clinicalCondition: Key pulse in limb assessment — loss of the posterior tibial pulse signals peripheral arterial disease; the vessel is a distal bypass target.
FJ2172.clinicalScenario: A patient with rest pain and a gangrenous toe has an occluded superficial femoral artery; a femoro–posterior tibial bypass is planned for limb salvage.

FJ2293.name: Right posterior ulnar recurrent artery
FJ2293.details: Branch of the ulnar artery ascending behind the medial epicondyle between its two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris region, anastomosing with the superior ulnar collateral artery around the elbow.
FJ2293.clinicalCondition: Elbow anastomosis — completes the periarticular network and lies near the ulnar nerve, relevant in elbow surgery.
FJ2293.clinicalScenario: During ulnar nerve transposition at the elbow, the surgeon preserves the posterior recurrent and collateral vessels feeding the nerve's vascular leash.

FJ1724.name: Right prefrontal artery
FJ1724.details: Cortical branch of the right MCA (candelabra group) ascending over the frontal operculum to supply the anterior prefrontal cortex.
FJ1724.clinicalCondition: Frontal opercular ischemia — contributes to executive dysfunction and, on the dominant side, expressive language deficits with MCA strokes.
FJ1724.clinicalScenario: A patient with an MCA branch occlusion shows impaired planning and verbal fluency; imaging localizes infarction to the right prefrontal cortical territory.

FJ3019.name: Right pulmonary artery
FJ3019.details: Branch of the pulmonary trunk; passes behind the ascending aorta and SVC, below the carina, into the right hilum, carrying deoxygenated blood to the right lung.
FJ3019.clinicalCondition: Pulmonary embolism — venous thrombus lodges here, abruptly blocking right lung perfusion and straining the right ventricle.
FJ3019.clinicalScenario: A 68-year-old develops sudden breathlessness and pleuritic pain three days after hip replacement; CT pulmonary angiography shows a large embolus occluding the right pulmonary artery.

FJ2294.name: Right radial artery
FJ2294.details: Continuation of the brachial artery from the cubital fossa; runs beneath brachioradialis, lies superficial at the wrist lateral to flexor carpi radialis, and completes the deep palmar arch.
FJ2294.clinicalCondition: Arterial line and graft harvest site — hand ischaemia follows if ulnar collateral flow through the palmar arches is inadequate.
FJ2294.clinicalScenario: An ICU nurse palpates the radial pulse and performs an Allen test before inserting an arterial line into an unconscious patient's right wrist.

FJ2295.name: Right radial recurrent artery
FJ2295.details: Small branch of the radial artery just below the elbow; ascends between brachioradialis and brachialis to anastomose with the radial collateral branch of profunda brachii at the elbow.
FJ2295.clinicalCondition: Elbow collateral circulation — this anastomosis helps maintain forearm perfusion when the brachial artery is injured or occluded above the elbow.
FJ2295.clinicalScenario: After a supracondylar humeral fracture, a child's hand remains warm and pink despite a feeble brachial pulse, thanks to collateral flow through the radial recurrent anastomosis.

FJ2297.name: Right recurrent interosseous artery
FJ2297.details: Branch of the posterior interosseous artery near its origin; ascends deep to anconeus to anastomose with the middle collateral branch of profunda brachii behind the elbow.
FJ2297.clinicalCondition: Elbow collateral circulation — contributes a posterior route preserving forearm blood supply in brachial artery occlusion.
FJ2297.clinicalScenario: During surgical exposure of an injured elbow, the recurrent interosseous branch is identified and preserved to protect the collateral network around the joint.

FJ2038.name: Right renal artery
FJ2038.details: Lateral branch of the abdominal aorta at L1, just below the SMA; passes behind the IVC (longer than the left), enters the hilum, and divides into segmental end-arteries.
FJ2038.clinicalCondition: Renal artery stenosis — atherosclerosis or fibromuscular dysplasia narrows the artery, driving renin-mediated secondary hypertension.
FJ2038.clinicalScenario: A 58-year-old with resistant hypertension and an abdominal bruit has tight right renal artery stenosis on Doppler; blood pressure improves after angioplasty and stenting.

FJ2344.name: Right second common palmar digital artery
FJ2344.details: Branch of the superficial palmar arch running distally toward the second webspace, where it divides into proper palmar digital arteries for adjacent sides of index and middle fingers.
FJ2344.clinicalCondition: Digital ischaemia — laceration, embolus or thrombosis here threatens the facing sides of the two adjacent fingers.
FJ2344.clinicalScenario: A machinist lacerates his palm at the second webspace; brisk bleeding from the common palmar digital artery is controlled while finger perfusion is assessed.

FJ1950.name: Right second posterior intercostal artery
FJ1950.details: Branch of the superior intercostal artery descending into the second intercostal space; runs in the costal groove with its vein and nerve, supplying the chest wall.
FJ1950.clinicalCondition: Intercostal bleeding at thoracentesis — groove vessels are injured when a needle passes too close to the lower rib's upper edge wrongly.
FJ1950.clinicalScenario: During pleural aspiration for a right effusion, the needle is walked over the upper border of the rib below to spare the second intercostal neurovascular bundle.

FJ1677.name: Right splenial artery
FJ1677.details: Branch of the terminal (P4) part of the posterior cerebral artery curving around the splenium of the corpus callosum, supplying the splenium and adjacent precuneus.
FJ1677.clinicalCondition: Splenial infarction — rare PCA-territory lesion disconnecting the hemispheres and impairing interhemispheric visual transfer.
FJ1677.clinicalScenario: An elderly patient with a posterior cerebral artery stroke cannot name objects shown only in the left visual field, suggesting splenial involvement.

FJ1678.name: Right splenial artery
FJ1678.details: Terminal cortical branch of the right posterior cerebral artery reaching the splenium; supplies posterior callosal fibres linking the occipital and parietal lobes across the midline.
FJ1678.clinicalCondition: Callosal disconnection syndrome — the lesion isolates right visual cortex from left-hemisphere language areas.
FJ1678.clinicalScenario: After PCA occlusion, a patient reads words normally from the right visual field but fails with left-field words, localising damage to the splenium and its arterial supply.

FJ3579.name: Right subclavian artery
FJ3579.details: Arises from the brachiocephalic trunk behind the right sternoclavicular joint; arches over the first rib, its parts defined by scalenus anterior, becoming axillary at the rib's lateral border.
FJ3579.clinicalCondition: Subclavian steal syndrome — proximal stenosis reverses vertebral artery flow, causing arm claudication with posterior-circulation symptoms.
FJ3579.clinicalScenario: A 65-year-old reports dizziness when using his right arm; its blood pressure is 30 mmHg lower, and Doppler shows reversed right vertebral artery flow.

FJ1967.name: Right subcostal artery
FJ1967.details: Lowest paired branch of the thoracic aorta, accompanying the T12 (subcostal) nerve below the 12th rib across quadratus lumborum, supplying the posterior abdominal wall.
FJ1967.clinicalCondition: Surgical landmark — the subcostal neurovascular bundle is vulnerable in flank and lumbar incisions, risking bleeding and wall denervation.
FJ1967.clinicalScenario: During a posterior approach to the kidney, the surgeon identifies the subcostal bundle below the right 12th rib and protects it to avoid postoperative flank numbness.

FJ2298.name: Right subscapular artery
FJ2298.details: Largest branch of the third part of the axillary artery; descends on subscapularis, gives the circumflex scapular branch, then continues as the thoracodorsal artery.
FJ2298.clinicalCondition: Scapular collateral pathway — this anastomotic route around the scapula sustains the arm when the axillary artery is occluded.
FJ2298.clinicalScenario: In chronic axillary artery occlusion, angiography shows a hypertrophied subscapular–circumflex scapular collateral keeping the patient's arm viable before bypass planning.

FJ2308.name: Right superficial cervical artery
FJ2308.details: Superficial branch of the transverse cervical artery ascending across the posterior triangle deep to trapezius, supplying trapezius and the skin and muscles of the neck.
FJ2308.clinicalCondition: Posterior triangle bleeding — encountered and ligated during neck dissection or lymph node biopsy in this region.
FJ2308.clinicalScenario: While excising a suspicious posterior triangle lymph node, the surgeon ligates a bleeding superficial cervical branch while protecting the spinal accessory nerve.

FJ3614.name: Right superficial epigastric artery
FJ3614.details: Small branch of the femoral artery just below the inguinal ligament; pierces the fascia lata and ascends in superficial fascia toward the umbilicus, supplying lower abdominal wall skin.
FJ3614.clinicalCondition: Flap design landmark — its territory and course are used when planning groin and lower abdominal skin flaps.
FJ3614.clinicalScenario: A plastic surgeon maps the superficial epigastric artery with handheld Doppler before raising a groin flap for hand reconstruction.

FJ2179.name: Right superficial medial plantar artery
FJ2179.details: Superficial branch of the medial plantar artery (from posterior tibial) running beneath abductor hallucis, supplying medial sole skin and contributing branches to the great toe.
FJ2179.clinicalCondition: Diabetic forefoot perfusion — medial plantar flow contributes to healing potential of medial forefoot and great-toe ulcers.
FJ2179.clinicalScenario: A diabetic patient with a medial forefoot ulcer has audible plantar Doppler flow, supporting conservative offloading and wound care rather than revascularisation.

FJ2300.name: Right superficial palmar arterial arch
FJ2300.details: Mainly the continuation of the ulnar artery in the palm, completed laterally by the superficial palmar branch of the radial artery; lies deep to the palmar aponeurosis, giving common palmar digital arteries.
FJ2300.clinicalCondition: Allen test — a complete, patent arch guarantees finger perfusion if the radial artery is cannulated or harvested.
FJ2300.clinicalScenario: Before harvesting the radial artery for coronary bypass grafting, a modified Allen test confirms the superficial palmar arch fills the hand from the ulnar artery alone.

FJ1726.name: Right superior cerebellar artery
FJ1726.details: Branch of the basilar artery just before its bifurcation, passing below the oculomotor nerve around the midbrain to supply the superior cerebellum and upper pons/midbrain tegmentum.
FJ1726.clinicalCondition: Superior cerebellar artery infarction — produces ipsilateral limb ataxia with contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation.
FJ1726.clinicalScenario: A patient presents with vertigo, right-sided limb clumsiness and loss of pain sensation over the left body; MRI shows infarction in the right superior cerebellar territory.

FJ1936.name: Right superior epigastric artery
FJ1936.details: Terminal branch of the internal thoracic artery descending into the rectus sheath behind rectus abdominis, anastomosing with the inferior epigastric artery and supplying the upper abdominal wall.
FJ1936.clinicalCondition: Rectus sheath haematoma — branch rupture bleeds into the sheath, producing a painful mass mimicking an acute abdomen.
FJ1936.clinicalScenario: An anticoagulated patient develops a painful right upper abdominal mass after violent coughing; CT confirms a rectus sheath haematoma from a superior epigastric branch.

FJ1935.name: Right superior intercostal artery
FJ1935.details: Branch of the costocervical trunk from the second part of the subclavian artery; descends over the necks of the first two ribs, giving the first and second posterior intercostal arteries.
FJ1935.clinicalCondition: Coarctation collateral — hugely dilated intercostal branches bypass an aortic coarctation and erode rib lower borders.
FJ1935.clinicalScenario: An adult with undiagnosed aortic coarctation shows inferior rib notching on chest radiography from enlarged superior intercostal collateral arteries.

FJ2373.name: Right superior ulnar collateral artery
FJ2373.details: Branch of the brachial artery in the mid-arm descending with the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle, anastomosing with ulnar recurrent branches around the elbow.
FJ2373.clinicalCondition: Elbow collateral circulation — sustains forearm and ulnar nerve perfusion when the brachial artery is compromised.
FJ2373.clinicalScenario: During cubital tunnel release, the superior ulnar collateral artery is found beside the ulnar nerve and carefully preserved with it.

FJ2303.name: Right suprascapular artery
FJ2303.details: Branch of the thyrocervical trunk passing laterally above the suprascapular ligament into the supraspinous fossa, then through the greater scapular notch to supply supraspinatus and infraspinatus.
FJ2303.clinicalCondition: Scapular anastomosis and notch landmark — 'artery above, nerve below' the ligament guides surgery for suprascapular nerve entrapment.
FJ2303.clinicalScenario: A patient has suprascapular notch decompression; the surgeon recalls the artery passes above the ligament while the nerve passes beneath it.

FJ3617.name: Right testicular artery
FJ3617.details: Paired anterior branch of the abdominal aorta at L2; descends retroperitoneally, crosses the ureter, and enters the inguinal canal within the spermatic cord to supply testis and epididymis.
FJ3617.clinicalCondition: Testicular torsion — cord twisting strangles this artery; salvage depends on detorsion within about six hours.
FJ3617.clinicalScenario: During emergency exploration for suspected torsion, the cord is untwisted and testicular arterial inflow checked to judge whether the testis remains viable.

FJ1675.name: Right thalamogeniculate artery
FJ1675.details: Posterolateral branch of the P2 segment of the posterior cerebral artery supplying the lateral thalamus, including the ventral posterolateral nucleus and lateral geniculate region.
FJ1675.clinicalCondition: Thalamic pain syndrome (Dejerine–Roussy) — lateral thalamic infarct causes contralateral sensory loss followed by burning neuropathic pain.
FJ1675.clinicalScenario: Weeks after a small thalamic stroke, a patient develops burning pain and allodynia over the left arm and leg, classic for thalamic pain syndrome.

FJ1720.name: Right thalamoperforating artery
FJ1720.details: Posteromedial perforating branch from the P1 segment of the posterior cerebral artery, entering the posterior perforated substance to supply the medial thalamus and rostral midbrain.
FJ1720.clinicalCondition: Paramedian thalamic infarction — occlusion produces hypersomnolence, memory loss and vertical gaze palsy.
FJ1720.clinicalScenario: A man found excessively sleepy, with upgaze paralysis and amnesia, has a paramedian thalamic infarct from thalamoperforating artery occlusion on MRI.

FJ2345.name: Right third common palmar digital artery
FJ2345.details: Branch of the superficial palmar arch travelling toward the third webspace, dividing into proper palmar digital arteries for adjacent sides of the middle and ring fingers.
FJ2345.clinicalCondition: Webspace ischaemia risk — injury here endangers the facing halves of two neighbouring fingers.
FJ2345.clinicalScenario: A glass injury at the third webspace bleeds briskly; exploration finds the third common palmar digital artery divided and repairs it to preserve ring-finger perfusion.

FJ2305.name: Right thoracodorsal artery
FJ2305.details: Continuation of the subscapular artery onto the costal surface of latissimus dorsi, running with the thoracodorsal nerve; forms the vascular pedicle of the latissimus dorsi flap.
FJ2305.clinicalCondition: Flap pedicle at risk — damage during axillary node clearance removes the latissimus flap reconstructive option.
FJ2305.clinicalScenario: During axillary clearance for breast cancer, the thoracodorsal pedicle is carefully preserved so a latissimus dorsi flap remains available for reconstruction.

FJ2307.name: Right thyrocervical trunk
FJ2307.details: Short branch of the first part of the subclavian artery, lateral to the vertebral origin; quickly divides into inferior thyroid, suprascapular and transverse cervical arteries.
FJ2307.clinicalCondition: Neck surgery landmark — its branches cross the operative field in thyroidectomy and neck dissection and may bleed briskly.
FJ2307.clinicalScenario: At thyroidectomy, the surgeon traces the inferior thyroid artery back to the thyrocervical trunk for control while protecting the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

FJ2309.name: Right transverse cervical artery
FJ2309.details: Branch of the thyrocervical trunk crossing the posterior triangle above the brachial plexus, deep to trapezius, dividing into superficial cervical and dorsal scapular branches.
FJ2309.clinicalCondition: Trapezius flap pedicle — also at risk of injury during posterior triangle lymph node biopsy.
FJ2309.clinicalScenario: A reconstructive surgeon raises a trapezius flap for a neck defect, basing it on the transverse cervical artery confirmed patent on preoperative imaging.

FJ2310.name: Right ulnar artery
FJ2310.details: Larger terminal branch of the brachial artery from the cubital fossa; descends beneath forearm flexors, enters the hand through Guyon's canal beside the pisiform, chiefly forming the superficial palmar arch.
FJ2310.clinicalCondition: Hypothenar hammer syndrome — repeated palm trauma thromboses the artery against the hook of the hamate.
FJ2310.clinicalScenario: A carpenter who uses his palm as a hammer develops cold, painful right ring and little fingers; imaging shows ulnar artery thrombosis at the hamate.

FJ2973.name: Right upper lobar artery
FJ2973.details: First major branch of the right pulmonary artery at the hilum, arising eparterially (above the bronchus) to supply the apical, posterior and anterior segments of the right upper lobe.
FJ2973.clinicalCondition: Segmental pulmonary embolism — emboli lodging here produce upper-lobe perfusion defects and pleuritic pain.
FJ2973.clinicalScenario: A breathless patient after a long-haul flight has a wedge-shaped right upper-lobe perfusion defect; CT confirms embolus in the right upper lobar arterial branch.

FJ1725.name: Right vertebral artery
FJ1725.details: First branch of the subclavian artery; ascends through the foramina transversaria of C6–C1, curves over the atlas, pierces the dura, and joins its fellow to form the basilar artery.
FJ1725.clinicalCondition: Vertebral artery dissection — intimal tear after neck trauma or manipulation causes posterior-circulation stroke in young patients.
FJ1725.clinicalScenario: A 40-year-old develops occipital headache and vertigo days after whiplash; angiography shows right vertebral artery dissection with cerebellar infarction.

FJ2646.name: Second right anterior branch of anterior interventricular branch of left coronary artery
FJ2646.details: Second diagonal branch of the anterior interventricular (LAD) artery, coursing over the anterolateral wall of the left ventricle and supplying that region.
FJ2646.clinicalCondition: Diagonal branch stenosis — produces anterolateral ischaemia; size decides whether it warrants grafting alongside the LAD.
FJ2646.clinicalScenario: Angiography in a patient with exertional angina shows a tight lesion in the second diagonal branch with a normal LAD trunk, managed after heart-team review.

FJ2736.name: Second septal branch of right posterior interventricular artery
FJ2736.details: Septal perforator from the posterior interventricular (posterior descending) artery entering the posterior interventricular septum; contributes supply to the posterior septum and AV conduction region.
FJ2736.clinicalCondition: Conduction ischaemia — posterior descending territory infarction involving septal branches can precipitate AV block.
FJ2736.clinicalScenario: Following an inferior myocardial infarction, a patient develops transient complete heart block attributed to ischaemia of septal branches from the posterior descending artery.

FJ2732.name: Septal branch of anterior interventricular artery
FJ2732.details: Perforating branch of the LAD diving at right angles into the interventricular septum, supplying its anterior two-thirds, including the right bundle branch and left anterior fascicle.
FJ2732.clinicalCondition: Septal infarction — proximal LAD occlusion infarcts the septum and commonly causes bundle branch block.
FJ2732.clinicalScenario: An anterior STEMI patient develops a new right bundle branch block; the culprit proximal LAD lesion threatens the septal perforators supplying conduction tissue.

FJ2733.name: Septal branch of anterior interventricular artery
FJ2733.details: One of several septal perforators arising along the LAD's course in the anterior interventricular groove, penetrating deeply to nourish the septal myocardium.
FJ2733.clinicalCondition: Post-infarct ventricular septal rupture — septal branch territory necrosis can perforate days after anterior MI.
FJ2733.clinicalScenario: Four days after an anterior infarct, a patient develops a harsh new murmur and shock; echocardiography shows septal rupture in perforator territory.

FJ2734.name: Septal branch of anterior interventricular artery
FJ2734.details: Septal perforating branch of the anterior interventricular artery; the first (largest) perforator also contributes to the AV bundle region via septal anastomoses.
FJ2734.clinicalCondition: Septal ischaemia in LAD disease — reduced perforator flow contributes to septal hypokinesis on imaging.
FJ2734.clinicalScenario: Stress echocardiography in a patient with mid-LAD stenosis shows septal hypokinesis, reflecting compromised septal perforator supply during exertion.

FJ2091.name: Set of calcaneal branches of posterior tibial artery
FJ2091.details: Medial and lateral calcaneal branches of the posterior tibial artery forming an anastomotic network over the calcaneal tuberosity, supplying the heel skin and fat pad.
FJ2091.clinicalCondition: Heel ulceration — calcaneal network perfusion determines whether heel pressure sores in neuropathic feet heal or progress.
FJ2091.clinicalScenario: A neuropathic diabetic patient with a heel pressure sore has intact calcaneal Doppler flow, supporting conservative offloading rather than amputation.

FJ2195.name: Set of calcaneal branches of posterior tibial artery
FJ2195.details: Calcaneal twigs of the posterior tibial artery (with peroneal contributions) ramifying beneath the tendo calcaneus to supply the posterior heel and adjacent plantar skin.
FJ2195.clinicalCondition: Heel flap and amputation planning — preserved calcaneal flow is essential for posterior flap viability in below-knee amputation.
FJ2195.clinicalScenario: Before a below-knee amputation, the surgeon confirms posterior tibial calcaneal branch flow so the long posterior flap will survive.

FJ2092.name: Set of common plantar digital arteries
FJ2092.details: Branches of the plantar arch (from the lateral plantar artery) running distally between the metatarsals, each dividing into proper plantar digital arteries and joined by perforating branches.
FJ2092.clinicalCondition: Forefoot ischaemia — embolic or diabetic occlusion here produces painful blue toes and distal gangrene.
FJ2092.clinicalScenario: A patient with atrial fibrillation presents with a painful blue second toe; an embolus lodged in a common plantar digital artery is suspected.

FJ2196.name: Set of common plantar digital arteries
FJ2196.details: Distal divisions of the plantar arch in the forefoot, coursing in the intermetatarsal spaces toward the webs and bifurcating to supply adjacent toes.
FJ2196.clinicalCondition: Critical limb ischaemia assessment — forefoot runoff through these arteries influences toe salvage decisions.
FJ2196.clinicalScenario: Angiography in a patient with a non-healing forefoot ulcer shows patent common plantar digital arteries, favouring toe-sparing debridement over amputation.

FJ2093.name: Set of dorsal digital arteries
FJ2093.details: Small arteries on the dorsum of the toes derived from the dorsal metatarsal system, supplying dorsal skin and nail beds and anastomosing with plantar digital arteries distally.
FJ2093.clinicalCondition: Toe perfusion assessment — dorsal digital flow supplements plantar supply and is checked before toe surgery.
FJ2093.clinicalScenario: Before excising a subungual lesion, the surgeon confirms dorsal and plantar digital flow to the toe with a handheld Doppler.

FJ2197.name: Set of dorsal digital arteries
FJ2197.details: Paired small arteries along the dorsal aspects of the fingers from the dorsal metacarpal arteries, supplying the dorsal skin, nail fold and distal phalanx region.
FJ2197.clinicalCondition: Raynaud phenomenon — digital vasospasm involving these and palmar digital arteries causes triphasic colour change.
FJ2197.clinicalScenario: A young woman with Raynaud phenomenon shows white-blue-red colour changes in cold weather, with normal digital arterial flow between attacks.

FJ2318.name: Set of dorsal digital arteries
