FJ2435.details: One of three semilunar cusps guarding the aortic orifice; its pocket-like sinus fills in diastole, snapping the valve shut and preventing reflux into the left ventricle.
FJ2435.clinicalCondition: Aortic regurgitation — cusp prolapse or destruction permits diastolic backflow into the left ventricle.
FJ2435.clinicalScenario: A 68-year-old with past rheumatic fever has a blowing early diastolic murmur and wide pulse pressure; echo shows a prolapsing aortic cusp.

FJ2420.name: Anterior leaflet of mitral valve
FJ2420.details: Larger mitral leaflet facing the aortic valve, in fibrous continuity with it; chordae tendineae from both papillary muscles anchor its free edge during systole.
FJ2420.clinicalCondition: Mitral valve prolapse — leaflet billows into the left atrium, causing late systolic murmur.
FJ2420.clinicalScenario: A young woman with palpitations has a midsystolic click; echo shows anterior leaflet prolapse with mild mitral regurgitation.

FJ2421.name: Anterior leaflet of tricuspid valve
FJ2421.details: Largest tricuspid leaflet, between right atrium and ventricle; chordae attach to the anterior papillary muscle; prevents systolic reflux into the right atrium.
FJ2421.clinicalCondition: Ebstein anomaly — leaflet displaced apically into ventricle, causing severe tricuspid regurgitation.
FJ2421.clinicalScenario: A cyanotic newborn with massive cardiomegaly and a holosystolic murmur has downward-displaced tricuspid leaflets on echo.

FJ2425.name: Cavity of left atrium
FJ2425.details: Chamber receiving the four pulmonary veins; contains the trabeculated left atrial appendage; smooth-walled posteriorly; empties through the mitral valve into the left ventricle.
FJ2425.clinicalCondition: Atrial appendage thrombus — blood stasis in fibrillation forms clots causing embolic stroke.
FJ2425.clinicalScenario: An elderly man with an irregular pulse develops sudden right-sided weakness; imaging shows thrombus in the left atrial appendage.

FJ2422.name: Cavity of left ventricle
FJ2422.details: Main pumping chamber receiving blood through the mitral valve and ejecting through the aortic valve; lined by trabeculae carneae and housing two papillary muscles.
FJ2422.clinicalCondition: Left ventricular hypertrophy — chronic pressure overload thickens the wall, impairing diastolic filling.
FJ2422.clinicalScenario: A hypertensive man with exertional dyspnea has concentric left ventricular thickening with preserved ejection fraction on echo.

FJ2424.name: Cavity of right atrium
FJ2424.details: Chamber receiving the superior and inferior venae cavae and coronary sinus; contains crista terminalis, fossa ovalis, and the SA node near the SVC opening.
FJ2424.clinicalCondition: Atrial septal defect — left-to-right shunt enlarges the right atrium and pulmonary circulation.
FJ2424.clinicalScenario: A child with a fixed split second heart sound and flow murmur has a secundum ASD with right atrial enlargement on echo.

FJ2423.name: Cavity of right ventricle
FJ2423.details: Crescentic chamber receiving tricuspid inflow and ejecting via the infundibulum through the pulmonary valve; the moderator band carries the right bundle branch.
FJ2423.clinicalCondition: Pulmonary hypertension — chronic pressure overload hypertrophies, then fails, the thin-walled ventricle.
FJ2423.clinicalScenario: A COPD patient with ankle edema and raised JVP has a dilated, hypertrophied right ventricle on echo.

FJ1731.name: Fourth ventricle
FJ1731.details: Diamond-shaped CSF cavity between pons and medulla anteriorly and cerebellum posteriorly; drains through the median and two lateral apertures into the subarachnoid space.
FJ1731.clinicalCondition: Medulloblastoma — childhood posterior fossa tumor obstructs CSF flow, causing hydrocephalus.
FJ1731.clinicalScenario: A six-year-old with morning headaches, vomiting, and papilledema has a midline cerebellar mass compressing the fourth ventricle on MRI.

FJ1752.name: Interventricular foramen
FJ1752.details: Short channel (of Monro) connecting each lateral ventricle to the third ventricle, bounded by fornix and thalamus; CSF passes through toward the cerebral aqueduct.
FJ1752.clinicalCondition: Colloid cyst — benign cyst at the foramen causes intermittent obstructive hydrocephalus.
FJ1752.clinicalScenario: A young adult with positional headaches and one drop attack has a hyperdense lesion at the foramen of Monro on CT.

FJ2417.name: Left anterior cusp of pulmonary valve
FJ2417.details: One of three semilunar cusps of the pulmonary valve at the right ventricular outflow tract; prevents diastolic backflow from the pulmonary trunk into the ventricle.
FJ2417.clinicalCondition: Pulmonary regurgitation — cusp damage after endocarditis or surgical repair leaks blood into the RV.
FJ2417.clinicalScenario: A man repaired for tetralogy of Fallot in childhood now shows free pulmonary regurgitation and right ventricular dilation on echo.

FJ1767.name: Left lateral ventricle
FJ1767.details: C-shaped CSF cavity within the left cerebral hemisphere with frontal, body, occipital, and temporal parts; choroid plexus produces CSF; drains via the interventricular foramen.
FJ1767.clinicalCondition: Intraventricular hemorrhage — blood within the ventricle, common in prematurity, risks hydrocephalus.
FJ1767.clinicalScenario: A premature neonate with falling hematocrit and bulging fontanelle shows blood filling the left lateral ventricle on cranial ultrasound.

FJ2426.name: Left posterior cusp of aortic valve
FJ2426.details: Semilunar cusp of the aortic valve on the left side; the left coronary artery arises from the aorta just above its sinus; supports competent diastolic closure.
FJ2426.clinicalCondition: Infective endocarditis — vegetations on the cusp risk systemic emboli and valve destruction.
FJ2426.clinicalScenario: An IV drug user with fever and a new diastolic murmur has a vegetation on an aortic cusp with severe regurgitation.

FJ2427.name: Posterior cusp of pulmonary valve
FJ2427.details: One of three semilunar cusps of the pulmonary valve; its sinus fills in diastole so the cusps coapt and block reflux from the pulmonary trunk.
FJ2427.clinicalCondition: Pulmonary valve stenosis — fused cusps obstruct right ventricular outflow, producing ejection murmur.
FJ2427.clinicalScenario: A child with exertional dyspnea and a harsh systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border has doming pulmonary cusps on echo.

FJ2432.name: Posterior leaflet of mitral valve
FJ2432.details: Smaller, scalloped (P1–P3) mitral leaflet attached to the posterior annulus; receives chordae from both papillary muscles and coapts with the anterior leaflet in systole.
FJ2432.clinicalCondition: Mitral annular calcification — calcium stiffens the posterior annulus in elderly patients.
FJ2432.clinicalScenario: An elderly diabetic woman has dense posterior annular calcification with mild mitral stenosis on echo.

FJ2433.name: Posterior leaflet of tricuspid valve
FJ2433.details: Smallest tricuspid leaflet along the inferior annulus; chordae attach to the posterior papillary muscle; coapts with the other leaflets to prevent reflux into the right atrium.
FJ2433.clinicalCondition: Functional tricuspid regurgitation — RV dilation stretches the annulus so normal leaflets fail coaptation.
FJ2433.clinicalScenario: A patient with pulmonary hypertension and a pulsatile liver has severe tricuspid regurgitation despite structurally normal leaflets.

FJ2434.name: Right anterior cusp of pulmonary valve
FJ2434.details: Anterior semilunar cusp of the pulmonary valve at the right ventricular outflow tract, just below the pulmonary trunk bifurcation; guards the pulmonary orifice in diastole.
FJ2434.clinicalCondition: Pulmonary valve endocarditis — rare infection, usually with IV drug use or congenital disease.
FJ2434.clinicalScenario: A febrile IV drug user with septic pulmonary infiltrates has a vegetation on a pulmonary valve cusp on echo.

FJ1814.name: Right lateral ventricle
FJ1814.details: C-shaped CSF cavity within the right cerebral hemisphere; choroid plexus produces CSF; drains through the right interventricular foramen into the third ventricle.
FJ1814.clinicalCondition: Obstructive hydrocephalus — blocked drainage dilates the ventricle and raises intracranial pressure.
FJ1814.clinicalScenario: A man with morning headaches and papilledema shows a dilated right lateral ventricle from foraminal obstruction on CT.

FJ2431.name: Right posterior cusp of aortic valve
FJ2431.details: Posterior (non-coronary) semilunar cusp of the aortic valve; no coronary artery arises above it; it lies close to the interatrial septum and conduction tissue.
FJ2431.clinicalCondition: Aortic root abscess — endocarditis here invades the conduction system causing heart block.
FJ2431.clinicalScenario: A man with prosthetic valve endocarditis develops new AV block; echo shows an abscess beside the posterior aortic cusp.

FJ2436.name: Septal leaflet of tricuspid valve
FJ2436.details: Tricuspid leaflet attached directly to the ventricular septum by short chordae; lies close to the AV node and bundle of His within the septum.
FJ2436.clinicalCondition: Ebstein anomaly — septal leaflet displaced downward, atrializing part of the right ventricle.
FJ2436.clinicalScenario: A teenager with cyanosis and palpitations has an apically displaced septal leaflet and a huge right atrium on echo.

FJ1730.name: Third ventricle
FJ1730.details: Slit-like midline CSF cavity within the diencephalon between the two thalami; receives the foramina of Monro anteriorly and continues into the cerebral aqueduct posteriorly.
FJ1730.clinicalCondition: Aqueductal stenosis — blocked outflow dilates the lateral and third ventricles.
FJ1730.clinicalScenario: An infant with a rapidly enlarging head and sunset eyes shows dilated lateral and third ventricles with a normal fourth on MRI.

FJ2438.name: Wall of left atrium
FJ2438.details: Thin, mainly smooth wall receiving the pulmonary veins; the appendage portion is ridged by pectinate muscles; the posterior wall lies directly against the esophagus.
FJ2438.clinicalCondition: Atrio-esophageal fistula — ablation heating of the posterior wall can perforate into esophagus.
FJ2438.clinicalScenario: Weeks after atrial fibrillation ablation, a patient develops fever and stroke-like episodes; CT shows air between left atrium and esophagus.

FJ2439.name: Wall of right atrium
FJ2439.details: Wall combining the smooth sinus venarum with the rough pectinate region, divided by the crista terminalis; the SA node lies subepicardially near the SVC junction.
FJ2439.clinicalCondition: Pacemaker lead perforation — the thin wall can be pierced, causing pericardial effusion.
FJ2439.clinicalScenario: A day after pacemaker insertion, an elderly woman becomes hypotensive with raised JVP; echo shows effusion from a lead tip through the atrial wall.

FJ2428.name: Wall of ventricle
FJ2428.details: Three-layered wall of endocardium, myocardium, and epicardium; spirally arranged ventricular muscle makes the left ventricular wall about three times thicker than the right.
FJ2428.clinicalCondition: Ventricular free-wall rupture — transmural infarction weakens the wall, causing tamponade.
FJ2428.clinicalScenario: Five days after a large myocardial infarction, a man collapses with pulseless electrical activity; echo shows pericardial blood from wall rupture.

FJ1734.name: Anterior commissure
FJ1734.details: Compact white-matter bundle crossing the midline just rostral to the columns of the fornix; interconnects olfactory structures and the middle/inferior temporal gyri of the two hemispheres.
FJ1734.clinicalCondition: Stereotactic landmark — the anterior commissure–posterior commissure line is the standard reference plane for deep brain stimulation targeting and imaging.
FJ1734.clinicalScenario: A neurosurgeon planning globus pallidus DBS for dystonia aligns the MRI fusion to the patient's anterior commissure before calculating target coordinates.

FJ1837.name: Anterior part of left superior temporal gyrus
FJ1837.details: Front portion of the superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere; participates in auditory processing and early analysis of speech sounds, just anterior to primary auditory cortex.
FJ1837.clinicalCondition: Temporal lobe epilepsy — anterior temporal foci produce déjà vu, rising epigastric sensation, and lip-smacking automatisms.
FJ1837.clinicalScenario: A 24-year-old repeatedly experiences sudden intense familiarity with strangers and a rising stomach sensation, then smacks her lips unresponsively for one minute.

FJ1838.name: Anterior part of right superior temporal gyrus
FJ1838.details: Non-dominant counterpart of the anterior superior temporal gyrus; processes pitch, melody, and the emotional tone (prosody) of speech rather than word meaning.
FJ1838.clinicalCondition: Receptive aprosodia — right temporal lesions flatten comprehension of emotional tone despite intact word understanding.
FJ1838.clinicalScenario: After a right temporal stroke, a man interprets his wife's joking remarks as angry insults because he can no longer read tone of voice.

FJ1761.name: Brachium of left inferior colliculus
FJ1761.details: Bundle of ascending auditory fibers running from the left inferior colliculus laterally to the left medial geniculate body of the thalamus.
FJ1761.clinicalCondition: Central auditory processing deficit — midbrain auditory pathway lesions impair sound localization despite normal pure-tone hearing.
FJ1761.clinicalScenario: A patient with a small midbrain infarct hears tones normally on audiometry but cannot tell from which side a voice is calling.

FJ1735.name: Brachium of left superior colliculus
FJ1735.details: Fiber bundle carrying retinal and optic tract input from the left side to the superior colliculus and pretectal nuclei, serving visual reflexes and pupillary responses.
FJ1735.clinicalCondition: Dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) syndrome — nearby compression abolishes the light reflex pathways that travel with these fibers.
FJ1735.clinicalScenario: A teenager with a pineal tumor cannot look upward, and his pupils react poorly to light but constrict normally on near effort.

FJ1809.name: Brachium of right inferior colliculus
FJ1809.details: Ascending auditory fibers linking the right inferior colliculus to the right medial geniculate body; one link in the central auditory pathway to the temporal cortex.
FJ1809.clinicalCondition: Tectal glioma — slowly growing midbrain roof tumors may first disturb central hearing and gaze before causing hydrocephalus.
FJ1809.clinicalScenario: A child with a tectal glioma is found to have subtle difficulty understanding speech in noisy classrooms despite normal ear examinations.

FJ1736.name: Brachium of right superior colliculus
FJ1736.details: Right-sided bundle conveying visual input from the optic tract toward the superior colliculus, coordinating reflexive eye and head turning toward visual stimuli.
FJ1736.clinicalCondition: Parinaud syndrome — loss of upward gaze and light–near dissociation from dorsal midbrain compression near this pathway.
FJ1736.clinicalScenario: An MRI for headaches in a young woman shows a pineal cyst compressing the tectal region; examination confirms impaired upgaze.

FJ1737.name: Central canal of spinal cord
FJ1737.details: Narrow CSF-filled channel running the length of the cord, lined by ependyma, continuous above with the fourth ventricle; largely obliterated in adults.
FJ1737.clinicalCondition: Syringomyelia — canal expansion forms a syrinx that destroys crossing pain and temperature fibers first.
FJ1737.clinicalScenario: A 30-year-old burns her hands repeatedly without pain; examination shows loss of pain and temperature over both shoulders in a cape distribution with preserved touch.

FJ1781.name: Cerebellum
FJ1781.details: Posterior fossa structure below the tentorium with two hemispheres and a midline vermis; fine-tunes movement, balance, and eye movements via deep nuclei and three peduncles.
FJ1781.clinicalCondition: Cerebellar stroke or hemorrhage — produces vertigo, vomiting, gait ataxia, and risks fatal tonsillar herniation.
FJ1781.clinicalScenario: An elderly hypertensive man develops sudden vertigo, vomiting, and inability to walk, then becomes drowsy as his cerebellar hematoma swells.

FJ1830.name: Cerebellum
FJ1830.details: Coordinates voluntary movement and posture; vermis governs trunk and gait, hemispheres govern ipsilateral limb coordination, flocculonodular lobe governs balance and eye movements.
FJ1830.clinicalCondition: Medulloblastoma — the commonest malignant childhood posterior fossa tumor arising in the cerebellar vermis.
FJ1830.clinicalScenario: A 6-year-old has morning headaches, vomiting, and a wobbling gait; MRI shows a midline cerebellar mass obstructing the fourth ventricle.

FJ1738.name: Cerebral aqueduct
FJ1738.details: Slender channel through the midbrain connecting the third and fourth ventricles; surrounded by periaqueductal gray; narrowest point of the CSF pathway.
FJ1738.clinicalCondition: Aqueductal stenosis — congenital narrowing causes obstructive (non-communicating) hydrocephalus in infants and children.
FJ1738.clinicalScenario: An infant's head circumference crosses percentiles rapidly; she has a bulging fontanelle and downward-deviated eyes, and MRI shows a blocked aqueduct.

FJ1741.name: Commissure of fornix of forebrain
FJ1741.details: Transverse fibers (hippocampal commissure, psalterium) crossing beneath the corpus callosum, interconnecting the crura of the fornix and the two hippocampal formations.
FJ1741.clinicalCondition: Limbic seizure spread — commissural fibers allow temporal lobe seizures to propagate to the opposite hippocampus.
FJ1741.clinicalScenario: Video-EEG in a patient with bilateral temporal epilepsy shows discharges crossing rapidly between hippocampi through commissural pathways.

FJ1311.name: Communicating branch of left nasociliary nerve with left ciliary ganglion
FJ1311.details: Sensory root of the ciliary ganglion: fibers from the eyeball (via short ciliary nerves) passing through the ganglion without synapsing to reach the nasociliary nerve.
FJ1311.clinicalCondition: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus — viral reactivation in this sensory pathway threatens corneal sensation and vision.
FJ1311.clinicalScenario: A shingles patient with vesicles on the left nasal tip is referred urgently because the same sensory root serves the globe itself.

FJ1362.name: Communicating branch of right nasociliary nerve with right ciliary ganglion
FJ1362.details: Right-sided sensory root of the ciliary ganglion, conveying sensory fibers from the cornea, iris, and ciliary body centrally via the nasociliary nerve without synapsing.
FJ1362.clinicalCondition: Corneal hypesthesia — interruption of this sensory limb weakens the blink reflex and risks neurotrophic keratitis.
FJ1362.clinicalScenario: After orbital surgery, a patient's right cornea no longer triggers blinking when touched, and he develops a painless corneal ulcer.

FJ1742.name: Corpus callosum
FJ1742.details: Largest cerebral commissure, about 200 million fibers in rostrum, genu, trunk, and splenium, linking corresponding cortical areas of the two hemispheres.
FJ1742.clinicalCondition: Callosotomy / split-brain — surgical section for intractable epilepsy disconnects hemispheres, causing intermanual conflict and left-hand anomia.
FJ1742.clinicalScenario: After callosotomy, a patient cannot name an object palpated by his left hand but can select it correctly from a group by sight.

FJ1743.name: Habenula
FJ1743.details: Small epithalamic nucleus at the posterior diencephalon near the pineal gland; relays limbic forebrain signals (via stria medullaris) to midbrain monoamine centers, modulating reward and aversion.
FJ1743.clinicalCondition: Habenular commissure calcification — a normal age-related finding used radiologically as a midline landmark for detecting pineal shift.
FJ1743.clinicalScenario: On a head CT after trauma, the radiologist notes the calcified habenular commissure sits midline, arguing against a mass displacing the pineal region.

FJ1760.name: Hypothalamus
FJ1760.details: Forms the floor and lower walls of the third ventricle; its nuclei regulate temperature, hunger, thirst, sleep, autonomic output, and pituitary hormone release.
FJ1760.clinicalCondition: Central diabetes insipidus — posterior hypothalamic/pituitary stalk damage abolishes ADH secretion, causing polyuria and polydipsia.
FJ1760.clinicalScenario: After pituitary surgery, a patient passes 6 liters of dilute urine daily and craves ice water; sodium rises until desmopressin is given.

FJ1808.name: Hypothalamus
FJ1808.details: Diencephalic control center connected to the pituitary by the infundibulum; supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei produce ADH and oxytocin; lateral and ventromedial nuclei govern feeding.
FJ1808.clinicalCondition: Craniopharyngioma — this suprasellar tumor compresses the hypothalamus, causing obesity, endocrine failure, and visual loss in children.
FJ1808.clinicalScenario: A 9-year-old stops growing, gains weight rapidly, and fails peripheral vision testing; imaging shows a calcified suprasellar cystic mass.

FJ1293.name: Inferior branch of left oculomotor nerve
FJ1293.details: Lower division of CN III entering the orbit through the superior orbital fissure; supplies medial rectus, inferior rectus, and inferior oblique, and carries parasympathetics to the ciliary ganglion.
FJ1293.clinicalCondition: Oculomotor palsy — divisional lesions in the cavernous sinus or orbit paralyze most eye movements and dilate the pupil.
FJ1293.clinicalScenario: A diabetic woman develops a painful left eye that sits "down and out" with a dilated pupil; imaging excludes an aneurysm.

FJ1344.name: Inferior branch of right oculomotor nerve
FJ1344.details: Right lower division of CN III; motor to medial rectus, inferior rectus, inferior oblique, with the parasympathetic branch to the ciliary ganglion arising from the inferior oblique branch.
FJ1344.clinicalCondition: Pupil-involving third nerve palsy — parasympathetic involvement suggests compression (aneurysm) rather than microvascular ischemia.
FJ1344.clinicalScenario: A man with sudden severe headache has a right ptosis, a "down-and-out" eye, and a fixed dilated pupil from a posterior communicating artery aneurysm.

FJ1763.name: Interpeduncular fossa
FJ1763.details: Midline space between the two cerebral peduncles at the midbrain base; contains the oculomotor nerve exit, mammillary bodies, posterior perforated substance, and the basilar artery bifurcation above.
FJ1763.clinicalCondition: Basilar tip aneurysm — aneurysms arising opposite this fossa can compress CN III and the midbrain.
FJ1763.clinicalScenario: A patient with a "top of the basilar" aneurysm presents with a unilateral third nerve palsy and fluctuating consciousness.

FJ1811.name: Interpeduncular fossa
FJ1811.details: Depression on the ventral midbrain between the crura; perforated by vessels supplying the medial midbrain and traversed by the emerging third cranial nerve.
FJ1811.clinicalCondition: Weber syndrome — a lesion of the adjacent peduncle here causes ipsilateral CN III palsy with contralateral hemiparesis.
FJ1811.clinicalScenario: A stroke patient cannot move her right eye or lift its lid, while her left arm and leg are weak with an upgoing plantar response.

FJ1764.name: Lamina terminalis
FJ1764.details: Thin sheet forming the anterior wall of the third ventricle, stretching from the optic chiasm to the rostrum of the corpus callosum; contains the organum vasculosum.
FJ1764.clinicalCondition: Surgical corridor — fenestrating the lamina terminalis is used to treat hydrocephalus and approach third-ventricular tumors.
FJ1764.clinicalScenario: During aneurysm surgery after subarachnoid hemorrhage, the neurosurgeon opens the lamina terminalis to drain CSF and reduce postoperative hydrocephalus.

FJ1812.name: Lamina terminalis
FJ1812.details: Anterior boundary of the third ventricle lying immediately behind the anterior communicating artery complex; a key landmark in anterior circulation aneurysm surgery.
FJ1812.clinicalCondition: Anterior communicating artery aneurysm rupture — bleeding here floods the basal cisterns and may damage nearby hypothalamic and septal structures, impairing memory.
FJ1812.clinicalScenario: A survivor of AComA rupture becomes apathetic and confabulates, reflecting injury to the basal forebrain adjacent to the lamina terminalis.

FJ1753.name: Left amygdala
FJ1753.details: Almond-shaped nuclear complex in the left medial temporal lobe, anterior to the hippocampus; central hub for fear, emotional learning, and assigning emotional significance to stimuli.
FJ1753.clinicalCondition: Temporal lobe epilepsy — amygdalar seizures produce sudden fear, déjà vu, and olfactory hallucinations as auras.
FJ1753.clinicalScenario: A woman describes episodes beginning with an unexplained burnt-rubber smell and intense dread, followed by staring and unresponsiveness.

FJ1732.name: Left angular gyrus
FJ1732.details: Cortical region of the dominant inferior parietal lobule curving around the posterior superior temporal sulcus; integrates reading, writing, calculation, and left–right orientation.
FJ1732.clinicalCondition: Gerstmann syndrome — dominant angular gyrus lesions cause agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, and left–right disorientation.
FJ1732.clinicalScenario: After an MCA stroke, a teacher can speak fluently but cannot write, do simple sums, or tell her left hand from her right.

FJ1283.name: Left anterior ethmoidal nerve
FJ1283.details: Branch of the nasociliary nerve leaving the orbit through the anterior ethmoidal foramen; supplies anterior ethmoid sinuses, anterior dura, nasal cavity, and (as external nasal nerve) nasal tip skin.
FJ1283.clinicalCondition: Anterior ethmoidal nerve block — targeted anesthesia for nasal and sinus surgery; its companion artery is a source of severe epistaxis.
FJ1283.clinicalScenario: An ENT surgeon infiltrates near the anterior ethmoidal foramen to anesthetize the nasal dorsum before reconstructing a fractured nose.

FJ1754.name: Left caudate nucleus
FJ1754.details: C-shaped basal ganglion arching in the wall of the lateral ventricle; head, body, and tail. Receives associative cortical input and participates in motor, cognitive, and reward circuits.
FJ1754.clinicalCondition: Huntington disease — selective caudate atrophy widens the frontal horns, producing chorea and psychiatric decline.
FJ1754.clinicalScenario: A 38-year-old with fidgety involuntary movements and depression has a father who died "shaking"; MRI shows squared-off, enlarged frontal horns from caudate loss.

FJ1288.name: Left ciliary ganglion
FJ1288.details: Small parasympathetic ganglion in the left orbit behind the globe; parasympathetic root from CN III synapses here; postganglionic fibers reach sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle via short ciliary nerves.
FJ1288.clinicalCondition: Adie tonic pupil — postganglionic damage denervates the sphincter, causing a dilated pupil with slow light–near response.
FJ1288.clinicalScenario: A young woman notices one pupil larger than the other; it constricts sluggishly to light but slowly and fully when she reads.

FJ1739.name: Left cingulate gyrus
FJ1739.details: Limbic cortical strip arching above the corpus callosum; anterior parts mediate emotion, motivation, and pain affect, posterior parts contribute to visuospatial and memory processing.
FJ1739.clinicalCondition: Akinetic mutism — bilateral anterior cingulate damage leaves patients awake but profoundly apathetic and unmoving.
FJ1739.clinicalScenario: After rupture of an anterior cerebral artery aneurysm, a patient lies with eyes open but neither speaks nor moves spontaneously.

FJ1756.name: Left fornix of forebrain
FJ1756.details: Arched white-matter tract carrying hippocampal output fibers from the left hippocampus, through crus, body, and column, mainly to the mammillary bodies; key Papez circuit link.
FJ1756.clinicalCondition: Forniceal injury amnesia — damage during colloid cyst surgery or by tumors causes severe anterograde memory loss.
FJ1756.clinicalScenario: A patient whose third-ventricular colloid cyst was removed cannot retain new information, forgetting conversations within minutes despite intact intelligence.

FJ1290.name: Left frontal nerve
FJ1290.details: Largest branch of the ophthalmic division (V1), running forward under the orbital roof outside the muscle cone; divides into supraorbital and supratrochlear sensory branches.
FJ1290.clinicalCondition: Supraorbital neuralgia — irritation of its terminal branches causes stabbing forehead pain with tenderness at the supraorbital notch.
FJ1290.clinicalScenario: A cyclist develops sharp, electric forehead pains after wearing a tight helmet strap; pressing the supraorbital notch reproduces the pain.

FJ1783.name: Left fusiform gyrus
FJ1783.details: Spindle-shaped gyrus on the inferior occipitotemporal surface; houses the fusiform face area, specialized for recognizing faces and expert visual categories.
FJ1783.clinicalCondition: Prosopagnosia — fusiform lesions (usually right or bilateral) abolish face recognition while general vision persists.
FJ1783.clinicalScenario: After a posterior cerebral artery stroke, a man recognizes his wife only by her voice, insisting familiar faces look like strangers.

FJ1757.name: Left globus pallidus
FJ1757.details: Medial segment of the lentiform nucleus; its internal part is the basal ganglia output nucleus, tonically inhibiting the thalamus via GABAergic fibers; external part regulates the indirect pathway.
FJ1757.clinicalCondition: Pallidal DBS target — stimulating or lesioning GPi relieves Parkinson disease dyskinesias and dystonia.
FJ1757.clinicalScenario: A young man with generalized dystonia twisting his neck and trunk improves markedly after bilateral globus pallidus interna stimulator implantation.

FJ1759.name: Left hippocampus
FJ1759.details: Seafloor-shaped gray matter in the medial temporal lobe forming the floor of the inferior horn; essential for consolidating declarative memories; outputs via the fornix.
FJ1759.clinicalCondition: Mesial temporal sclerosis — hippocampal scarring is the commonest substrate of drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy.
FJ1759.clinicalScenario: An MRI for refractory seizures shows a shrunken, bright left hippocampus; the patient has automatisms and postictal confusion weekly despite medication.

FJ1762.name: Left inferior colliculus
FJ1762.details: Rounded prominence of the midbrain tectum below the superior colliculus; obligatory relay where ascending auditory fibers converge before passing to the medial geniculate body.
FJ1762.clinicalCondition: Central hearing disorders — bilateral collicular damage impairs sound localization and speech-in-noise perception.
FJ1762.clinicalScenario: A soldier after blast-related midbrain injury passes standard hearing tests but cannot follow conversation in a crowded mess hall.

FJ1744.name: Left inferior frontal gyrus
FJ1744.details: Gyrus below the inferior frontal sulcus; its pars opercularis and triangularis in the dominant hemisphere form Broca's area (areas 44–45) for speech production.
FJ1744.clinicalCondition: Broca (expressive) aphasia — lesions cause effortful, telegraphic speech with relatively preserved comprehension.
FJ1744.clinicalScenario: After a left MCA stroke, a man says only "wife... hospital... tomorrow," clearly understanding questions but unable to form sentences.

FJ1746.name: Left inferior temporal gyrus
FJ1746.details: Lowest temporal convolution on the lateral surface; part of the ventral visual stream for object and word-form recognition, adjacent to the visual word form area.
FJ1746.clinicalCondition: Temporal lobe seizures and semantic deficits — dominant inferior temporal lesions disturb naming and category knowledge.
FJ1746.clinicalScenario: A patient with dominant inferior temporal glioma progressively loses the ability to name animals while retaining fluent grammar.

FJ1296.name: Left infratrochlear nerve
FJ1296.details: Small terminal branch of the nasociliary nerve passing below the trochlea; supplies skin and conjunctiva at the medial canthus, lacrimal sac, and medial eyelids.
FJ1296.clinicalCondition: Dacryocystitis pain localization — inflammation of the lacrimal sac is felt in this nerve's medial canthal territory.
FJ1296.clinicalScenario: A woman with a swollen, tender lump below the inner corner of her left eye has tearing and pus expressed from the punctum.

FJ1748.name: Left insula
FJ1748.details: Cortical island buried in the lateral sulcus beneath the opercula; anterior insula handles taste, interoception, and autonomic integration; supplied by M2 branches of the MCA.
FJ1748.clinicalCondition: Insular stroke — associated with dysphagia, cardiac arrhythmias, and loss of taste or visceral sensation.
FJ1748.clinicalScenario: Following an insular infarct, a patient develops new atrial fibrillation and reports that food has lost all flavor.

FJ1750.name: Left internal capsule
FJ1750.details: Compact white-matter sheet between caudate/thalamus medially and lentiform nucleus laterally; posterior limb carries corticospinal fibers, genu corticobulbar, anterior limb frontopontine fibers.
FJ1750.clinicalCondition: Lacunar stroke — a small capsular infarct causes pure motor hemiparesis because fibers are densely packed.
FJ1750.clinicalScenario: A hypertensive man wakes with equal weakness of the right face, arm, and leg, no sensory loss, and MRI shows a 9 mm posterior limb lacune.

FJ1300.name: Left lacrimal nerve
FJ1300.details: Smallest branch of the ophthalmic nerve (V1), running along the lateral orbital wall above lateral rectus to the lacrimal gland; carries sensation and conveys parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the gland.
FJ1300.clinicalCondition: Lacrimal gland lesions — tumors or dacryoadenitis here cause superotemporal orbital pain and swelling in its territory.
FJ1300.clinicalScenario: A patient with painful swelling at the upper outer left orbit and an S-shaped eyelid deformity is diagnosed with acute dacryoadenitis.

FJ1766.name: Left lateral geniculate body
FJ1766.details: Six-layered thalamic relay for vision on the underside of the pulvinar; receives retinal ganglion fibers in the optic tract and projects via optic radiations to calcarine cortex.
FJ1766.clinicalCondition: Geniculate lesion field defects — vascular injury produces characteristic contralateral homonymous sectoranopia.
FJ1766.clinicalScenario: A patient loses wedge-shaped portions of the right visual field in both eyes after a small anterior choroidal artery infarct.

FJ1318.name: Left long ciliary nerve
FJ1318.details: Two or three branches of the nasociliary nerve piercing the sclera near the optic nerve; carry sensory fibers from the cornea and uvea plus sympathetic fibers to dilator pupillae.
FJ1318.clinicalCondition: Herpetic keratitis — herpes simplex travels these sensory fibers to the cornea, causing dendritic ulcers and reduced corneal sensation.
FJ1318.clinicalScenario: A contact-lens wearer has a branching corneal ulcer that stains with fluorescein, and touching the cornea with a wisp barely triggers a blink.

FJ1816M.name: Left medial geniculate body
FJ1816M.details: Thalamic auditory relay forming a small elevation below the pulvinar; receives fibers via the brachium of the inferior colliculus and projects to the primary auditory cortex.
FJ1816M.clinicalCondition: Auditory agnosia contribution — bilateral medial geniculate or projection lesions prevent recognition of sounds despite intact hearing thresholds.
FJ1816M.clinicalScenario: After bilateral thalamic strokes, a patient hears a telephone ring but cannot identify what the sound is.

FJ1787.name: Left middle frontal gyrus
FJ1787.details: Broad gyrus between superior and inferior frontal sulci; dorsolateral prefrontal cortex subserving working memory and executive function; frontal eye field lies at its posterior end.
FJ1787.clinicalCondition: Frontal eye field lesions — destructive lesions deviate the eyes and head toward the side of the lesion.
FJ1787.clinicalScenario: During a seizure arising near the left frontal eye field, a patient's eyes and head are driven forcefully to the right.

FJ1789.name: Left middle temporal gyrus
FJ1789.details: Convolution between the superior and inferior temporal sulci; dominant posterior part participates in language comprehension and semantic processing; lies near motion-sensitive visual areas posteriorly.
FJ1789.clinicalCondition: Wernicke-type comprehension deficits — posterior dominant temporal lesions impair understanding and produce paraphasias.
FJ1789.clinicalScenario: A stroke patient speaks in fluent jargon, answers questions irrelevantly, and is unaware that nobody understands him.

FJ1310.name: Left nasociliary nerve
FJ1310.details: Branch of the ophthalmic nerve (V1) entering the orbit within the common tendinous ring; crosses above the optic nerve and gives ethmoidal, long ciliary, and infratrochlear branches.
FJ1310.clinicalCondition: Hutchinson sign — herpes zoster vesicles on the nasal tip predict ocular involvement because both share this nerve.
FJ1310.clinicalScenario: An elderly man with shingles vesicles on the left side and tip of his nose is sent for same-day slit-lamp examination.

FJ1791.name: Left occipital lobe
FJ1791.details: Posterior cerebral lobe containing primary visual cortex along the calcarine sulcus; receives geniculate input via optic radiations and processes the contralateral visual hemifield.
FJ1791.clinicalCondition: Posterior cerebral artery stroke — causes contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing.
FJ1791.clinicalScenario: A woman suddenly cannot see anything to her right; perimetry shows a right homonymous hemianopia, but central acuity is preserved.

FJ1312.name: Left ophthalmic nerve
FJ1312.details: Purely sensory first division of the trigeminal nerve, passing in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus and through the superior orbital fissure; divides into frontal, lacrimal, and nasociliary branches.
FJ1312.clinicalCondition: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus — V1 reactivation threatens the eye; the afferent limb of the corneal reflex also travels here.
FJ1312.clinicalScenario: A doctor testing reflexes finds that touching the left cornea blinks neither eye, while touching the right blinks both, localizing damage to left V1.

FJ1313.name: Left optic nerve
FJ1313.details: Cranial nerve II conveying about 1.2 million ganglion cell axons from the left retina to the chiasm; myelinated by oligodendrocytes and invested by meninges, so raised CSF pressure affects it.
FJ1313.clinicalCondition: Optic neuritis — demyelinating inflammation causes painful, subacute monocular visual loss in multiple sclerosis.
FJ1313.clinicalScenario: A 28-year-old woman loses vision in her left eye over three days, with pain on eye movement and a relative afferent pupillary defect.

FJ1772.name: Left optic nerve
FJ1772.details: Second cranial nerve, a tract of the CNS rather than a peripheral nerve; fibers from the temporal retina stay ipsilateral while nasal fibers later cross at the chiasm.
FJ1772.clinicalCondition: Papilledema — transmitted raised intracranial pressure swells the disc, threatening vision if prolonged.
FJ1772.clinicalScenario: Fundoscopy in a patient with morning headaches shows blurred, elevated optic discs bilaterally; lumbar puncture confirms high opening pressure.

FJ1773.name: Left optic tract
FJ1773.details: Posterior continuation of the visual pathway from the chiasm to the left lateral geniculate body, carrying temporal retinal fibers of the left eye and nasal fibers of the right eye.
FJ1773.clinicalCondition: Tract lesion hemianopia — damage causes an incongruous contralateral homonymous hemianopia with a relative afferent pupillary defect.
FJ1773.clinicalScenario: A tumor extending from the pituitary region produces a right-sided homonymous field loss that differs in shape between the two eyes.

FJ1785.name: Left parahippocampal gyrus
FJ1785.details: Gyrus on the medial temporal surface below the hippocampus, including entorhinal cortex; gateway for cortical input to the hippocampus and crucial for memory and scene recognition.
FJ1785.clinicalCondition: Earliest Alzheimer pathology — neurofibrillary tangles begin in the entorhinal/parahippocampal region years before dementia.
FJ1785.clinicalScenario: A 68-year-old repeatedly gets lost driving familiar routes and mislays items; volumetric MRI shows medial temporal atrophy.

FJ1797.name: Left postcentral gyrus
FJ1797.details: Primary somatosensory cortex (areas 3, 1, 2) immediately behind the central sulcus; receives contralateral touch, proprioception, pain, and temperature via the ventral posterior thalamus.
FJ1797.clinicalCondition: Cortical sensory loss — lesions impair stereognosis, graphesthesia, and two-point discrimination with crude touch relatively spared.
FJ1797.clinicalScenario: After a small parietal stroke, a man cannot identify a coin placed in his right hand with eyes closed, though pinprick feels normal.

FJ1315.name: Left posterior ethmoidal nerve
FJ1315.details: Small branch of the nasociliary nerve leaving via the posterior ethmoidal foramen; supplies posterior ethmoid air cells and the sphenoid sinus; it is sometimes absent.
FJ1315.clinicalCondition: Sinus surgery landmark — its foramen lies near the optic nerve, guiding safe ethmoid dissection in endoscopic surgery.
FJ1315.clinicalScenario: During FESS for chronic sinusitis, the surgeon identifies the posterior ethmoidal canal and stays below it to avoid the orbit and optic nerve.

FJ1800.name: Left precentral gyrus
FJ1800.details: Primary motor cortex (area 4) forming the anterior bank of the central sulcus; somatotopically organized (motor homunculus) and origin of most corticospinal fibers for the contralateral body.
FJ1800.clinicalCondition: Upper motor neuron weakness — MCA superior-division strokes here paralyze the contralateral face and arm predominantly.
FJ1800.clinicalScenario: A patient presents with right lower facial weakness and a clumsy, weak right hand; MRI confirms an infarct in the left precentral "hand knob."

FJ1776.name: Left putamen
FJ1776.details: Lateral part of the lentiform nucleus, separated from the globus pallidus by the lateral medullary lamina; main input nucleus of the motor loop, receiving dopaminergic nigral fibers.
FJ1776.clinicalCondition: Hypertensive putaminal hemorrhage — a classic deep bleed causing contralateral hemiparesis, gaze deviation, and depressed consciousness.
FJ1776.clinicalScenario: A 60-year-old with uncontrolled hypertension collapses with left-sided weakness; CT shows a 4 cm hemorrhage centered in the right putamen's counterpart region with mass effect.

FJ1777.name: Left stria medullaris of thalamus
FJ1777.details: Slender fiber bundle running along the dorsomedial thalamus at the roof of the third ventricle, carrying septal and anterior hypothalamic fibers to the habenular nuclei.
FJ1777.clinicalCondition: Third-ventricle surgical landmark — it marks the roof line used to orient approaches to pineal-region and ventricular tumors.
FJ1777.clinicalScenario: During endoscopic removal of a colloid cyst, the surgeon uses the stria medullaris and choroid plexus to confirm orientation inside the third ventricle.

FJ1778.name: Left stria terminalis
FJ1778.details: Slender limbic tract running in the sulcus between caudate nucleus and thalamus, carrying amygdalar output fibers to the septal area, hypothalamus, and bed nucleus of the stria terminalis.
FJ1778.clinicalCondition: Anxiety and stress circuitry — this amygdala output pathway mediating sustained threat responses is implicated in anxiety and PTSD.
FJ1778.clinicalScenario: Researchers studying a veteran with hypervigilance note altered connectivity in the stria terminalis–bed nucleus pathway on functional imaging.

FJ1779.name: Left superior colliculus
FJ1779.details: Layered tectal nucleus receiving retinal and cortical visual input; generates saccadic eye movements and reflexive head–eye orienting toward sudden visual or auditory stimuli.
FJ1779.clinicalCondition: Parinaud syndrome — tectal compression from pineal tumors abolishes upward gaze and convergence–retraction nystagmus appears.
FJ1779.clinicalScenario: A boy with precocious puberty from a germinoma cannot elevate his eyes, and his lids retract when he attempts upgaze.

FJ1833.name: Left superior frontal gyrus
FJ1833.details: Gyrus above the superior frontal sulcus; its medial posterior part contains the supplementary motor area, involved in planning and initiating internally generated movements and speech.
FJ1833.clinicalCondition: Supplementary motor area syndrome — resection causes transient contralateral akinesia and mutism that recovers over weeks.
FJ1833.clinicalScenario: After removal of a medial frontal tumor, a patient barely moves her right side or speaks for ten days, then recovers almost fully.

FJ1835.name: Left superior parietal lobule
FJ1835.details: Parietal region above the intraparietal sulcus integrating proprioceptive and visual information for skilled movement, stereognosis, and spatial manipulation.
FJ1835.clinicalCondition: Cortical sensory dysfunction — lesions cause astereognosis and impaired position sense in the contralateral limbs.
FJ1835.clinicalScenario: A woman with a superior parietal infarct cannot judge where her right arm is without looking and fumbles tying her shoelaces.

FJ1325.name: Left supra-orbital nerve
FJ1325.details: Lateral terminal branch of the frontal nerve exiting the supraorbital notch/foramen; supplies forehead, scalp to the vertex, frontal sinus, and upper eyelid.
FJ1325.clinicalCondition: Supraorbital nerve block — anesthetizing it at the notch numbs the forehead for laceration repair and minor surgery.
FJ1325.clinicalScenario: In the emergency department, a doctor blocks the left supraorbital nerve to painlessly suture a 5 cm forehead laceration in a child.

FJ1841.name: Left supramarginal gyrus
FJ1841.details: Dominant inferior parietal cortex capping the posterior end of the lateral sulcus; part of the perisylvian language network involved in phonological processing and repetition.
FJ1841.clinicalCondition: Conduction aphasia — lesions disconnect comprehension from production, causing fluent speech with poor repetition.
FJ1841.clinicalScenario: A patient speaks fluently and understands commands but, asked to repeat "no ifs, ands, or buts," produces garbled approximations and grows frustrated.

FJ1326.name: Left supratrochlear nerve
FJ1326.details: Medial terminal branch of the frontal nerve passing above the trochlea; supplies the medial forehead, glabella, medial upper eyelid, and root of the nose.
FJ1326.clinicalCondition: Regional forehead anesthesia — combined supratrochlear and supraorbital blocks anesthetize the entire forehead for flap surgery.
FJ1326.clinicalScenario: Before excising a basal cell carcinoma from the central forehead, the surgeon blocks both medial nerves to obtain a bloodless, pain-free field.

FJ1782.name: Left thalamus
FJ1782.details: Large diencephalic gray mass forming the lateral wall of the third ventricle; relays all sensory modalities except smell, plus motor and limbic information, to the cortex.
FJ1782.clinicalCondition: Thalamic pain syndrome (Dejerine–Roussy) — posterolateral infarcts cause contralateral sensory loss followed by burning, allodynic pain.
FJ1782.clinicalScenario: Months after a thalamic stroke, a man develops severe burning pain in his right arm whenever clothing brushes the skin.

FJ1330.name: Left trochlear nerve
FJ1330.details: Cranial nerve IV, the only nerve exiting the dorsal brainstem and crossing before emergence; has the longest intracranial course and supplies the superior oblique muscle alone.
FJ1330.clinicalCondition: Fourth nerve palsy — vertical diplopia worst on looking down and in, with compensatory head tilt away from the lesion; often traumatic.
FJ1330.clinicalScenario: After a head injury, a cyclist sees double descending stairs and tilts his head to the right to fuse images, indicating a left superior oblique weakness.

FJ1768.name: Mammillary body
FJ1768.details: Paired pea-like hypothalamic nuclei on the ventral diencephalon behind the infundibulum; receive hippocampal fibers via the fornix and project to the anterior thalamus in the memory circuit.
FJ1768.clinicalCondition: Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome — thiamine deficiency causes mammillary body hemorrhage and atrophy with profound amnesia and confabulation.
FJ1768.clinicalScenario: A malnourished alcoholic patient, treated for confusion and ataxia, is left inventing detailed false memories to fill his memory gaps.

FJ1815.name: Mammillary body
FJ1815.details: Round hypothalamic relay of the Papez circuit, connected anteriorly to the hippocampus by the fornix and posteriorly by the mammillothalamic tract to the anterior thalamic nuclei.
FJ1815.clinicalCondition: Korsakoff psychosis — selective mammillary damage explains why memory fails while other cognition is relatively preserved.
FJ1815.clinicalScenario: MRI in a patient with chronic alcoholism and dense anterograde amnesia shows shrunken, signal-abnormal mammillary bodies.

FJ1769.name: Medulla oblongata
FJ1769.details: Lowest brainstem segment from pons to the foramen magnum; contains cardiac, respiratory, and vasomotor centers and the nuclei of cranial nerves IX–XII plus decussating pyramids.
FJ1769.clinicalCondition: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome — PICA infarction causes vertigo, ipsilateral facial and contralateral body sensory loss, dysphagia, and Horner syndrome.
FJ1769.clinicalScenario: A man develops vertigo, hoarseness, and inability to swallow, with loss of pain sensation on his left face and right limbs.

FJ1831.name: Medulla oblongata
FJ1831.details: Houses the dorsal respiratory group, nucleus ambiguus, hypoglossal nucleus, and the area postrema on the floor of the fourth ventricle; vital autonomic reflexes are integrated here.
FJ1831.clinicalCondition: Medial medullary syndrome — anterior spinal artery occlusion paralyzes the ipsilateral tongue and contralateral limbs with proprioception loss.
FJ1831.clinicalScenario: A stroke patient protrudes his tongue toward the weak side and has right arm and leg weakness with loss of vibration sense.

FJ1770.name: Midbrain
FJ1770.details: Shortest brainstem segment around the cerebral aqueduct; contains the tectum (colliculi), tegmentum with red nucleus and substantia nigra, and the cerebral peduncles; nuclei of CN III and IV.
FJ1770.clinicalCondition: Weber syndrome — a ventral midbrain lesion causes ipsilateral third nerve palsy with contralateral hemiplegia.
FJ1770.clinicalScenario: A patient has a drooping right eyelid, a dilated pupil, and weakness of the left arm and leg after a midbrain infarct.

FJ1817.name: Midbrain
FJ1817.details: Rostral brainstem between diencephalon and pons; its substantia nigra pars compacta provides dopaminergic input to the striatum, and its periaqueductal gray modulates pain.
FJ1817.clinicalCondition: Parkinson disease — degeneration of nigral dopaminergic neurons here depletes striatal dopamine, causing bradykinesia, rigidity, and tremor.
FJ1817.clinicalScenario: A 65-year-old with a shuffling gait, pill-rolling tremor, and masked facies improves on levodopa, reflecting his midbrain neuronal loss.

FJ1771.name: Optic chiasm
FJ1771.details: Flattened X-shaped structure above the pituitary fossa where nasal retinal fibers cross; temporal fibers stay ipsilateral; related above to the lamina terminalis and below to the pituitary stalk.
FJ1771.clinicalCondition: Bitemporal hemianopia — compression from below by a pituitary adenoma destroys the crossing nasal fibers first.
FJ1771.clinicalScenario: A woman with galactorrhea reports repeatedly bumping into door frames; field testing shows loss of both temporal visual fields.

FJ1818.name: Optic chiasm
FJ1818.details: Partial decussation of the optic nerves anterior to the hypothalamus; fibers are retinotopically arranged, with inferior nasal fibers looping briefly into the opposite nerve (Wilbrand knee).
FJ1818.clinicalCondition: Chiasmal glioma and craniopharyngioma — intrinsic or suprasellar tumors produce progressive, often asymmetric bitemporal field defects in children.
FJ1818.clinicalScenario: A child with failing school vision and growth failure has a suprasellar calcified mass compressing the chiasm from above.

FJ1793.name: Orbital gyrus
FJ1793.details: Gyri on the inferior frontal lobe resting on the orbital roof (orbitofrontal cortex); involved in decision-making, social behavior, impulse control, and olfactory association.
FJ1793.clinicalCondition: Orbitofrontal damage — trauma or tumors cause disinhibition, poor judgment, and personality change with intact intellect.
FJ1793.clinicalScenario: After a frontal head injury, a formerly reserved accountant becomes tactless and impulsive, although his memory and IQ test normally.

FJ1794.name: Orbital gyrus
FJ1794.details: Ventral prefrontal cortex above the orbit, divided by the olfactory sulcus into medial and lateral parts; receives taste and smell input and evaluates reward value.
FJ1794.clinicalCondition: Foster Kennedy syndrome context — frontal basal tumors near this region can present with anosmia and behavioral change before visual signs.
FJ1794.clinicalScenario: A slowly growing olfactory groove meningioma is discovered after a woman loses her sense of smell and her family reports personality change.

FJ1774.name: Peduncle of midbrain
FJ1774.details: Massive ventral midbrain column (crus cerebri) carrying descending corticospinal, corticobulbar, and corticopontine fibers from cortex to cord, pons, and medulla.
FJ1774.clinicalCondition: Cerebral peduncle lesion — combined with CN III involvement it produces the crossed signs of Weber syndrome.
FJ1774.clinicalScenario: An MRI-confirmed peduncular infarct explains a patient's ipsilateral dilated pupil together with contralateral spastic hemiparesis.

FJ1821.name: Peduncle of midbrain
FJ1821.details: The crus cerebri is somatotopically arranged — medial fibers for head, lateral for lower limb — and forms the lateral boundary of the interpeduncular fossa.
FJ1821.clinicalCondition: Kernohan phenomenon — contralateral peduncle compression against the tentorial edge can cause hemiparesis falsely localizing to the lesion side.
FJ1821.clinicalScenario: In a patient with a large subdural hematoma, weakness appears on the same side as the clot, puzzling juniors until tentorial notching is explained.

FJ1775.name: Pons
FJ1775.details: Bulging middle brainstem segment between midbrain and medulla; basis pontis relays cortex to cerebellum, tegmentum houses nuclei of CN V–VIII and the reticular formation.
FJ1775.clinicalCondition: Pontine hemorrhage — classically causes coma, pinpoint pupils, quadriparesis, and hyperthermia in hypertensive patients.
FJ1775.clinicalScenario: A hypertensive man is found comatose with 1 mm reactive pupils and flaccid quadriplegia; CT shows a large central pontine bleed.

FJ1822.name: Pons
FJ1822.details: Contains the abducens and facial nuclei in its caudal tegmentum, the trigeminal nuclei more rostrally, and the pneumotaxic centers modulating medullary respiration.
FJ1822.clinicalCondition: Locked-in syndrome — ventral pontine infarction spares consciousness but abolishes all movement except vertical eye movements and blinking.
FJ1822.clinicalScenario: After basilar artery thrombosis, a fully aware patient communicates by blinking in code because only her eyelid and vertical gaze muscles work.

FJ1799.name: Posterior commissure
FJ1799.details: Fiber bundle crossing the midline just above the cerebral aqueduct opening, ventral to the pineal gland; interconnects pretectal and interstitial nuclei involved in vertical gaze and pupillary reflexes.
FJ1799.clinicalCondition: Pretectal syndrome — lesions here disrupt the light reflex interconnections, producing light–near dissociation.
FJ1799.clinicalScenario: A patient with a pineal region tumor has pupils that fail to react to light but constrict briskly when she focuses on her thumb.

FJ1839.name: Posterior part of left superior temporal gyrus
FJ1839.details: Rear portion of the dominant superior temporal gyrus, constituting Wernicke's area; decodes spoken language and is essential for comprehension and meaningful speech output.
FJ1839.clinicalCondition: Wernicke (receptive) aphasia — posterior temporal stroke causes fluent nonsense speech with severely impaired comprehension.
FJ1839.clinicalScenario: A man talks rapidly in well-formed but meaningless sentences and cannot follow the simple command to close his eyes.

FJ1840.name: Posterior part of right superior temporal gyrus
FJ1840.details: Non-dominant homologue of Wernicke's area; interprets prosody, melody, and speaker intent rather than literal word meaning, supporting emotional communication.
FJ1840.clinicalCondition: Receptive aprosodia — lesions render patients unable to detect sarcasm, emotion, or emphasis in speech.
FJ1840.clinicalScenario: A right temporal stroke patient takes every joke literally and complains that family members "sound angry all the time."

FJ1829.name: Right amygdala
FJ1829.details: Limbic nuclear complex in the right medial temporal lobe; evaluates threat and emotional salience, drives autonomic fear responses, and modulates memory for emotional events.
FJ1829.clinicalCondition: Klüver–Bucy features — bilateral amygdala damage (e.g., herpes encephalitis) causes placidity, hyperorality, and loss of fear.
FJ1829.clinicalScenario: Recovering from herpes encephalitis, a previously anxious patient becomes abnormally docile, mouths inedible objects, and shows no fear of snakes.

FJ1733.name: Right angular gyrus
FJ1733.details: Non-dominant inferior parietal cortex at the junction of temporal and parietal lobes; contributes to spatial attention, number processing, and theory-of-mind functions.
FJ1733.clinicalCondition: Hemispatial neglect contribution — right parietal lesions cause patients to ignore the left side of space.
FJ1733.clinicalScenario: A stroke patient eats only from the right half of his plate and shaves only the right side of his face.

FJ1333.name: Right anterior ethmoidal nerve
FJ1333.details: Nasociliary branch exiting the right anterior ethmoidal foramen; supplies the anterior ethmoid sinuses, anterior cranial fossa dura, upper nasal cavity, and nasal tip via its external nasal continuation.
FJ1333.clinicalCondition: Sluder-type nasal neuralgia differential — anterior ethmoidal irritation can refer pain to the forehead and orbit.
FJ1333.clinicalScenario: A patient with chronic anterior ethmoid sinusitis describes deep aching pain behind the right eye that eases after decongestion.

FJ1802.name: Right caudate nucleus
FJ1802.details: C-shaped striatal nucleus hugging the lateral ventricle on the right; partners with the putamen in motor and associative circuits and in procedural learning.
FJ1802.clinicalCondition: Caudate infarcts — small strokes cause cognitive slowing, abulia, and subtle movement disorders rather than dense paralysis.
FJ1802.clinicalScenario: A patient with a right caudate head infarct becomes apathetic and disorganized, neglecting his business despite normal limb strength.

FJ1339.name: Right ciliary ganglion
FJ1339.details: Parasympathetic relay in the right orbit lateral to the optic nerve; preganglionic fibers from the Edinger–Westphal nucleus (via CN III) synapse, supplying pupil constriction and accommodation.
FJ1339.clinicalCondition: Tonic pupil and surgical risk — the ganglion may be injured in orbital surgery, producing a permanently dilated, poorly reactive pupil.
FJ1339.clinicalScenario: After repair of a right orbital floor fracture, a patient complains that one pupil stays large and reading blurs at near.

FJ1740.name: Right cingulate gyrus
FJ1740.details: Limbic cortex above the corpus callosum on the right; its anterior division integrates emotion with autonomic responses and attention; part of the Papez circuit.
FJ1740.clinicalCondition: Cingulate seizures — produce complex automatisms, emotional outbursts, and autonomic changes mimicking psychiatric episodes.
FJ1740.clinicalScenario: A teenager has stereotyped spells of sudden fear, shouting, and fumbling hand movements that were misdiagnosed for years as behavioral problems.

FJ1804.name: Right fornix of forebrain
FJ1804.details: Right limb of the arched hippocampal output tract; fibers sweep from the hippocampus beneath the corpus callosum and descend in the column toward the mammillary bodies.
FJ1804.clinicalCondition: Memory circuit interruption — forniceal damage disconnects hippocampus from diencephalon, replicating diencephalic amnesia.
FJ1804.clinicalScenario: A cavernous malformation bleeding near the right fornix leaves a student unable to remember lessons despite normal attention and language.

FJ1341.name: Right frontal nerve
FJ1341.details: Branch of the right ophthalmic nerve coursing forward beneath the orbital roof; purely sensory, dividing into supraorbital and supratrochlear branches for forehead sensation.
FJ1341.clinicalCondition: Post-traumatic forehead anesthesia — orbital roof fractures can injure this nerve, numbing the forehead and scalp.
FJ1341.clinicalScenario: After a blowout injury repair, a patient reports complete numbness of the right forehead up to the hairline.

FJ1784.name: Right fusiform gyrus
FJ1784.details: Inferotemporal gyrus on the right housing the fusiform face area; the right side is dominant for holistic face recognition and processing of facial expression.
FJ1784.clinicalCondition: Acquired prosopagnosia — right fusiform stroke is the classic cause of inability to recognize familiar faces.
FJ1784.clinicalScenario: A portrait photographer after a right occipitotemporal infarct cannot recognize his own children in photographs, though he identifies objects normally.

FJ1805.name: Right globus pallidus
FJ1805.details: Medial lentiform nucleus on the right; external segment modulates the indirect pathway, internal segment provides inhibitory basal ganglia output to the thalamus and brainstem.
FJ1805.clinicalCondition: Carbon monoxide poisoning — selectively necroses both globus pallidi, causing parkinsonism and cognitive impairment.
FJ1805.clinicalScenario: Weeks after faulty-heater exposure, a survivor develops a shuffling gait and apathy; MRI shows symmetric pallidal necrosis.

FJ1807.name: Right hippocampus
FJ1807.details: Medial temporal memory structure on the right, specialized relatively more for visuospatial and navigational memory; forms new episodic memories with its cortical partners.
FJ1807.clinicalCondition: Right hippocampal sclerosis — causes temporal lobe epilepsy with visuospatial memory deficits rather than verbal ones.
FJ1807.clinicalScenario: A taxi driver with right mesial temporal sclerosis begins getting lost on familiar routes and fails map-based memory testing.

FJ1810.name: Right inferior colliculus
FJ1810.details: Tectal auditory relay on the right, integrating binaural cues for sound localization before relaying to the medial geniculate body via its brachium.
FJ1810.clinicalCondition: Midbrain auditory dysfunction — lesions impair localization of sounds arising from the contralateral side.
FJ1810.clinicalScenario: A patient with a right tectal plate cavernoma consistently mislocalizes voices to his left when his eyes are closed.

FJ1745.name: Right inferior frontal gyrus
FJ1745.details: Non-dominant inferior frontal cortex, homologue of Broca's area; governs expressive prosody (emotional melody of speech) and response inhibition.
FJ1745.clinicalCondition: Expressive aprosodia — right inferior frontal lesions produce flat, monotone speech despite normal language content.
FJ1745.clinicalScenario: After a right frontal stroke, a salesman speaks in a dull monotone and colleagues wrongly assume he is depressed.

FJ1747.name: Right inferior temporal gyrus
FJ1747.details: Lowest lateral temporal convolution on the right; ventral-stream area for visual object recognition, including color and form integration with the fusiform cortex.
FJ1747.clinicalCondition: Visual object agnosia — bilateral or right inferior temporal lesions prevent recognition of objects by sight alone.
FJ1747.clinicalScenario: A patient can describe a key's shape and copy its drawing perfectly yet cannot say what the object is until he holds it.

FJ1347.name: Right infratrochlear nerve
FJ1347.details: Terminal nasociliary twig emerging below the pulley of the superior oblique; provides sensation to the medial canthus, caruncle, lacrimal sac, and medial conjunctiva of the right eye.
FJ1347.clinicalCondition: Medial canthal anesthesia landmark — its block supplements eyelid anesthesia for chalazion and canalicular surgery.
FJ1347.clinicalScenario: An oculoplastic surgeon anesthetizes the medial canthal region before probing a blocked right nasolacrimal duct in an infant.

FJ1749.name: Right insula
FJ1749.details: Buried cortex of the right lateral sulcus; dominant for sympathetic autonomic representation, interoceptive awareness, and risk/emotion processing; supplied by insular MCA branches.
FJ1749.clinicalCondition: Insular epilepsy and autonomic storms — seizures here trigger visceral sensations, laryngeal constriction, and heart-rate swings.
FJ1749.clinicalScenario: A patient describes seizures beginning with a choking throat sensation and racing heart, later localized to the right insula on stereo-EEG.

FJ1751.name: Right internal capsule
FJ1751.details: White-matter V-shaped sheet on the right whose posterior limb funnels corticospinal fibers for the left body; supplied by lenticulostriate and anterior choroidal arteries.
FJ1751.clinicalCondition: Anterior choroidal artery syndrome — posterior capsular infarction causes hemiparesis, hemisensory loss, and homonymous hemianopia.
FJ1751.clinicalScenario: A diabetic patient develops left-sided weakness, numbness, and a left visual field cut from a single deep infarct.

FJ1351.name: Right lacrimal nerve
FJ1351.details: Ophthalmic branch running along the upper border of lateral rectus to the right lacrimal gland; conveys sensation and delivers postganglionic parasympathetic fibers for tear secretion.
FJ1351.clinicalCondition: Dry eye from secretomotor interruption — damage reduces reflex tearing on the affected side.
FJ1351.clinicalScenario: A patient after lateral orbitotomy has a dry, gritty right eye with markedly reduced Schirmer test wetting.

FJ1813.name: Right lateral geniculate body
FJ1813.details: Six-layered visual thalamic nucleus on the right; magnocellular layers process motion, parvocellular layers detail and color; projects to the right calcarine cortex.
FJ1813.clinicalCondition: Lateral geniculate lesions — rare strokes produce sector-shaped contralateral homonymous field defects.
FJ1813.clinicalScenario: Perimetry in a patient with a small right thalamic infarct shows matching wedge defects in the left fields of both eyes.

FJ1369.name: Right long ciliary nerve
FJ1369.details: Nasociliary branches piercing the right sclera around the optic nerve; carry corneal sensation and sympathetic fibers (from the internal carotid plexus) to the dilator pupillae.
FJ1369.clinicalCondition: Neurotrophic keratitis — loss of this sensory supply after herpetic or surgical injury leads to painless corneal breakdown.
FJ1369.clinicalScenario: An elderly diabetic develops a non-healing right corneal epithelial defect with almost no pain, alerting doctors to sensory denervation.

FJ1816.name: Right medial geniculate body
FJ1816.details: Auditory thalamic relay on the right receiving the brachium of the inferior colliculus; sends acoustic radiations through the sublenticular internal capsule to Heschl's gyri.
FJ1816.clinicalCondition: Thalamic auditory relay lesions — contribute to impaired speech-sound discrimination when bilateral.
FJ1816.clinicalScenario: Bilateral thalamic infarcts leave a patient able to hear a doorbell yet unable to distinguish spoken words from noise.

FJ1788.name: Right middle frontal gyrus
FJ1788.details: Dorsolateral prefrontal region on the right between the frontal sulci; sustains attention, working memory, and monitoring; its posterior part adjoins the frontal eye field.
FJ1788.clinicalCondition: Dysexecutive syndrome — lesions cause disorganization, poor planning, and impaired multitasking with preserved basic intellect.
FJ1788.clinicalScenario: A manager with a right frontal meningioma begins missing deadlines and making uncharacteristic errors juggling routine tasks.

FJ1790.name: Right middle temporal gyrus
FJ1790.details: Lateral temporal convolution on the right involved in semantic processing, social perception, and biological-motion recognition near the superior temporal sulcus.
FJ1790.clinicalCondition: Social perception deficits — right temporoparietal lesions impair reading of facial expressions and intentions.
FJ1790.clinicalScenario: A patient after right temporal surgery repeatedly misreads neutral facial expressions as hostile during rehabilitation testing.

FJ1361.name: Right nasociliary nerve
FJ1361.details: Ophthalmic division branch entering the right orbit through the superior orbital fissure within the tendinous ring; gives the sensory root to the ciliary ganglion and ethmoidal and infratrochlear branches.
FJ1361.clinicalCondition: Orbital apex syndrome — compression here combines V1 sensory loss with multiple ocular motor palsies.
FJ1361.clinicalScenario: A patient with a right orbital apex tumor has forehead numbness, a dull cornea, ptosis, and a frozen globe.

FJ1792.name: Right occipital lobe
FJ1792.details: Posterior lobe housing the right visual cortex along the calcarine sulcus; upper bank receives the inferior visual field, lower bank the superior field, from the left hemifield of both eyes.
FJ1792.clinicalCondition: Cortical blindness and Anton syndrome — bilateral occipital damage blinds patients who may deny their blindness.
FJ1792.clinicalScenario: After bilateral PCA strokes, a man insists he can see while walking into furniture and confabulating descriptions of the room.

FJ1363.name: Right ophthalmic nerve
FJ1363.details: Sensory first trigeminal division traversing the cavernous sinus wall to the superior orbital fissure; supplies the globe, conjunctiva, forehead, scalp, and nasal cavity via three branches.
FJ1363.clinicalCondition: Cavernous sinus thrombosis — V1 involvement gives forehead sensory loss alongside chemosis and ocular motor palsies.
FJ1363.clinicalScenario: A septic patient develops a swollen, protruding right eye, forehead numbness, and paralyzed eye movements, signaling cavernous sinus spread.

FJ1364.name: Right optic nerve
FJ1364.details: Cranial nerve II carrying axons from the right retina; its intraorbital, canalicular, and intracranial segments are vulnerable respectively to orbital, bony, and suprasellar pathology.
FJ1364.clinicalCondition: Optic nerve glioma — a childhood tumor, often with neurofibromatosis type 1, causing painless proptosis and visual loss.
FJ1364.clinicalScenario: A 5-year-old with café-au-lait spots develops gradual painless protrusion of the right eye and declining vision.

FJ1819.name: Right optic nerve
FJ1819.details: CNS tract ensheathed by meninges and CSF; ganglion cell axons from the nasal retina will cross at the chiasm, temporal fibers remain uncrossed.
FJ1819.clinicalCondition: Traumatic optic neuropathy — fractures or contusion at the optic canal cause severe vision loss after head injury.
FJ1819.clinicalScenario: After a road-traffic accident, a patient's right eye perceives only hand movements despite a normal-looking globe and clear media.

FJ1820.name: Right optic tract
FJ1820.details: Band of fibers sweeping from the chiasm around the cerebral peduncle to the right lateral geniculate body, encoding the left visual hemifield.
FJ1820.clinicalCondition: Optic tract syndrome — lesion causes left homonymous hemianopia, a left relative afferent defect, and bow-tie optic atrophy.
FJ1820.clinicalScenario: A craniopharyngioma patient loses the left field in both eyes and shows characteristic band atrophy of the right optic disc.

FJ1786.name: Right parahippocampal gyrus
FJ1786.details: Medial temporal gyrus on the right, including entorhinal and parahippocampal cortex specialized for spatial scenes and contextual memory; feeds information into the hippocampus.
FJ1786.clinicalCondition: Topographical disorientation — right parahippocampal lesions destroy recognition of landmarks and familiar environments.
FJ1786.clinicalScenario: A retired postman with a right medial temporal infarct can no longer navigate his own neighborhood of forty years.

FJ1798.name: Right postcentral gyrus
FJ1798.details: Primary somatosensory cortex on the right receiving left-body sensation; its hand and face areas are disproportionately large, reflecting receptor density.
FJ1798.clinicalCondition: Sensory seizures — focal discharges produce marching tingling that spreads across the contralateral body (Jacksonian sensory march).
FJ1798.clinicalScenario: A woman describes episodes where tingling starts in her left thumb, climbs the arm, then involves the left cheek over two minutes.

FJ1366.name: Right posterior ethmoidal nerve
FJ1366.details: Inconstant nasociliary branch through the right posterior ethmoidal foramen, supplying posterior ethmoid cells and sphenoid sinus mucosa; closely related to the optic canal region.
FJ1366.clinicalCondition: Sphenoid sinusitis referral — deep vertex or occipital headache may be the only symptom of posterior sinus disease near this nerve.
FJ1366.clinicalScenario: A patient with weeks of dull vertex headache and normal neurology has CT evidence of isolated right sphenoid sinus opacification.

FJ1801.name: Right precentral gyrus
FJ1801.details: Right primary motor cortex driving the left body; large pyramidal (Betz) cells give rise to corticospinal axons; leg area lies medially in the paracentral lobule.
FJ1801.clinicalCondition: Focal motor seizures — precentral discharges cause clonic jerking of the contralateral face or limbs.
FJ1801.clinicalScenario: A man has stereotyped episodes of left facial twitching spreading to the left hand; MRI reveals a small right precentral cavernoma.

FJ1823.name: Right putamen
FJ1823.details: Lateral lentiform component on the right; input station of the basal ganglia motor circuit, topographically organized and richly supplied by lenticulostriate vessels.
FJ1823.clinicalCondition: Lenticulostriate lacunes and hemorrhage — small deep infarcts here cause lacunar hemiparesis affecting the left side.
FJ1823.clinicalScenario: A hypertensive smoker develops pure motor weakness of the left arm and leg; MRI shows a small right putaminal lacunar infarct.

FJ1824.name: Right stria medullaris of thalamus
FJ1824.details: Fiber ridge along the dorsomedial right thalamus at the third-ventricle roof, conveying limbic forebrain afferents to the habenular nucleus of the epithalamus.
FJ1824.clinicalCondition: Epithalamic pathway relevance — this limbic–midbrain link modulating monoamine release is under study in depression and chronic pain.
FJ1824.clinicalScenario: A functional imaging study of treatment-resistant depression highlights altered habenular connectivity fed by this stria medullaris pathway.

FJ1826.name: Right superior colliculus
FJ1826.details: Right tectal visual-reflex center coordinating saccades and orienting movements toward the left visual field; receives retinal, cortical, and auditory spatial input.
FJ1826.clinicalCondition: Saccadic dysfunction — collicular region lesions slow or abolish reflexive gaze shifts toward contralateral stimuli.
FJ1826.clinicalScenario: A patient with a pineal tumor is slow to look toward objects appearing in his left field, keeping his head turned instead.

FJ1834.name: Right superior frontal gyrus
FJ1834.details: Superior frontal convolution on the right; supports working memory and self-monitoring, with supplementary and presupplementary motor areas on its medial surface.
FJ1834.clinicalCondition: Medial frontal (anterior cerebral artery) stroke — causes contralateral leg weakness and abulia from SMA and cingulate involvement.
FJ1834.clinicalScenario: After an ACA infarct, a woman has a weak, stiff left leg and sits for hours without initiating conversation.

FJ1836.name: Right superior parietal lobule
FJ1836.details: Parietal area above the intraparietal sulcus on the right, integrating proprioception and vision for reaching, grasping, and spatial attention to both sides.
FJ1836.clinicalCondition: Optic ataxia — superior parietal damage within Balint syndrome makes visually guided reaching inaccurate.
FJ1836.clinicalScenario: A patient with bilateral parieto-occipital infarcts repeatedly misses a cup placed directly in front of her, groping past it.

FJ1376.name: Right supra-orbital nerve
FJ1376.details: Lateral terminal branch of the right frontal nerve emerging through the supraorbital notch; sensory to the forehead, anterior scalp, frontal sinus, and upper lid.
FJ1376.clinicalCondition: Migraine trigger-site relevance — supraorbital nerve irritation is implicated in frontal migraine pain and treated by blocks or decompression.
FJ1376.clinicalScenario: A chronic migraineur obtains weeks of relief after a diagnostic supraorbital block confirms the right nerve as her pain generator.

FJ1842.name: Right supramarginal gyrus
FJ1842.details: Non-dominant inferior parietal cortex arching over the posterior lateral sulcus; contributes to empathy, phonological working memory, and overcoming emotional egocentricity.
FJ1842.clinicalCondition: Neglect spectrum — combined right inferior parietal lesions underlie severe left-sided inattention and anosognosia.
FJ1842.clinicalScenario: A patient with a right MCA stroke denies her left arm is paralyzed and claims it belongs to her husband.

FJ1377.name: Right supratrochlear nerve
FJ1377.details: Medial frontal nerve branch passing above the trochlea of the right orbit; supplies the glabella, medial forehead, and nasal root skin and conjunctiva.
FJ1377.clinicalCondition: Glabellar anesthesia for surgery — this nerve is blocked for excisions and flap repairs of the medial forehead and nasal bridge.
FJ1377.clinicalScenario: Before repairing a dog bite across the nasal bridge, the surgeon injects above the right trochlea to numb the wound edges.

FJ1827.name: Right thalamus
FJ1827.details: Right half of the diencephalic relay station; ventral posterior nuclei relay left-body sensation, geniculate bodies relay vision and hearing, and anterior nuclei serve memory circuits.
FJ1827.clinicalCondition: Pure sensory stroke — a small ventral posterior thalamic lacune causes numbness of the entire left side.
FJ1827.clinicalScenario: A hypertensive patient reports that her whole left side, including face and trunk, has "gone to sleep" without any weakness.

FJ1381.name: Right trochlear nerve
FJ1381.details: Cranial nerve IV supplying the right superior oblique; exits dorsally, decussates, and winds around the midbrain — its long course makes it the nerve most vulnerable to closed head trauma.
FJ1381.clinicalCondition: Traumatic fourth nerve palsy — vertical, torsional diplopia with the eye higher on the affected side and head tilt to the opposite shoulder.
FJ1381.clinicalScenario: A boxer sees double reading in bed and tilts his head left; examination confirms a weak right superior oblique.

FJ1832.name: Septum of telencephalon
